News.title: Royal Navy drones secretly sent data to China through ‘heartbeat communications’ after years of Beijing spying fears
News.content:
SPY drones used by British special forces have been secretly sending data to China amid concerns over espionage from Beijing.

Cameras in the drones used by elite Navy forces contain components which were made in China and have reportedly been transmitting information back to Beijing.



The K3 Scout surveillance drones have been part of the Royal Marines’ £12million fleet since March.

After finding the breach, the Ministry of Defence has reportedly been forced to remove all internet connectivity from the cameras, the Telegraph reports.



The drones were from major British defence contractor Kraken Technology Group which sourced the cameras from a third party.

The third party is said to have given assurances about the equipment’s security.



After the breach was discovered, an investigation revealed that cameras were sending “heartbeat communications” to an IP address in China.

This data confirms the devices were online and functioning as they should be.

The MoD said no systems were compromised or transmitted externally.

A source said the drones had been part of the UK’s future defence package offered to help secure movement in the Strait of Hormuz.



They added that preparations had already been conducted on the drones and the find was a “major failure to check origins of components and we have lost confidence in the platform.”

A spokesperson for the MoD said: “The first duty of government is national security, and we take the security of our equipment, networks and data extremely seriously.

“A routine cyber vulnerability assessment identified an issue affecting a Kraken Unmanned Surface Vessel sub-system used by the Royal Navy.

“A thorough investigation found no evidence of MOD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.

“Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment.”



This comes as the Labour Party tries to maintain relations with the Chinese Communist Party despite the looming threat the country poses.

Last month, a huge Chinese embassy was given the green light after a High Court challenge against the planning permission was dismissed.

The vast complex at Royal Mint Court, near the Tower of London, was approved despite concerns it could lead to terror attacks and the suppression of protests.

The Sun previously revealed that staff at British defence firms were told not to take phones to Wes Streeting’s first speech as Shadow Defence Secretary over fears of Chinese spying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Streeting spoke at an arms fair packed with Chinese firms – including an electronic warfare specialist that lists signals “cracking” as a flagship service.



Workers at Britain’s List X defence firms – which hold secret government contracts – were advised to leave phones, tablets and other devices outside the exhibition hall where Streeting delivered his keynote address.

News.title: Married doctor who Lucy Letby was ‘infatuated’ with could be identified if Lucy Letby has retrial, says Tory MP
News.content:
LUCY Letby campaigner David Davis MP says the anonymity order given to a doctor she was infatuated with is likely to be reviewed in the wake of his death.

The MP said it could take place at any future retrial.



The Sun on Sunday revealed how the medic, who was granted anonymity and referred to in court as Doctor A, died last month.

Mr Davies said: “I don’t think this changes much, I assume that the anonymity orders will be reviewed in the event of a retrial.”



At trial, prosecutors alleged Lucy would create “crisis situations” to gain his sympathy.

Her supporters later turned on him because he said in court that she might have “manipulated” him.



The married registrar – known as Doctor A – previously gave evidence against Letby during her trial for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others.

It is understood the medic – who was in his 50s – had been ill before passing away last month.

Prosecutors alleged Letby was infatuated with the physician and would create “crisis situations” by attacking infants to ensure he would be bleeped to attend.

Although the pair exchanged 1,300 messages and enjoyed day trips to London, Letby denied a romance and insisted they were simply “trusted friends”.



The 2024 Thirlwall Inquiry later found the doctor had been “misled” and “maybe manipulated” into giving Letby information about the babies she had attacked.

Letby continues to claim her innocence while serving a whole-life sentence at Bronzefield Prison.

News.title: Cops hunt firebomb maniacs after week-long arson rampage through Scots towns
News.content:
DETECTIVES have launched a manhunt after four cars were firebombed less than two miles apart.

Thugs torched the motors in two Lanarkshire towns in a nine-day wrecking spree.



In the first attack, a vehicle on Hamilton’s Sneddon Terrace was set on fire at around 2.20am on July 24.

Two other motors were targeted in nearby Reid Street at around 3.40am six days later.



The maniacs left a Mini and a black estate car burnt out.

Shocking footage showed both vehicles ablaze as fire crews arrived to put out the flames.



Pictures later revealed the charred wrecks of the cars with the estate’s bonnet lying mangled.

Meanwhile, officers are hunting two masked suspects over another car attack in Ivy Place, Blantyre, at 11.40pm on August 2.

Police said the suspects were dressed head-to-toe in black. They were spotted pushing a bicycle around the time of the blaze.

Last night, Police Scotland confirmed inquiries into all three attacks remained ongoing.



It is understood the force is treating the Hamilton attacks as linked while keeping an open mind on the incident in Blantyre.

No one was injured in any of the blazes.

Detective Constable Stuart Adams said: “I am appealing to anyone who was in the area to think if they noticed anything suspicious or unusual.

“I would also appeal to any motorists with dash-cam to check their footage for any images which could assist our investigation.

“Any information could prove relevant.”

News.title: Brit teen, 16, dead and two siblings badly injured after ‘terrible accident’ on family holiday as tributes pour in
News.content:
'FOREVER LOVED' Brit teen, 16, dead and two siblings badly injured after ‘terrible accident’ on family holiday as tributes pour in

A BRITISH teenager has died in a “terrible accident” on a family holiday which also left her two siblings badly injured.

Abbie Lainton, 16, from Swindon, died while on vacation in the Dominican Republic with her heartbroken friends and school paying tribute.



Family friend Becky Jamieson described Abbie as a “beautiful” young girl who was loved by everyone who knew her.

She said in an emotional statement that Abbie lost her life on July 30, with her sister Carley and brother Bradley also being left badly injured.



It remains unclear how the siblings got into danger.

Becky continued: “Abbie had her whole life ahead of her. She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results.

“She was so loved by her family, friends and everyone who knew her.

“For Abbie, forever 16, forever loved and never forgotten.”

A GoFundMe page, which was set up to help Abbie’s family, has already received more than £5,000 in donations.

Abbie’s former school Tanwood School for Performing Arts, also honoured her in a statement.



A spokesperson said: “Abbie joined Tanwood as a dinky dot and was part of an exceptional group of dancers who formed strong friendships which spilled over to the audience when they performed together.

“She always performed with a huge smile, and those beautiful feet.

“We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time.

“You will always be in our hearts.”

Abbie joined Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club at a later date where she excelled and took part in competitions around the world.



The club invited people to come together and remember Abbie as well as celebrate her life and share memories.

A spokesperson for the club said: “There are simply no words that feel enough.

“Abbie was a much-loved member of our Swindon Lightning family.

“Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years.

“She brought so much light to our gym, and her loss has left us all heartbroken.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our thoughts, love and deepest condolences are with Abbie’s family and loved ones during this unimaginable time.”

News.title: Islamist terrorists who plotted to blow up 10 planes must not be eligible for early release from prison
News.content:
Too dangerous

IT could have been the worst mass murder in criminal history.

A gang of Islamist terrorists plotted to blow ten passenger jets out of the sky with liquid explosives smuggled through Heathrow disguised in hand luggage as drinks, shampoo and toothpaste.



Had the plot succeeded, up to 10,000 innocent people could have been killed — three times the death toll of the 9/11 attacks on New York’s Twin Towers.

Britain was spared that unimaginable slaughter thanks to the bravery, skill and ingenuity of MI5 and the police, who smashed the conspiracy just days before the planned attacks.



But three of the men convicted of conspiracy to murder — Waheed Zaman, Ibrahim Savant and Arafat Waheed Khan — could soon be eligible for parole after serving 20 years of their life terms.

These were not misguided young men caught up in some minor offence.



They were convicted of planning mass murder on an appalling scale.

All three recorded “martyrdom” videos, intended to be released by al-Qaeda after the attacks.

The British public has had enough of violent criminals being released early while victims and their families are left to live with the consequences.

The Parole Board must not allow pressure to ease prison overcrowding to cloud their cold-headed judgment when considering these cases.



Some prisoners are just too dangerous to release.

These terrorists should be among them.

Off to prison

BRITAIN’S overcrowded prisons are at breaking point — yet 10,000 foreign lags are taking up scarce places.

Most of them would have been booted out long ago if their home countries had agreed to take them back.

Instead, the Government has been forced to free thousands of offenders early to stop the system collapsing.



So Nigel Farage’s idea to ship foreign convicts to serve their sentences 5,500 miles away in the grim jails of El Salvador is worth exploring.

It would end the sickening spectacle of violent crooks being freed halfway through their sentence.

And make foreign visitors think twice about bringing criminal activities to Britain.

Back to work

FRESH back from holiday, Andy Burnham will embark on a cost of living tour tomorrow — and recycle an idea first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago.

He will re-announce plans to end “subscription traps” which deliberately make it tricky for people to stop recurring charges after ordering online.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Perhaps when he’s delivered his latest “easy win”, the PM might find time to turn his mind to more pressing issues.

Like the economy, illegal migration, hospital waiting lists and rebuilding our hollowed-out Armed Forces.

News.title: Andy Burnham kicks off cost-of-living tour with reheated Labour pledge to crack down on subscription traps
News.content:
ANDY Burnham will kick off his cost-of- living tour tomorrow with a reheated pledge first announced by Labour in 2023.

The PM is promising to end so-called subscription traps that lure customers into costly and hard-to-cancel online plans for the likes of streaming services.



Back from his holiday, Mr Burnham will accuse Westminster of “telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life” for too long.

But the crackdown on subscription traps was first unveiled by Sir Keir Starmer three years ago and started in April before his resignation.



It will force companies to give customers clearer information when subscriptions are automatically renewed at a higher cost, and impose a 14-day cooling-off period allowing them to cancel after a trial.

Like Sir Keir — who was seen playing football yesterday in an Arsenal strip — Mr Burnham claims this will save an average £14 a month for every unwanted subscription, ending an estimated total of £1.6billion a year being wasted.

The only difference in the cut-and-paste policy appears to be the PM bringing forward the date from spring next year to January.

Mr Burnham is also announcing plans to end rip-off discounts whereby sellers deliberately raise their prices before slashing them to give the impression of a bargain.

He will launch a consultation to see whether such practices should be banned by law.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Burnham has already run out of ideas.



“Labour’s tax hikes have sent costs soaring for hardworking families and destroyed jobs.

“Consultations and reheated measures won’t make up for that.”

News.title: Terrorists who planned to kill thousands in liquid bomb jet plot could be freed in WEEKS as they launch parole bids
News.content:
THREE Al-Qaeda terrorists who were part of the infamous plot to blow up airliners with liquid explosives could be released back on the streets within weeks.

Their 2006 al-Qaeda-inspired plan to hide liquid explosives in drinks bottles changed air travel around the world.



It also sparked airport chaos, cost airlines millions and ultimately forced the aviation industry to invest in sophisticated new scanners.

All three, who are British citizens of Pakistani descent, are now ­eligible to ask the Parole Board to decide whether the danger they once represented can safely be managed outside prison.



They were sentenced to life with a minimum of 20 years after a jury heard they recorded chilling “martyrdom videos” in preparation for suicide attacks.

Ibrahim Savant, of Stoke Newington, North London, Arafat Waheed Khan and Waheed Zaman, both of Walthamstow, East London, were recruited by Abdulla Ahmed Ali.

Zaman has a Parole Board hearing listed for September 7.

Khan’s case will be considered on September 21, while Savant is due before the board on November 12.

If the Parole Board considers them rehabilitated they could be freed by Christmas.

Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said last night: “The public will be rightly appalled that these appalling individuals could soon be back on our streets.



“Our justice system is fundamentally broken when people convicted of conspiracy to commit mass murder on such a terrifying scale are even considered for release. They should be locked up for life.”

Tory Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy added: “It’s unconscionable that Islamist terrorists — who planned to blow up planes, killing hundreds of innocent civilians — should be let out of prison.

“If they are, the public will rightly be outraged.”



Police moved against the plotters on August 10, 2006, amid fears that an attack could be imminent.

The UK terror threat level was raised to “critical” and normal hand luggage was initially banned from flights leaving British airports.

Thousands of passengers were caught in huge queues in the peak summer holiday season.



British Airways cancelled 1,280 flights in eight days and later estimated that the disruption had cost it £40million.

The conspirators planned to manufacture bombs using liquid explosives which could be concealed inside bottles of drinks including Oasis and Lucozade.

The main charges were to contain hydrogen peroxide and other chemicals capable of producing the highly unstable explosive TATP.

Small detonators fashioned using components from disposable cameras could then have been used to ­trigger explosions in mid-air.

Within months, restrictions were introduced limiting liquids in hand luggage to containers of no more than 100ml, which had to be presented for security screening inside transparent one-litre plastic bags.



Bottles of water were routinely surrendered at airport security.

Shampoo, toothpaste, deodorant, perfume, suncream and cosmetics were decanted into tiny containers.

The annoying and time- consuming process became as familiar to holidaymakers as passports and boarding cards.



Manufacturers and retailers responded with travel-sized ­toiletries, while passengers also bought empty 100ml bottles and transparent security bags.

The global market for such items is now valued at £5.7billion.

Airports have since spent millions installing CT security scanners capable of detecting liquid explosives technology, which is finally allowing some of the restrictions to be relaxed.

Yet the scale of the atrocity which prompted them could have been almost unimaginable.

The plot centred on plans to destroy multiple passenger aircraft travelling simultaneously from Britain to the US and Canada.



Flights from Heathrow to San Francisco, Toronto, Montreal, Chicago, Washington DC and New York were among those considered.

Investigators discovered discussions involving an operation which could potentially have used up to 18 suicide bombers.

Six suspects recorded martyrdom videos denouncing the West and explaining their willingness to die.

The recordings were intended to be distributed by al-Qaeda supporters after the attacks.

At the centre of the conspiracy was Abdulla Ahmed Ali.



Ali and fellow plotters Assad Sarwar and Tanvir Hussain were eventually convicted of conspiring specifically to murder passengers by detonating liquid bombs aboard transatlantic aircraft.

Ali was sentenced to life with a minimum term of 40 years.

Sarwar received a minimum of 36 years and Hussain 32 years.

Another conspirator, Umar Islam, was convicted of conspiracy to murder and sentenced to life with a minimum term of 22 years.



But bringing Savant, Khan and Zaman to justice proved consider-ably more complicated.

They were cleared of conspiring specifically to blow up aircraft after prosecutors failed to prove they knew the intended targets of the suicide operation were airliners.



But the Crown argued that the evidence nevertheless showed each had committed himself to taking part in a murderous suicide attack.

Then-Director of Public Prosecutions Sir Keir Starmer authorised the exceptional step of seeking another trial after deciding there remained a realistic prospect of conviction.

In 2010 a third jury convicted all three of conspiracy to murder.

Jailing the trio for life, Mr Justice Holroyde told them: “Each of you agreed to join with others in this conspiracy, with each of you intending that you would kill members of the general public and yourselves by acting as a suicide bomber.”

The three are now eligible to ask the Parole Board to decide if the danger they once represented can safely be managed outside prison.



But Ghaffar Hussain, a former counter-terror officer on the Government’s Prevent programme, told The Sun: “For terrorists who intended on killing hundreds of innocent people, life sentences should mean lifelong imprisonment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Threat assessment with such individuals is notoriously difficult and released terrorists have reoffended before. We need to be very careful.”

The Parole Board said: “Reviews are undertaken thoroughly and with extreme care. Protecting the public is our number one priority.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s ten-year journey to No10 is over but now the real battles begin – he has to deliver on promises
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM’S path to power has been an epic political odyssey.

While other Prime Ministers enjoyed swifter triumphs, his ten-year journey to Downing Street has been plagued by setbacks, detours and outright failure.



Heavily defeated in two ­Labour leadership contests, he stubbornly refused to give up.

Instead, he retreated 200 miles to Manchester, to build a power base and plot his route back to Westminster.



He returned as King of the North to seize the crown in an almost bloodless coup just three weeks ago.

And now? He’s spent the last week on holiday.



After a decade of scheming, Burnham apparently needs a breather before tackling the little matter of running the country.

He’ll need the rest.

Because, like Odysseus, our new PM will soon discover that getting home is only half the battle.

Homer’s hero had barely made it back to Ithaca before he was forced to take on a hall full of grasping suitors wooing his wife.



Burnham’s homecoming will be no less bruising.

His own monsters are already waiting: a £3trillion mountain of debt, threadbare Armed Forces, a battalion of disgruntled Starmer loyalists and, lurking in the shadows, Labour’s hard left.

Fasten your seatbelts. When Parliament returns next month it’ll be pure political box office.



Already the problems are piling up for Andysseus.

His biggest challenge is clear: to deliver on his promise to get things done and put “hope in every heart”.

Feelgood vibes and instant giveaways, like the £2 cap on bus fares and 86p-a-week cut in energy bills, have given Labour a Burnham bounce and sent expectations sky high.

But soon an impatient public will demand real change — and some already suspect he’ll end up like the rest of them: big on promises and short on delivery.

Labour’s decision to free thousands of offenders from prison early — including the killers of PC Andrew Harper — is Burnham’s first big test.



He raised hopes of an intervention when he “paused” the process.

But anger went off the scale when he claimed he was powerless to halt their release, with 850,000 people signing a protest petition.

Now he’s wisely decided to explore other options.



Like Pandora’s box, the scheme has released future misery and mayhem, which may soon come back to haunt the PM.

His proud boast of assembling the first Cabinet with more women than men will ring hollow if 9,000 domestic abusers walk free in the next three years.

Burnham must resolve this brewing crisis before his next major test in just three weeks — taking on the Mino-Tory.

Kemi Badenoch is gearing up for her first Commons joust with the new PM by watching old videos of his performance at the despatch box.

Burnham’s at his best when delivering passionate arguments.



But as a minister he lacked the razor-sharp wit and quickfire repartee of top parliamentary gladiators and is easily rattled when put on the spot.

His top team will no doubt put him through his paces when he returns from his sunbed to prepare him for something he has so far avoided: full public scrutiny.

The Conservative leader is bound to challenge him on the real-life Trojan horse: the small boats used by illegal migrants and criminals to enter Britain.

Burnham has promised to be “relentless” in tackling the crisis.



Yet 2,000 have made the perilous crossing since he became PM and he cannot allow things to drift as Keir Starmer did.

But his real Achilles’ heel is the estimated £96billion in new spending pledges — to build more council houses, fix social care and beef up our Armed Forces.

Where is the money coming from?

Britain is £3trillion in debt. That’s £43,000 for every man, woman and child.



But now there’s talk in Number 10 North and South about tampering with fiscal rules to allow more borrowing.

Taxpayers already fork out £12million in interest charges every HOUR, twice what we spend on defence.

The market gods will unleash their fury if Burnham dares to borrow more.

His only real options are to break a manifesto pledge not to increase taxes, already at an 80-year high, or to take the axe to the bloated £334billion welfare bill.

Burnham must use his clout to drive through the necessary cuts before his power ebbs away.



He has undoubtedly brought a new air of optimism to government.

But after years of economic mayhem and political upheaval, Britain still feels like a ship searching for its Ithaca.

The past four Prime Ministers have promised that home is just beyond the horizon, only for another storm to blow them off course.

Will Burnham’s voyage be as treacherous as The Odyssey, or will he steer us to calmer waters?

We’ll soon discover whether he’s a hit or a myth.



THE Prime Minister’s flagship plan to move power out of Westminster is being run by a civil ­servant . . . from London.

Sam Lister, the new director general of No 10 North, spends four days a week in the ­Manchester office, clocking up an £800 weekly bill for hotel and rail fares as he commutes from the capital.

And there was me thinking Burnham wanted to improve job opportunities for northerners.

KILLJOY council chiefs want to end the centuries-old tradition of ordering a pint while standing at the bar.



They plan to call time on “vertical drinking” by imposing compulsory table service on busy pubs.

But how do the clipboard-wielding party poopers plan to enforce the rule?

Can we expect spot-checks from inspectors using protractors to check the angle at which we are seated?

“Pardon me, sir, but you are leaning at 31 degrees, which is nearly upright.

“I’m going to ask you to sit back in your chair or leave.”



What happens if we slouch after feeling worse for wear after two pints?

Or if we have a few too many and find ourselves horizontal?

Well, here’s a message for those councils thinking of following the crackdown proposed by the City of Westminster:

British pubs have survived the plague, the Blitz, a smoking ban and the pandemic.

They’ve even survived the advent of karaoke and won’t be beaten by a bunch of meddling jobsworths.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

We’ll remain on our feet at the bar.

And we won’t stand for this nonsense.

News.title: A31 fire live: New Forest wildfire breaks out as drivers told 'flee if you want to stay alive'
News.content:
The A31 remains closed following the vehicle fire

Firefighters are tackling the blaze after 160 calls were made following a vehicle fire that spread to dry heathland

A31 fire live: New Forest wildfire breaks out as drivers told 'flee if you want to stay alive'

A huge fire has broken out after a vehicle fire spread to dry heathland on the A31 in the New Forest, Hampshire.

More than 20 fire engines are trying to extinguish the blaze after a vehicle fire spread.

Members of the public made 160 calls reporting the vehicle on fire on the eastbound A31 just after 5.24pm.

The road is closed in both directions. The westbound carriageway is closed between the M27 J2 (Ower) and the A338 (Ringwood).

The eastbound carriageway is closed between the A338 and M27 J1 (Cadnam).

News.title: Royal Navy's £12m drones 'secretly sent data to China' in huge security breach
News.content:
Royal Navy's £12m drones 'secretly sent data to China' in huge security breach

Questions are now being asked over the UK government's bid to thaw relations with China, but Ministry of Defence officials have insisted no sensitive data was leaked

View 2 Images File Royal Navy photo (Image: PA)

A £12m fleet of Royal Navy drones secretly sent information to China, according to reports.

‌



An investigation has revealed that cameras fitted to new K3 Scout spy drones transmitted ‘heartbeat communications’ to an IP address in China, reports The Telegraph. The discovery was reportedly made at the Special Boat Service’s HQ in Poole, Dorset, after the £12m fleet of drones, produced by UK supplier Kraken Technology Group, entered service in March.

‌



The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has denied any sensitive information has fallen into the hands of Chinese officials, as it's thought the cameras sent data which confirmed the cameras were functioning as normal.

‌



An MoD spokesperson said: “A routine cyber vulnerability assessment identified an issue affecting a Kraken Unmanned Surface Vessel sub-system used by the Royal Navy. A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.

“Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment.”

Kraken added a 'full audit' has taken place. A spokesperson for Kraken said: “We are aware that some third-party, [US] national defence authorisation act-compliant cameras had a small number of components originating from outside the UK.

‌



View 2 Images Keir Starmer was the first UK leader to visit China earlier this year since Theresa May in 2018 (Image: PA)

“After a full audit by both Kraken and the Royal Navy we are confident no sensitive information has ever been shared outside of intended channels and any potential vulnerabilities have been identified and closed.”

‌



The revelations could lead to more questions over Britain’s relationship with China.

Earlier this year, the government approved construction of a new Chinese embassy complex at Royal Mint Court, which is located near highly-valuable underground cables used by city traders. Its approval sparked fears Chinese agents could spy on market information.

Labour has attempted to thaw relations with Beijing since coming to power, with Keir Starmer visiting the country in late January. He was the first British Prime Minister to conduct a diplomatic mission to China since Theresa May in 2018.

News.title: Met Office issues rare extreme red heat warning update as 36C forecast Thursday
News.content:
Met Office issues rare extreme red heat warning update as 36C forecast Thursday

The Met Office have issued a heat warning update as scorching temperatures are likely to cause chaos across the UK this week as the country faces its fifth heatwave

View 4 Images A heat health warning may be on the cards this week (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

The Met Office have issued a rare extreme red heat warning update as temperatures are expected to skyrocket to 36C on Thursday.

‌



The forecaster has warned that as highs are predicted this week, there will be possible impacts to railway lines and power networks.

‌



The Met Office has said they are considering issuing rare amber or red extreme heat warnings.

‌



View 4 Images Another heatwave is expected to strike (Image: Graham Hunt/BNPS)

The scorching temperatures will see parts of the UK bake in their fifth heatwave of the summer.

Monday will be slightly cooler before temperatures rise again on Tuesday.

‌



“We’ll probably see highs reaching the mid-30s quite widely on Wednesday, and indeed on Thursday too for England and Wales,” Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said.

“On Wednesday, probably the Midlands, maybe a little bit further south, the M4 corridor, west of London, up towards the Midlands, is where we might have a small chance of reaching 36C in one or two spots.

“But Thursday at this stage looks the most likely hottest day of the week.

‌



“So 36C is a fairly reasonable probability locally on Thursday and there’s a small chance it could get even higher than that.”

View 4 Images A heat health warning is likely according to the Met Office (Image: Ben Whitley/PA Wire)

Due to recent warm conditions half of England and Wales has been plunged into drought and more regions could be declared when officials meet at the National Drought Group on Monday.

‌



Mr Morgan said: “If it wasn’t for this incredible summer that we’re currently seeing, then we’d be talking about these temperatures as being really, very unusual.

“But of course, we’ve had such an exceptional summer, people have become a bit used to it.

“There is a potential for impacts, so impacts to infrastructure, things like railway lines and power networks, impacts to vulnerable people as well.”

‌



Health alerts are already in place as officials have warned that vulnerable people will be impacted in the upcoming hot weather.

Yellow heat health alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency are in place for the East Midlands, West Midlands, South East, South West, East of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, and London and currently continue until 9pm on Tuesday.

These may well be extended as the hot weather continues.

‌



View 4 Images Several areas are in drought due to the conditions (Image: Akira Suemori/Shutterstock)

Meanwhile, the Met Office is considering issuing rare extreme heat warnings ahead of the scorching temperatures forecast later in the week.

“We sometimes issue extreme heat warnings, amber and red warnings, which we did back in June, so that’s under consideration at the moment,” Mr Morgan said.

Article continues below

Another record is set to tumble this week after Sunday was the 34th day so far this year when temperatures exceeded 30C somewhere in the UK, equalling the record from 1995.

So far, the extreme weather of summer 2026 has included two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

Two more heatwaves in July, the driest July in England and Wales since records began in 1836, have fuelled drought and wildfires.

News.title: Fighter jets intercept aircraft over Donald Trump's golf course after air restriction violation
News.content:
Fighter jets intercept aircraft over Donald Trump's golf course after air restriction violation

The flight restrictions were in place over the Bedminster area, where US President Donald Trump was expected to spend the weekend during the LIV Golf New York tournament

View 3 Images F-16 fighters jets (file image) (Image: AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

US fighter jets intercepted general aviation aircraft which violated temporary flight restrictions near US President Donald Trump's golf course.

‌



It is being reported that two aircraft were involved in the incident.

‌



The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) said its F-16 fighter jets intercepted the aircraft over Bedminster, New Jersey, on Sunday, August 9.

‌



Flight restrictions were in place over the Bedminster area. Mr Trump was expected to spend the weekend in the area while his golf club hosted the LIV Golf New York tournament from August 6 to 9.

View 3 Images LIV Golf New York - Day Four (Image: Getty)

Video footage captured the interception and showed the F-16 fighter jet close in on a small aircraft near Jefferson Township, outside Bedminster.

‌



The aircraft were escorted out of the restricted area by NORAD aircraft, officials said.

Before Mr Trump landed in New Jersey, NORAD said that it would enforce multiple Federal Aviation Administration-established temporary flight restrictions over the region for the weekend.

View 3 Images (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

Temporary flight restrictions are issued to limit aircraft operations in specified areas.

It is usually done for presidential movements, major sporting events and national security worries, among other things.

General aviation pilots were reminded to check notices before every flight for the information on airspace restrictions and other flight protocols.

News.title: Fraud advice for music fans as more than one in 10 bought fake tickets in last year
News.content:
Fraud advice for music fans as more than one in 10 bought fake tickets in last year

More than one in 10 gig-goers have fallen victim to fake tickets in the last year, fresh polling shows, as ministers warn music fans of scammers on social media

View 2 Images Ministers described ticket fraud as an 'absolutely shameful crime' (Image: Getty)

More than one in 10 gig-goers have fallen victim to fake tickets in the last year, polling shows today, as ministers warn of scammers on social media.

‌



Some 14% of music fans surveyed bought a fake ticket, with over three-quarters (77%) of the tickets bought via online platforms, a study by O2 found. The polling found that no age group was immune to these scams, but those aged 18 to 24 faced the highest risk with 31% having been sold a fake ticket compared to 4% of those aged over 55.

‌



Researchers said some £150million has been lost to ticket fraud in the last year. Ticket fraud occurs when you buy tickets from a website or social media platform, but the tickets either don’t arrive or turn out to be fake.

‌



View 2 Images Ministers warned the public to remain vigilant as festival season continues and ahead of huge tours from artists including Ariana Grande (Image: Christopher Polk/2026GG/Penske Media via Getty Images)

Ministers described ticket fraud as an "absolutely shameful crime" and warned the public to remain vigilant as festival season continues and ahead of huge tours from Ariana Grande, The Weeknd and Bon Jovi. The government delivered £250m of investment to crackdown on fraud and protect the public earlier this year, as part of a new Fraud strategy.

It established a new Online Crime Centre to bring together police and industry to disrupt scams at source and boost support for victims. The Stop! Think Fraud campaign aims to make it easier for the public to recognise fraud and take steps to protect themselves, their family and friends.

‌



The Government has also committed to stamping out ticket touting, where tickets are bought at volume, often using automated bots, before being relisted on resale platforms at hugely inflated prices. Plans have been announced to make it illegal for tickets to live events to be resold for more than their original cost, which will eliminate the scourge of industrial-scale ticket touting.

Fraud Minister Lord Hanson said: “Fraud is an absolutely shameful crime, and this data shows that anyone can be a victim. Scammers exploit our excitement and desperation to see our favourite artists live. They post fake messages on social media seeking to catch fans when their guard is down in a last-minute rush for tickets.

“I urge everyone to Stop! Think Fraud before buying tickets – let’s not let scammers get in the way of enjoying concerts this summer.”

‌



Gareth Griffiths, Virgin Media O2's d irector of partnerships and sponsorship, said: “Ticketing scams are a blight on the UK's live music industry, and it's heartbreaking to see so many fans being targeted. Seeing your favourite artist live should be an exciting experience, not one that leaves you out of pocket or turned away at the door.

"That's why O2 is encouraging fans to stay vigilant, buy tickets only from official authorised services and use capped fan-to-fan resale platforms when a show is sold out.”

::: Censuswide polled 2,000 people in the UK between June 23 and 29.

Article continues below

What you should do to keep yourself safe from ticket fraud:

If you’re offered tickets for something in high demand don’t let the fear of missing out rush your decision. Take a moment to stop, think, and check if the offer is genuine. Only buy tickets from an official ticketing website. Artists will always link to official ticket sellers in posts on their social media and official websites. Never move away from an official payment platform to make a direct payment via bank transfer or virtual currency. Use the site’s recommended payment methods to stay protected. Remember buying second hand tickets comes with risks and while some platforms may offer a refund for ticket scams, they cannot guarantee entry to a show.

This advice was issued by the Home Office.

News.title: UK jobs market finally showing 'rays of light' - especially if you're after permanent work
News.content:
UK jobs market finally showing 'rays of light' - especially if you're after permanent work

A decline in permanent jobs that has stretched on for 45 months has finally come to end, research from recruiters has revealed, showing a slither of sunshine on the horizon

View 3 Images The jobs market is still fragile despite signs or it stabilising

The jobs market is showing “rays of light” in a boost to those battling to find work, a report has found.

‌



Recruiters say a decline in workers getting permanent work that stretches all the way back to 2022, around the time failed Tory PM Liz Truss quit, has finally come to an end. The number of vacancies for temporary workers has also risen for the first time in two years, according to a report Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC) and accountancy giant KPMG.

‌



The finding will give hope to those who have found it increasingly difficult to bag a job. It will also prove another welcome sign for new PM Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey as they look for signs of recovery in the economy.

‌



View 3 Images Feedback from recruiters points to improvements in the jobs market (Image: GETTY)

That said, the latest research still shows how any upturn in the jobs market could be some way off. While the number of job hunters being placed in permanent jobs by recruiters stabilised in July, it followed 45 months of decline. It added: “Recruiters noted that demand for permanent staff remained subdued amid political and economic uncertainty and higher labour costs.”

The data also showed employers remain nervous about taking on permanent workers, highlighted by demand for temporary workers instead. Though modest, the rate of growth was the quickest seen since August 2023. On the flipside, the number of people looking for work rose again last month, extending a run of increases that goes back nearly three-and-a-half years.

‌



“The latest increases in staff supply were generally linked to redundancies and a lack of job opportunities,” the report said. Demand for permanent workers was sharpest among nurses, medical and car workers. The biggest decline was among shop workers and those in hotel and catering

View 3 Images The past few years has been that much harder to find permanent work (Image: Dima Berlin via Getty Images)

Maxine Bligh, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation’s chief membership and innovation officer, said: “Rays of light are beginning to break through for the job market as employers revive hiring plans. That makes it all the more important that the government takes decisions now that builds business confidence and momentum in hiring.

Article continues below

"This means action to bring the Industrial Strategy to life and exercising pragmatism around the implementation of the Employment Rights Act, particularly guaranteed hours proposals. The Autumn Budget is a great opportunity to give businesses the shot of confidence they need to hire and invest."

Callum Licence, group head of advisory at KPMG UK and Switzerland, said: “Despite ongoing uncertainty it’s encouraging that businesses are starting to press ahead with investment, which means across the board we are starting to see the data moving in the right direction. This is most pronounced in the continued rise of temporary work, where employers have been looking at flexible approaches and hiring has been growing for several months, and permanent hiring is starting to turn a corner.

“Over the past 45 months we have seen the longest recorded period of contraction in the permanent placements index, so to finally have it stable is a big milestone. With a new Government in place, businesses will be looking for signs that the new policies can translate into greater confidence to invest and hire”.

News.title: Brit teen, 16, dies and siblings badly injured in 'terrible accident' on family holiday
News.content:
Brit teen, 16, dies and siblings badly injured in 'terrible accident' on family holiday

A 16-year-old girl has died, and her two siblings have been seriously injured, while on a family in a tropical destination - tribute have poured in for the teen

View Image Abbie Lainton, 16, died on July 30 while on vacation in the Dominican Republic (Image: GoFundMe)

A teenager has died in an accident, and her two siblings were seriously injured, while on a family holiday.

‌



Abbie Lainton, 16, from Swindon, died on July 30 while on vacation in the Dominican Republic.

‌



The teen's former school, Tanwood School for Performing Arts, paid tribute to her in a statement.

‌



"Abbie joined Tanwood as a dinky dot and was part of an exceptional group of dancers who formed strong friendships which spilled over to the audience when they performed together," a spokesperson said in statement.

"She always performed with a huge smile, and those beautiful feet.

"We are all in complete shock at this heartbreaking news and send so much love and support to her family and friends at this unimaginable time.

‌



"You will always be in our hearts."

Abbie was also a member of Swindon Lightning Cheerleading club. She participated in competitions around the world.

A spokesperson for the club said: "There are simply no words that feel enough.

‌



"Abbie was a much-loved member of our Swindon Lightning family.

"Her kindness, infectious smile, unwavering encouragement and love for cheerleading touched the lives of so many athletes, coaches and families over the years."

A GoFundMe page has been established to assist her family. It did not provide details surrounding the accident.

‌



Becky Jamieson, who set up the fundraiser, described the Abbie as as someone who was loved by everyone who knew her.

"On July 30, 2026, Abbie Lainton tragically lost her life in a terrible accident while on holiday in the Dominican Republic," the page reads.

"Becky and Gary have lost their beautiful 16-year-old daughter, and Carley and Bradley were also badly injured in the accident.

Article continues below

"Abbie had her whole life ahead of her. She should have been enjoying the summer with her friends and looking forward to receiving her GCSE results."

The fundraiser concluded: "Forever 16, forever loved and never forgotten."

News.title: Record heatwaves expose hidden history - from Nazi motorbike to mammoth bones and 'lost' gardens
News.content:
A Nazi motorbike is one of the many secrets of history uncovered by Europe's record-breaking heatwave.

The Wehrmacht military motorcycle, the remains of two soldiers, and World War II ammunition were among items found on the riverbed amid record-low water levels along the Danube in Budapest at the weekend.

Mammoth bones believed to be several thousand years old were also discovered along the same river near Ryahovo, Bulgaria.

Across Europe, months of scorching hot temperatures and low rainfall have seen rivers, reservoirs and lakes turn up secrets that until now have been hidden from history, offering archaeologists a unique opportunity to retrieve important artefacts.

Parched, dry grass has meanwhile revealed the outlines of structures long since demolished and forgotten - including a grand 17th century formal garden that once stood on the grounds of Chatsworth House in Derbyshire.

News.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
News.content:
Consumers will benefit from an end to so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices", Andy Burnham has said.

The prime minister is bringing forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, to make it easier to cancel subscriptions.

Burnham is also planning to outlaw shops using fake "was" prices, which he said trick shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

Consumer group Which? said it has "repeatedly exposed businesses, including trusted household brands, ripping off customers with dodgy deals that aren't what they seem".

Its head of consumer rights policy, Sue Davies, welcomed the announcement and called for the government to bring the rules in "swiftly".

But Stride said: "The cost of living didn't become a problem last week, so you have to ask why it has taken Labour so long to enact legislation passed by the previous government."

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumer Act, passed under the Conservatives in 2024, cracked down on hidden fees, fake reviews online and made it easier for customers to cancel subscriptions.

The announcement is Burnham's latest intervention aimed at easing the cost of living, following a Â£2 bus fare cap in England and a VAT cut on household electricity bills.

But he is likely to come under pressure to make more significant changes in the Budget, which will be delivered by Chancellor John Healey on 28 October.

But Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

News.title: Brief relief ahead of fifth heatwave - as more areas could move into drought
News.content:
Much of the country will feel some relief from the heat early in the week before temperatures spike again.

On Monday, the air will feel a little fresher compared to the weekend with maximum temperatures in northern areas of the UK around 18 to 24C.

Further south, while cooler than Sunday, it will still be a very warm day with temperatures between 22 to 27C.

By Tuesday, warmer air will start to move back in across the UK with the highest temperatures across central southern England, the Midlands and east Wales.

Yellow heat-health alerts remain in force for much of England until 21:00 BST on Tuesday, though they are likely to be extended or upgraded as the heatwave nears.

Highs are likely to be around 27 to 30C.

Wednesday will see temperatures widely across England and Wales head into the high twenties and low thirties.

The peak of the extreme heat is set to arrive on Thursday, with temperatures reaching 36C (97F) in south-east England, and up to 35C likely across central and eastern England.

This would mark the fourth consecutive month where 35C has been reached in the UK â a new record.

Many locations will exceed their heatwave threshold of 25 to 28C â dependent on location â for the first day.

Some of the warmth will spread further north into northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures into the low to mid-20s Celsius.

As heat builds throughout the week, overnight temperatures will stay relatively high bringing some uncomfortable nights for sleeping.

Minimum temperatures may not go lower than 16 to 18C across England and Wales.

There's also a possibility of a 'tropical night' â where temperatures remain above 20C all night â in south-east England.

News.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez freezing her eggs and hasn't 'ruled out' presidential run
News.content:
New York Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has revealed she has decided to freeze her eggs and has shared her first steps in the process on social media.

The 36-year-old posted the clips on Sunday, hours before telling ABC News This Week she had not "ruled out the possibility" of running for president.

In the clips, Ocasio-Cortez shows herself taking an injection and talks through tips she has learnt, before answering questions about costs, clinical procedures, storage and how fertility care works under what she calls the US's "broken" medical system.

In an interview on ABC News she said she wanted to "normalise" conversations about the process.

She said it was important "especially in this political environment".

"This administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy," she said. "I think it's important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes," she added.

In an earlier post on Instagram she said she wanted to share the information even though there was a "political risk" in doing so.

When asked if she would run for president in the 2028 elections after being shown polling reflecting her popularity as a potential candidate, Ocasio-Cortez chuckled and tried to sidestep a direct answer.

"I'm focused on winning the midterms, I'm running for Congress right now," she said.

But when pushed as to whether she was open to it and whether it was a realistic prospect, she said: "I haven't ruled out the possibility and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."

"We have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans," she said.

After she was asked about a possible Senate run against minority leader Chuck Schumer, the US Senate's top Democrat, Ocasio-Cortez replied that "anything was possible".

The midterms are held every two years and fall in the middle of the president's four-year term of office.

They are due to be held in early November. Votes will be cast for all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, and a third of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for grabs.

News.title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
News.content:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear â plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to Â£50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was Â£101.94 with a pinafore, and Â£83.95 without â but this year it will cost families an average of Â£53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.

News.title: 'Spectacular' Game of Thrones stage spin-off opens at home of Shakespeare
News.content:
The first Game of Thrones stage spin-off has been launched by the Royal Shakespeare Company, and the verdict from most theatre critics is that it's a worthy addition to the epic fantasy franchise.

Game of Thrones: The Mad King, a prequel set shortly before the events of George RR Martin's first book and the all-conquering TV series, officially opened at the RSC in Stratford-upon-Avon this weekend.

The Telegraph awarded four stars to the "spellbinding spectacle", while the Guardian's four-star review said it features "spectacular stagecraft and plenty of modern resonance".

The Times was more lukewarm, giving three stars and saying the play "lacks pace, sex and gore".

News.title: You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check
News.content:
Millions of people will learn of the level of winter energy prices later this month, when Ofgem announces the quarterly price cap for the three months from October.

To help those who might struggle to pay, energy companies distribute the Â£150 Warm Home Discount to about six million households in the winter. Households in receipt of housing benefit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and universal credit qualify.

Households who are eligible should get the discount automatically, provided their supplier has over 1,000 customers.

However, that only happens if your name is on the bill and you are receiving one of these benefits. It can also help suppliers offer better support, such as repayment plans, to those who have energy debt.

Someone might not be named on their electricity bill if they have recently moved house.

Eligible customers on pre-payment meters who use a key or card to top up will also need to ensure that their household's account is registered in their name.

"If you know someone who might benefit, please start spreading the word and encourage them to check they are named on their energy bill," said Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

The government also said that 345,000 Scottish low-income households would now automatically receive the rebate in the winter, bringing Scotland's policy in line with England and Wales.

Previously, eligible Scottish households have had to apply for the scheme.

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid 'Dobby's grave'
News.content:
He said a colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam said he then discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

News.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
News.content:
The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said.

Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition.

New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died.

The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released by officials.

Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue.

A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company's founder Adam Schwartz said according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said.

The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said.

The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said.

Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered.

An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection.

"We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Family 'devastated' as hit-and-run driver who killed boy, 13, to have early prison release
News.content:
The family of a 13-year-old boy killed in a hit-and-run say they are "devastated" after being told the driver who caused his death has had his sentence reduced.

Kaylan Hippsley died three days after being struck by a car driven by Harley Whiteman on Brecon Road in Hirwaun, Rhondda Cynon Taf, on 29 February 2024.

Whiteman was originally sentenced to six years and nine months in prison and banned from driving for eight years and four months but, after Kaylan's family appealed, High Court judges increased the sentence to nine years.

Now, the family has been told Whiteman can be released under licence as early as this autumn as part of the UK government's Sentencing Act early release scheme.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Rare turtle to be sent back home in 5,000-mile 'incredibly emotional' trip
News.content:
It has taken almost two years to plan, including building a special temperature-controlled crate for him, and co-ordinating complex paperwork across two countries.

Rhossi normally lives in the sea, but has to travel out of the water â first by helicopter from Anglesey to London, then by cargo flight to Houston, Texas, USA.

It means the journey needs to be completed as quickly as possible, and staff have to be constantly on hand to make sure he does not dry out or dehydrate.

Davidson said: "We have to make sure that the shell is really well lubricated, so we spread Vaseline all over to stop it drying out and flaking off.

"The same for the skin â it's really delicate â and especially the eyes, which both have to be lubricated before he goes into the crate and again just before takeoff, or he will start to peel like someone getting sunburned.

"But I have had to go to the checkout in a chemist's with about eight tubes of KY Jelly and three tubs of Vaseline and explain what's happening when I get strange looks."

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7 million people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assault led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
News.content:
As the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.

Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.

At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th Century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.

Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.

Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning "on the ground" - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install".

"It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after three hit by car
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and dangerous driving after three pedestrians were hit by a car following reports of a disturbance.

The incident happened on Stokes Croft in Bristol at about 06:30 BST, according to Avon and Somerset Police.

A spokesperson for the force said one of the pedestrians was taken to hospital, but their injuries were not considered to be life-changing or life-threatening. The two others were not seriously injured.

A man police believe to be the car's driver was treated for facial injuries after his arrest.

Thomas Street, Hepburn Road, Stokes Croft and City Road are all closed while police make enquiries, with more officers than usual in the area as investigations continue.

The Best Off Licence in Stokes Croft was also damaged in the incident.

Bristol Supt Matt Ebbs said: "We would like to assure the public we do not believe there to be any wider threat.

"Anybody with concerns is welcome to speak to officers on the ground, but we would also appeal to anybody with CCTV, dashcam or mobile phone footage which may assist our enquiries to contact us."

News.title: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandise
News.content:
Celebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?

At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days.

It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.

While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.

Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care.

Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers.

"We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"

Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.

Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers.

Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.

News.title: New Zealand’s decision to recognise a new official language draws sharp criticism: ‘Embarrassing waste of time’
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Lawmakers in New Zealand have passed a bill to make English an official language of the country.

The move has sparked criticism from some lawmakers and linguistic experts who called it “virtue signalling and a waste of parliamentary time and money while raising the risk of marginalisation of te reo Māori and New Zealand Sign Language.

English has now been recognised as an official language alongside the Māori language and New Zealand sign language, giving it the same official status as the other two languages.

The English language bill became a law on 30 July. The law will not mean any new rules or changes are needed for it to continue being used in legal, political and government settings or documents.

English is already widely used in New Zealand’s courts and parliament, with more than 95 per cent of the population using it as a spoken language, according to government data in 2023. Only 4.3 per cent spoke Māori and 0.5 per cent used sign language.

The bill, which was campaigned by the nationalist New Zealand First party and the centre-right National Party, was passed in its third reading in the House of Representatives.

New Zealand's flag flutters in front of 'The Beehive', the executive wing of the New Zealand Parliament Buildings ( Reuters )

The coalition government and the main opposition Labour Party voted in favour of the bill, while the smaller opposition parties, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, voted against it.

Green MP Tamatha Paul said the decision was “a pathetic waste of the responsibility of this house”, adding that the “snowflake” government “see te reo Māori and they shiver in their boots.”

In the video of the speech, which has gone viral, and garnered more than six million views on Instagram, she said, “We had to march our asses to parliament demanding that the Indigenous first language of this country be recognised and not beaten out of the mouths of its native speakers.”

Dr Dean Knight, a professor of law at Te Herenga Waka Victoria University of Wellington, told Newsroom: “It doesn’t change practice at all, other than to the extent that people can look up in a statute and see, unsurprisingly, that English is an official language of the nation. It won’t change things a jot”.

“English is and has been an official language of this nation, by dint of custom and usage, for years and years and years. All the business of the state and the state apparatus is predominantly done in English. All this bill does is spell that out in legislation.”

Dr Sidney Wong, a linguist said, said official language status was required for languages that need protection and services, but English was not under any threat.

“The main reason why this bill was put in place was based on ideology – there was this perception that English was under threat, that it doesn’t have the prestige, and it needs that sort of legislative protection. But it doesn’t need that,” he told the Guardian.

During the debate, Labour MP Camilla Belich mocked the legislation, saying “I wondered if they might want to legislate for the changing of the seasons?”

They said Māori and New Zealand sign language were made official languages to protect linguistic minorities.

Defending the need for the legislation, lawmaker, representing the New Zealand First party, Casey Costello, said it was a practical measure.

“It aligns the statute book with longstanding practice, and provides a clear statement about the status of English within New Zealand’s official framework,” Ms Costello told the house.

“It is not trivial, unnecessary or a distraction to this House in a democracy to deliver for those who elected us to this House.”

Winston Peters, leader of minor populist New Zealand First party, had previously said Māori in public services was causing confusion.

A report presented to Parliament by the Justice Committee in June found widespread opposition to the bill. Of the 1,601 submissions received from individuals and organisations, nearly two-thirds opposed the proposal.

Critics argued that making English an official language would be an unnecessary use of resources, create unnecessary social division, and undermine the legal protections afforded to the country's two existing official languages by weakening legislation that safeguards their use, including in legal proceedings.

US president Donald Trump has said the US is "low-keying it" with Iran as talks to end their war and reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz appeared to have stalled.

"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he told Axios.Iran has set out a series of demands that it says the US must meet before it will sign off on a deal with Oman to partially open up the Strait, including the payment of compensation for war damages.

The head of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, said the Strait will remain shut until the US meet six conditions, including ending the war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq forever.

It comes as the US is pushing for defence companies to “dramatically” accelerate weapons production as the Iran war drains through their missile supplies.

Deputy defence secretary Steve Feinberg gave companies three weeks to lay out how they would “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.”

“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Mr Feinberg added in a memo obtained by The Washington Post.

“We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”
