World.title: Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first
World.content:
Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first

toggle caption Alex Brandon/AP

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected President Trump's 15-point peace plan for Gaza, saying Israeli forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely disarmed."

"We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," he said at a meeting with government ministers Sunday.

Netanyahu's comments come just over a week after President Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached a deal with the Palestinian militant group to completely give up its weapons.

"Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza. This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY," Trump wrote on social media in late July.

Sponsor Message

Under Trump's proposed peace deal, Board of Peace officials said Hamas and other militant groups would hand their arms over to a vetted international policing force.

But a senior Hamas official previously told NPR that the group would only hand over their weapons if Israel withdrew from parts of Gaza first.

The latest dispute follows an initial ceasefire reached between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, alongside Trump's broader 20-point Gaza plan.

That first phase of the peace plan halted major fighting, provided for the release of remaining hostages in exchange for some 2,000 Palestinian prisoners, increased humanitarian aid, and called for a partial Israeli withdrawal. More contentious issues – including Hamas's disarmament and further Israeli withdrawals – were left to later negotiations.

Trump's new 15-point roadmap, published on July 31, sought to move those unresolved issues forward. It envisioned Israel's withdrawal from Gaza and Hamas's disarmament as part of a phased process, rather than requiring Hamas to fully disarm before Israeli forces began pulling back.

The Board of Peace had already backed Netanyahu on that key point, saying on Aug. 3 that Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the Yellow Line until Hamas's weapons were fully decommissioned. Netanyahu's decision to emphasize his demand again comes less than three months before Israel's Oct. 27 election, with polls showing his coalition is at risk of losing its majority.

Sponsor Message

The apparent stalemate comes as Israel still controls roughly 70% of Gaza, according to Palestinian officials and aid agencies.

Hamas released a press statement Sunday saying it was still committed "to the roadmap agreed upon" in the agreement.

NPR's Anas Baba contributed to this report from Gaza.

World.title: Haunted by Hoover, Trump searches for an endgame in Iran
World.content:
Haunted by Hoover, Trump searches for an endgame in Iran

toggle caption KENT NISHIMURA/AFP via Getty Images

President Trump is confronting a question that has haunted presidents throughout history: how a war — one that has gone on longer than predicted — can reshape a presidency.

Behind the scenes and in public remarks, Trump has acknowledged seeking an agreement to end the Iran war in hopes of escaping comparisons to former President Herbert Hoover, the Republican whose name became synonymous with economic collapse after the Great Depression.

"I've studied presidents, some good, some bad, some great," he said at the June G7 summit in France. "Not too many are great and some really bad. We had one just recently. The one president I did not want to be was the late, great Herbert Hoover. I didn't want that and who knows what would have happened. But bad things happen."

Sponsor Message

Those remarks were more than an offhand remark. They reveal his sensibilities of what it means to be a good president and how he hopes to be remembered by history. It's recognition that he may be judged not only by what happens on the battlefield, but by the impacts on inflation, gas prices and voters' lives at home.

Historic parallels

Trump, born in 1946, grew up during a time when Hoover served as a cautionary example of what not to do during difficult economic times.

Hoover stuck to his Republican principles that the government shouldn't meddle in the economy — a decision many saw as one of the worst political mistakes of the 20th century.

"Trump often reveals what he's thinking with these comments he makes," said Tevi Troy, a presidential historian and former White House aide to George W. Bush. "They sound like asides, but I think they're indicative of his upbringing. He grew up in a period where Herbert Hoover was a very negative thing to be."

Trump is not the only Republican to face those fears.

During the financial crisis of 2008, President George W. Bush raised his own concerns in an Oval Office meeting congressional leaders urging them to approve his plan to stabilize the financial markets. Bush argued that it was better to take action — or risk being compared to Herbert Hoover.

Sponsor Message

"We're going to act. I'm not going to be Herbert Hoover," Bush told the leaders, presidential historian Russell Riley wrote in his book Inside the George W. Bush White House: An Oral History.

Ronald Reagan also faced Hoover comparisons during the recession of 1981 and 1982, but escaped the association when the economy rebounded.

"Any Republican president who gets hit with bad economic times faces the danger of being tagged as Herbert Hoover," Troy said. "You don't really hear people saying Jimmy Carter was Herbert Hoover. It's constantly something that happens to Republican presidents."

Urgent concerns

For Trump, that concern is more urgent as the war takes its toll on energy and inflation.

The risks of recession are higher today than they were prior to the war, but they're also not off the charts, according to Diane Swonk, chief economist at the accounting firm KPMG. But she said the risks get higher the longer that inflation persists and the Fed leaves it unaddressed, noting that inflation has persisted for five years.

Still, she cautioned against treating today's economy as a replay of Hoover's experience — noting the economy was much different then and there are much better tools today to prevent such a catastrophe.

"It's hard to get back to a Hoover-type situation where there are all these Hoovervilles," she said. "There were so many policy mistakes made back then that caused that situation and how it played out."

But the president has long understood that his political success may be defined by the performance of the economy – and he knows that a prolonged war can often reshape a presidency in unexpected ways.

World.title: There's a birth control backlash online. Can it explain the rise in abortions?
World.content:
There's a birth control backlash online. Can it explain the rise in abortions?

toggle caption Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

Right after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, there were many stories about how new state abortion bans were influencing people's birth control decisions, especially by prompting people to use long-acting or permanent options.

Research shows that it wasn't just anecdotal, the trend was real — more people got intrauterine devices and implants for birth control, and procedures like vasectomies and tubal ligation spiked.

Sponsor Message

These days, though, Dr. Caitlin Bernard, an OB-GYN in Indianapolis who helps lead a statewide free birth control program, says her patients aren't talking much about the abortion ban that's been in place in the state for years.

"This is just the normal status quo now," says Bernard, who was involved in a high-profile abortion case soon after Roe was overturned. "Other things that help you decide whether or not to use contraception are more top of mind."

Bernard says patients are questioning things like whether they would rather take a pill or have an IUD, and whether their insurance would cover both options. She also sees patients worried about finances in general and trying to avoid going to the doctor to steer clear of unexpected medical bills.

Contraception "maligned"

Bernard says there is one thing that is affecting her patient's decision-making more nowadays: Social media, and the rise of "Make America Healthy Again" and "trad wife" influencers. Both deliver messages about hormonal birth control being bad for women.

These types of videos are all over social media. While research shows that hormonal birth control options are safe and that they're effective at preventing pregnancy, many of these videos exaggerate potential side effects and minimize the downsides of non-hormonal birth control options. Most are posted by people who aren't medical professionals.

"There is definitely a social media phenomenon of wellness influencers with non-evidence-based personal experiences that are just ricocheting through the stratosphere," says Cynthia Harper, a contraception researcher at the University of California San Francisco. "That's overlapping with ideology and policy that women are supposed to be at home having a lot of babies, young," she says, referring to the pronatalist movement.

Sponsor Message

"These two things have come together and contraception has never been so maligned," she says.

Harper adds that there are also political forces working against birth control access. The Trump administration has cut fundingfor reproductive health providers across the country, and for the health system more broadly. Harper says those things have an impact. "Everything I see points to lower access to contraception," she says.

A twist after abortion bans: More abortions

Surprisingly, the number of abortions has actually gone up in the last few years as states have enacted bans.

Could it be that the cultural push against birth control is leading to more unplanned or unwanted pregnancies and therefore more abortions?

Harper thinks it's an intriguing hypothesis. To test if out, you'd have to do a study to survey people accessing abortion, she says, "and ask if it was the restricted access to contraception that was the reason for the pregnancy that they're seeking abortion care for."

Brittni Frederiksen, a women's health police researcher at the nonpartisan organization KFF, does not think that shifts in birth control use explains recent abortion numbers. "I actually think the number of abortions going up is likely just due to increased abortion accessibility, particularly with telehealth medication abortions," she says.

In telehealth medication abortion, patients are able to get abortion pills from a pharmacy or in the mail after a telehealth visit. It has grown dramatically in popularity since becoming available during the COVID-19 pandemic. Right now, a high-profile legal case from Louisiana aims to remove that option for patients all over the country.

As for the effect abortion bans have had on birth control? Frederiksen points to the women's health survey KFF conducts every two years that asks about birth control use.

"In 2024, 82% of sexually active reproductive age women were using contraception. 6% were not using contraception," she says. The rest were pregnant, trying to get pregnant or unable to conceive.

Sponsor Message

KFF just fielded the survey again this year. "I have given a brief look at the 2026 data, and it looks like the shares using contraception are pretty similar," she says.

Frederiksen says cultural attitudes towards birth control and political forces are changing, and funding cuts that affect access are happening, though perhaps in ways that aren't visible in the data yet.

World.title: This rising painter reimagines Renaissance art in a cocoa plantation in Cameroon
World.content:
This rising painter reimagines Renaissance art in a cocoa plantation in Cameroon

toggle caption Copyright The Artist/Courtesy Larkin Durey

Cameroonian painter Marc Padeu says that being an African artist means "being the heir to an extraordinarily rich history." But he also says it can mean "living and working on a continent where artistic infrastructure is virtually nonexistent."

Padeu's work often takes inspiration from religious paintings from the European Renaissance — but reimagines them, depicting people in Cameroon's cocoa plantations. London gallery Larkin Durey is currently holding an exhibition of Padeu's latest work.

toggle caption Courtesy of Larkin Durey

Oliver Durey, the gallery's director, said: "Mark's work is timeless. His visual style is simultaneously very contemporary but also deeply rooted in that old tradition — so there is something extremely fresh about it."

Padeu is from Bafang in the West Region of Cameroon and is part of the Bamileké ethnic group. The 36-year-old now lives in Yaoundé, the country's political capital. In an interview with NPR, Padeu explained his art — and what inspires him.

Can you talk about why you meld classic Western paintings with African scenes?

I wouldn't say that I'm trying to fuse Western painting with African scenes. For me, it's more a question of placing images that everyone recognizes within a setting that is familiar to me. I grew up in Cameroon, surrounded by plantations, villages and people who make their living from the land. That's the world I know best, so it's only natural that this is the setting in which I want to tell these stories.

Sponsor Message

At one point, I asked myself why certain images seemed to belong exclusively to Europe. Why should the Nativity, the Last Supper or Christ in Gethsemane always be depicted with the same faces and the same landscapes? Yet what they convey goes far beyond any particular place or era. They speak of love, sacrifice, fear, hope, family. These are profoundly human, universal experiences.

How did you become an artist?

It's certainly down to genetics, first and foremost. My mother is a fashion designer. She doesn't work much any more, but when I was younger, I used to see her fashion sketchbooks. So I inherited this talent from my mother. I was already drawing a lot at primary school and then at secondary school. I was the one who often helped teachers draw their demonstration sketches on the blackboard in front of my classmates. This often earned me a certain reputation at the various schools I attended.

Later on, I went on to study at the school of fine arts. I must say the timing was perfect in that respect. The very year I passed my A-levels, the Cameroonian government opened the country's very first art schools. So I'm part of the very first ever intake of graduates from that school. It was a very traditional course, based mainly on the study of art history.

toggle caption Private Collection, USA/Image copyright of the artist, courtesy of Larkin Durey

Is there one artist who inspired you most?

The African American painter Kerry James Marshall. Marshall was a significant discovery for me, not because I wanted to paint like him, but because he showed me that it was possible to reestablish Black bodies at the heart of the great tradition of painting. He never merely added Black figures to an art history that had already been written; he demonstrated that they were an integral part of it.

Sponsor Message

I do think, however, that our approaches subsequently take different directions. He is very interested in the social and political history of African American communities. My work is more permeated by philosophical and spiritual questions. I explore the major themes of existence: birth, sacrifice, death, hope, promise by embodying them in scenes from everyday life in Cameroon.

Is it right that you used to be a fresco painter in a church?

That's right. I created a few murals in the churches of Nkongsamba, where I was studying at the school of fine arts. At first, it was just a part-time job to earn a bit of money. But the murals were so successful that I was very quickly inundated with commissions, mainly of religious murals. The churches commissioned me to paint scenes inspired by the Bible: episodes from the life of Christ, the Virgin Mary, the various apostles, angels and certain saints.

One evening, whilst I was still painting on the scaffolding inside the town's grand cathedral, a few women from a prayer group entered the church and prostrated themselves before the still-unfinished mural. It gave me a very strange feeling. But above all, it was at that moment that I realized the power that images and representations can have.

toggle caption Private Collection, USA/Image copyright of the artist, courtesy of Larkin Durey

I have read that you take inspiration from religious paintings from Europe, especially from the Renaissance era.

Through constantly depicting these religious images, I began to take a deeper interest in them. I remember one in particular: The Coronation of the Virgin by Diego Velázquez. This painting, which I consider a masterpiece of composition, fascinated me to such an extent that I created my own reinterpretation, which I would call The Blue Virgin. The same is true of Caravaggio's The Incredulity of Saint Thomas, which I reinterpreted as The Blue Man of Njombé.

Sponsor Message

Can you tell us a bit more about The Blue Virgin — with its depiction of a woman whose skin and clothing is blue?

The Blue Virgin is one of the first works in which I sought to create a dialogue between Christian iconography and my own visual world. I depict a young African woman striking the serene, frontal pose of Renaissance Madonnas. Inspired by Diego Velázquez's The Coronation of the Virgin, this is not a Virgin in the religious or devotional sense. Rather, she is a symbolic figure. She embodies motherhood, promise and a form of silent presence. By giving her the features of a young Cameroonian woman, I wanted to show that these foundational figures of art history can be reinvented through other faces, other stories and other places.

The luminous skull resting on the figure's lap is undoubtedly the most important element in the painting. It refers to the memento mori [Latin for "remember you must die"] tradition, which features prominently in Western painting. In Christian iconography, the Virgin is often associated with the promise of life; here, that promise is set against the awareness of death. The color blue was not chosen here solely because it is traditionally the color of the Virgin Mary. It creates a sense of distance from reality. It distances the figure from the portrait, bringing it closer to the symbolic.

Can you explain how religion influences your work? Are you religious yourself?

My relationship with religion did not begin with the frescoes in churches. For as long as I can remember, my family has always been very religious. My mother is without a doubt the most devout person I know on this earth. This was already the case with my grandparents before her. My grandfather was a catechist [a teacher in the church]. However, I grew up caught between two spiritual traditions. My mother's family are very devout Catholics. My father's family, on the other hand, are not at all. They are animists [people who believe that animals, plants and various objects possess a spiritual essence] deeply rooted in the Bamiléké spiritual tradition. My father was, in fact, a member of a council that assists the village chief in making decisions for the community. So I have always navigated between these two spiritual traditions, as have most other Africans, for that matter.

Sponsor Message

How did you get the idea of putting classical figures in a clearly African setting — and not a glamorous setting but a setting of people who farm for a living, which is hard work?

My aim here is not to rewrite the history of painting. Over the years I have spent studying classical painting, I very quickly realized that the major themes it explores — namely birth, death, sacrifice, promise, hope and so on — are by no means exclusively European. They are quite simply human and can therefore be embodied by Africans, and of course by Cameroonians.

Having grown up in an environment where working the land plays a central role, it therefore seemed entirely natural to me to place at the heart of my work these men, women and children whom I know well, and with whom I once shared the grueling daily life of the plantation. The idea is to portray them with the same nobility and dignity as the figures of the great masters. So, indirectly, it is my own story that I am telling. It is myself that I am painting.

toggle caption Image copyright of the artist, courtesy of Larkin Durey

Your paintings feel very alive, like the people in them might move at any moment. Do you work from photographs or real life models?

My way of working is rather unusual — it's very personal. In fact, a painting can take several months, or even much longer, to take shape in my mind before I even begin to paint. I live with that image for a while. I think about it constantly, I transform it in my mind, I imagine different compositions until everything starts to fall into place.

Once this vision becomes clearer, I look for people who can bring it to life. Sometimes these are close friends or family members, sometimes acquaintances and sometimes people I meet over time. I don't work with professional models. I organize photo shoots, but I don't necessarily ask them to strike a specific pose. Although nothing is left to chance, I prefer to suggest a situation or an emotion and let them express themselves naturally in front of the camera.

Sponsor Message

These photographs form my raw material. I sometimes take dozens, or even more, for a single painting. The figures are often photographed separately, at different times, sometimes several months apart. Then, in my studio, I reconstruct the scene entirely from scratch. I reposition the bodies, alter the gazes, the lighting, the colors and the proportions. A final composition may thus bring together references taken at moments far apart in time.

I like to let an image mature for a long time before bringing it to life on the canvas. It is often in this waiting that the work finds its true purpose.

What does it mean to be a Cameroonian artist — an African artist — in 2026?

That's an excellent question. Being a Cameroonian or African artist in 2026 means, first and foremost, living and working on a continent where artistic infrastructure is virtually non-existent. We're talking here about sub-Saharan Africa. This means that recognition very often comes from outside the continent. We find ourselves in a kind of paradox: We're more visible in London, Berlin, Paris or New York than in Douala, Abidjan or Lagos. As African and Cameroonian artists, our careers therefore depend on an international ecosystem whose rules and contours we don't always fully understand.

However, being an African artist, a Cameroonian artist, also means being the heir to an extraordinarily rich history. We come from great kingdoms, often with recognized artistic traditions. Kingdoms that have weathered major historical and painful events, namely: the various slave trades, colonization, the struggles for independence, the diversity of languages and the coexistence of ancestral practices with monotheistic religions imported from the West. All this heritage that already exists within us is very often reflected in the works we create.

However, we do not remain prisoners of this history. We do not paint to represent Africa or Cameroon to the world but to reveal the world from the perspective of Cameroon, of Africa.

toggle caption Copyright The Artist/Courtesy Larkin Durey

What advice do you have for other aspiring African artists?

First and foremost, I would tell them not to try to be "African artists" but simply to become artists. Much like a politician, one's ethnic or geographical background cannot be a political platform. One's background is therefore merely a starting point for a broader openness to the world.

Sponsor Message

I would encourage them to broaden their horizons further. To study their personal history and their origins in depth. To learn about the history of art and to take a serious interest in philosophy.

I'd also tell them not to be afraid of time. These days, everything pushes us to produce quickly, to be visible straight away. Personally, I don't produce more than ten paintings a year, sometimes even fewer than seven. That suits me just fine. I'm constantly quite aware that I'll be doing this all my life, so that drives me to find a creative rhythm that I can easily sustain, given the high standards it demands over the very long term.

Finally, I'd remind them that art isn't just a profession, but a way of being, of existing in the world.

Are you ever asked if you are just imitating the great masters? Or trivializing these images by putting them in a cocoa plantation?

To be honest, I have never asked myself the question in those terms. All artists draw inspiration from those who came before them. Manet drew inspiration from Titian, Picasso from Velázquez and so did Francis Bacon. For my part, I enter into a dialogue with these images because they form part of our shared heritage. I do not seek to copy them but to extend them through my own perspective.

As for the idea that I might trivialize these works by transposing them into a cocoa plantation, I actually believe quite the opposite. Biblical stories feature ordinary people: fishermen, shepherds, craftsmen. They do not take place in extraordinary settings but at the heart of everyday life. Ultimately, what could be more natural than to bring them back to life today amongst the men and women who work the land? For me, there is something profoundly noble in these ordinary gestures.

toggle caption Copyright The Artist/Courtesy Larkin Durey

In a world where prejudice sadly still flourishes, have you run into discrimination?

In all honesty, I don't recall ever having personally been the victim of any form of discrimination. Perhaps I haven't been paying close enough attention to have noticed it? Or perhaps philosophy really does help me a great deal in this regard. However, I think it would be very naïve to say that prejudice does not exist in the art world. It can be present there just as it is in other areas of life. However, it is essential not to build one's career around it. If one makes prejudice the main subject of one's work or narrative, one gives it a prominence it does not deserve.

Sponsor Message

I therefore believe that the best response to discrimination is not to confront it head-on or to deny it but rather to produce works that defy all the categories into which people might seek to pigeonhole them.

What is your dream for your work, and what would you like people to think when they see it?

My professional dream hasn't changed much since the days when I used to paint murals in churches. I simply hope that my work reaches as many people as possible around the world.

You know, the world is in a really difficult state. With all these conflicts and natural disasters, as an artist, I feel a humble duty to do my bit for a happier world. George Bernard Shaw said: "Without art, the brutality of reality would make the world unbearable."

Marc Padeu: Memento Vivere is on view at the Larkin Durey gallery in London until August 14. The gallery regularly exhibits Padeu's work.

World.title: Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Aramco oil facility in Saudi Arabia, and other Middle East news
World.content:
Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Aramco oil facility in Saudi Arabia, and other Middle East news

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

Yemen's Houthis said they attacked an oil facility Sunday in southwestern Saudi Arabia, the latest attack by the Iranian-backed rebels on the kingdom.

Meanwhile, Iran has made new demands about the restart of negotiations and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Pentagon is pressing the U.S. defense industry to accelerate production of weapons.

Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the Houthis, said they targeted an Aramco refinery in the city of Jazan with a drone. The attack was in response to Saudi drones' breaching Yemen's airspace over the provinces of Hajjah and Saada, he said.

Sponsor Message

Early on Sunday, the Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery without casualties. The ministry said the fire was extinguished but it didn't describe its cause.

Sunday's Houthi attack is the latest in a series of missile and drone attacks that targeted Saudi Arabia and its shipping in the Red Sea.

A Yemeni government official said Sunday that the Houthis also attacked a crucial port on the Red Sea.

Fayed al-Noman, assistant undersecretary of the information ministry, said the Houthis fired missiles and drones on the Mocha port. It's one of the main ports under Yemen's internationally recognized government, renovated in recent years to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held ports in Hodeida.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

The escalation threatens to reignite Yemen's civil war more than four years after a 2022 truce stopped major fighting in the impoverished Arab country.

Iran: Negotiations with US "cannot resume" until conditions met

Speaking to reporters in Tehran on Sunday, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said an "exchange of messages through intermediaries" is continuing with the United States, but that doesn't constitute negotiations.

"From our perspective, negotiations cannot resume until the violations of the memorandum of understanding have ended and the United States has remedied the provisions of the memorandum that it violated," he said.

Sponsor Message

He added that negotiations with Oman about "new maritime routes" through the Strait of Hormuz were "in the final stages."

"This, however, does not mean that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen," Araghchi said. "An agreement on the routes may be reached, but reopening the strait is subject to a number of other conditions, which have been conveyed through intermediaries."

Iran says the strait won't open until the US 'corrects' its behavior

Similarly, Iran's powerful Supreme National Security Council has said the Strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States "corrects its behavior," issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway.

Iran's state broadcaster published the statement by the council's secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard.

toggle caption Pléiades © CNES 2026, Distribu/AP

The United States must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The U.S. must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It must "completely compensate" Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and "unconditionally" release frozen assets.

The U.S., which has wanted an acceptable deal first on the strait before ending the blockade, had no immediate comment. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and plan on compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.

According to the U.S. Central Command, the blockade has redirected 53 commercial vessels, disabled two, and boarded two through Saturday.

Pentagon pushes boost in weapons production

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement Saturday that the department was actively focused on boosting munitions acquisitions to provide "the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands."

Sponsor Message

The war with Iran has used up more of the U.S. military's already diminished stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors, says a new analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington think tank.

Parnell said the push for speedier delivery was part of a broader modernization effort that predated the five-month-old conflict.

Details emerge about potential Iran-Oman deal

The Strait of Hormuz, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, was considered an international waterway before the war.

But Iran and Oman are working to finalize a temporary deal that would reopen the strait with ships entering the strait through a route close to Iran and exiting through a route close to Oman, according to two people familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Ships would cross the strait without paying fees or tolls during the interim period.

The agreement is designed to restore an earlier, separate agreement between the U.S. and Iran and restart a 60-day clock for the two countries to negotiate over Iran's nuclear program.

According to the two people who spoke about the talks, the deal is endorsed by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council and expected when finalized to be jointly announced by Iran, Oman, the U.S., and the International Maritime Organization of the United Nations. But the people stressed the terms could still change before the deal is final.

World.title: 80-year-old woman killed in Summerland, B.C., wildfire: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

RCMP have confirmed a fatality in the explosive wildfire that forced mass evacuations from Summerland, B.C., over the weekend.

The Bald Range wildfire broke out shortly after 5 p.m. PT on Friday about 15 kilometres from the city, and grew rapidly, forcing tactical evacuations — some involving firefighting helicopters.

Penticton RCMP said Sunday it had confirmed at least one person died as a result of the fire.

Police said an 80-year-old woman "died suddenly" while trying to flee the fire with her family.

"Police believe her death to be a result of the wildfire," the RCMP said.

WATCH | RCMP confirms fatality in wildfire near Summerland: B.C. wildfires: Thousands flee Summerland, RCMP confirms death of 80-year-old | Duration 6:42 British Columbia's unprecedented wildfire emergency has forced thousands to flee from the community of Summerland and some surrounding areas. The RCMP also confirmed the death of an 80-year-old woman who was trying to flee on Friday.

Police said the B.C. Coroners Service was investigating, and that there were no other known fatalities related to the fire.

As of Sunday, the fire had grown to 136 square kilometers in size. About 12,000 residents, along with people in surrounding areas including southern Peachland remain under evacuation orders.

The remainder of Peachland and areas south of Summerland and west of Penticton are on evacuation alerts. The Penticton Indian Band has also declared a state of emergency.

Smoke from the fire has led to multiple flight cancellations at the Kelowna airport.

Interior Health said it helped transport more than 200 residents out of Summerland and into safe locations, and has set up a hotline for families looking to reunite with loved ones.

Downtown Summerland spared

A city official said Sunday that Summerland's downtown has survived the fire intact.

"I was in downtown Summerland myself yesterday as late as 2 a.m. [PT] and everything is fine," Summerland Chief Administrative Officer Graham Statt told a Regional District of Okangan-Similkameen livestream on Sunday.

"There is active fires around the community still that are being dealt with and there are some hotspots and stuff ... but downtown Summerland hasn’t been destroyed, anything like that.”

Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes, however, said there were losses in the area.

"We know structures have been lost. We don’t know how many," Holmes said.

A look at the Bald Range fire burning between Summerland and Peachland as seen from Naramata, B.C., on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Holmes added there was no timeline for residents to return, adding that power lines are down and water supplies are likely contaminated.

"Until we know all of that infrastructure is safe, we can’t really let people back," he said.

"We will be leaning on the province for support to make sure that everything is safe for people to get back and return to their homes," he said.

Statt said planning is underway for a phased re-entry.

Some groups, like those who work with livestock, have been allowed temporary access to care for animals, he said.

Heavy smoke from the Bald Range wildfire near Okanagan Lake is blanketing Penticton, B.C., on Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

'Gut wrenching'

Leah Gibbs, who lives at the base of Bald Range above Summerland, said she knew it was time to evacuate when she saw a helicopter refill water from her family's property.

"When we drove out, we could see the horses running around into the flames and into the smoke," she said.

"It was gut wrenching," she added. "Not knowing whether they would live or die and not knowing if you would have a house to go home to."

Evacuees from the Bald Range fire are pictured at the evacuation centre in Penticton, B.C., on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Many residents are now sheltering in Penticton, which has set up a resource hub for evacuees. Due to limited accommodations, evacuees are being urged to stay with friends or family if possible.

Not everyone wanted to flee.

Jim Ure has been a Summerland resident for the past 34 years.

"[I] don’t want to see it go away. Hence I might stay," he explained. "My wife said she wants to go."

Provincial and local emergency officials have urged everyone to obey evacuation orders, and say defying them puts lives at risk.

Firefight far from over

Much of the province's southern Interior is currently listed at the federal government 's highest level of drought intensity.

"It is very drought driven. There’s a lot of drought in the Okanagan right now," said Nicole Bonnett, BCWS incident commander on the Bald Range fire.

Bonnett said overnight relief wasn’t as strong as anticipated due to a lack of moisture. The service said in its Sunday update that if skies clear, "fire behaviour will increase significantly" due to increasing winds throughout the day.

The wildfire service said its focus on Sunday was limiting fire growth in the drainage between Fish Lake and Garnet Valley, and that fire growth to the south remains a concern.

Across B.C., there are roughly 13,200 properties on evacuation order and another 5,800 under evacuation alert – affecting approximately 21,700 and 10,600 people respectively.

World.title: RCMP investigating homicide of 12-year-old Edmonton boy after remains found in northern Alberta
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

RCMP say they are investigating the homicide of a 12-year-old Edmonton boy after remains were found in a rural area of northern Alberta.

In a news release on Sunday, police said Athabasca RCMP officers responded to a report of human remains found on Thursday, Aug. 6, just before 3:30 a.m.

Police said an autopsy was completed on Friday at the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Edmonton, and the boy’s manner of death was deemed a homicide.

RCMP Cpl. Gina Slaney told CBC News in an interview that the boy had not been reported missing to police prior to Thursday, and his family has been notified of his death.

Police said investigators are seeking the public’s assistance with the case.

“If you were around Highway 813 near Calling Lake or Range Road 213A (referred to as the ‘C-Road’), on Aug. 6, 2026, between 12 a.m. and 4:30 a.m., and have dash cam video, please contact Athabasca RCMP,” the news release said.

Calling Lake is located more than 200 kilometres north of Edmonton.

The RCMP Major Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.

World.title: 'No more caving': Poilievre's letter to Carney urges him not to concede to U.S. tariff demands
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up with the United States.

In a letter to Carney that was shared with reporters, Poilievre and his Canada-U.S. relations critic, Shuvaloy Majumdar, said Ottawa has given in to several of Trump's demands in the last year.

The pair cited scrapping the digital service tax, removing Canada's counter-tariffs and cutting the United States into a deal to share net toll revenue from the recently opened Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich.

Poilievre and Majumdar argued against Carney's previous claim that no deal is better than a bad deal by pointing to job losses in manufacturing-heavy Canadian cities that rely on cross-border supply chains.

"For the past year and a half, you have backed down to one American demand after another while getting nothing in return, with concession after concession," Poilievre tells Carney in the letter.

WATCH | Canada weighs ending U.S. booze bans for tariff relief. Not so fast, say provinces: Canada weighs ending U.S. booze bans for tariff relief. Not so fast, say provinces | Duration 4:11 Canada could be willing to end provincial bans on U.S. liquor and make concessions on dairy products in exchange for relief from U.S. tariffs, sources tell CBC News, but provinces are already pushing back.

"Worse, you have lost ground with American tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum doubling and broadening and tariffs on lumber tripling."

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving."

A new round of 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on a range of Canadian goods is set to take effect on Aug. 19. Trade talks between the nations have intensified ahead of that deadline.

The Conservatives reiterated their call to strengthen Canada's negotiating position with the creation of a strategic reserve of critical minerals, which would be open to countries that provide tariff-free access to their own markets.

Canada and Mexico both indicated last month that they want to see the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) extended for another 16-year term. The United States instead opted to let the agreement move to rolling annual reviews.

Dairy farmers urge PM against making concessions

The U.S. has cited the supply management system that protects Canadian dairy as a key trade irritant, and Trump has repeatedly complained about the level of U.S. dairy farmers' access to Canada's market.

Carney said Thursday his government is loyal to the supply management system as the group Dairy Farmers of Canada urged the government not to offer concessions regarding its industry in trade talks.

The dairy group has also said Canada has already made several concessions, only to be met each time with fresh demands.

WATCH | U.S. senator says there's 'momentum' toward trade deal after LeBlanc meeting: U.S. senator says there's 'momentum' toward trade deal after LeBlanc meeting | Duration 10:57 North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer says 'this is the moment' to get a Canada-U.S. trade deal. Plus, Power & Politics guest host Katie Simpson asks Cramer what wildfire smoke 'punishment' Canada can expect from U.S. President Donald Trump.

According to industry sources who spoke to CBC News, the Canadian government is preparing to meet some U.S. demands — including ending bans on American alcohol sales — in exchange for tariff relief.

In addition to ending the booze bans, the Canadian side is considering lifting retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and making some changes on dairy, the sources said. They didn't say what changes were on the table in regards to the dairy sector.

In exchange, Canada is pushing for the U.S. to drop the new 50 per cent tariffs, as well as relief from the sectoral tariffs on industries such as steel and aluminum, and a joint announcement that talks on the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) will resume in the fall.

World.title: 3-year-old girl hospitalized after Maple Ridge, B.C., bear attack
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A bear attack in Maple Ridge, B.C., on Sunday has left a three-year-old girl in hospital.

Maple Ridge RCMP said the attack happened around 11:30 a.m. PT, outside the girl's home on 240 Street near 124 Avenue.

According to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service, the girl was playing on the deck in her family's back yard when the attack happened.

A parent intervened and chased the bear away, it added.

The RCMP said in a statement the girl was taken to hospital via air ambulance " out of an abundance of caution due to her age."

"She is currently in hospital with non-life-altering injuries."

RCMP at the scene of a bear attack in Maple Ridge on Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026. (Shane MacKichan)

Police said the bear showed a "high degree of interest" in the area, returning several times while officers were on site.

Around noon, officers encountered the bear and shot it, "to protect public safety," as "the bear had showed signs of aggression and already attacked a small child," the RCMP said.

The bear was hit, and fled into a wooded area, police said.

A B.C. Conservation Officer Service predator attack team has taken over efforts to track the bear.

People in the surrounding area are being advised to stay alert and stay indoors.

Anyone who sees the bear is asked to contact the B.C. Conservation Officer Service at 1-877-952-7277 .

World.title: N.L. has a hard bread shortage — but why do we eat it in the first place?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Grocery stores across Newfoundland and Labrador have been struggling to keep hard bread in stock since a fire at the Purity factory in March put a crimp in the company’s baking operations.

Purity is the province’s primary provider of hard bread, also called hard tack, ship’s biscuit, and sea biscuit — a dry, unleavened bread made of flour, water and salt.

But why is the jaw-breaking baked good so popular here?

Dehydrated bread has been a mainstay of the traveller’s diet since ancient times. Because it’s long lasting and easy to carry, military leaders issued it to soldiers on campaign when they couldn’t count on being able to access enough local provisions to feed an army.

Roman legionaries received bucellatum , a twice-baked bread, among their field rations. King Richard the Lionheart loaded his ships with “ biskit ” when he left for the Crusades in 1190.

The non-perishable fare was also a useful provision for sailors, who could spend weeks or months at sea and often needed enough supplies to see them not only to their destination but home again afterward.

Basque seasonal fishermen brought hard bread to the coasts of Newfoundland and Labrador in the 1500s.

Between the sail out, the fishing season, and the journey home, they could be away for six months at a stretch, and they packed enough for nine months in case their ships became locked in ice and they were stranded for the winter.

When the British visited the region, they stocked up on hard bread, too.

In 1620, Richard Whitbourne, an English mariner who briefly served as governor of Renews, published a record of all the supplies he had brought with him on a trip to the colony of Newfoundland from Great Britain.

At the top of the list is “eleven thousand [weight] of Bisket bread,” the equivalent of nearly 5,600 kilograms, and enough to feed 40 people for 12 months.

After European settlement, fishing families baked their own “soft” bread at home, but they continued to rely on hard bread when they were out at sea, berry picking or hunting.

Proper hard bread couldn’t be home baked. It was made from a special winter wheat flour and slowly dried in a kiln or an evaporation loft to remove all its moisture, giving it its longevity.

Like most other food that couldn’t be caught locally or grown in a kitchen garden, hard bread had to be imported. By the 1770s, Newfoundland was dependent on the American colonies not only for hard bread but for flour and livestock, as well as rum, sugar and molasses shipped up from the West Indies.

In 1775, as tensions escalated between the British Crown and its American colonists after the Boston Tea Party, the House of Commons passed an act to restrict trade out of Massachusetts .

The American reaction was unexpected: the colonies closed ranks and retaliated. New York, Philadelphia and most other major ports cut off all trade to Newfoundland.

It was a strategic move intended to strike at the heart of the European food fishery. Without American supplies to keep them going, Newfoundland settlers wouldn’t be able to fish and the British would lose a key food source.

The ban couldn’t have come at a worse time. It was spring, and Newfoundlanders had exhausted their provisions over the winter.

There was panic. People hoarded wheat, and the price of goods skyrocketed.

Near the end of the American Civil War, artist Winslow Homer designed a set of collector’s cards showing an unvarnished view of life in the Union army. Here, a soldier spits out his first bite of hard tack. (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

By 1776, America was at war with Great Britain, and Newfoundland was starving.

European suppliers eventually scaled up production to meet Newfoundland’s needs, though the trade ban led to long-term inflation in the price of food. The town of Hamburg, Germany, cornered the market on hard bread, so much so that Newfoundlanders nicknamed it Hamburg bread.

Hard bread wasn’t manufactured locally until the Scottish Rennie brothers opened a flour mill and bakery in St. John’s in the 1830s — Rennie’s Mill, which gave its name to the river and the road. Their baking equipment was imported from Hamburg.

The demand for hard bread didn’t slacken. If anything, it increased.

In his travels across Newfoundland in the 1850s, Anglican bishop Edward Feild described “tea and biscuit” as “the ordinary hospitality extended to visitors.” He and his companions were so desperate for “soft” bread they provided flour to local women to bake it for them.

By the 1880s, 180,000 residents were eating 40 million hard biscuits a year , over 200 per person.

A large portion of those biscuits would have gone into the traditional dish fish and brewis. Pronounced “brews,” brewis is made by soaking hard bread in water overnight then boiling it to soften it before serving it with salt cod.

In 1885, Nova Scotia journalist George Patterson wrote that brewis “occupies almost the same place at a Newfoundlander’s breakfast-table that baked beans are supposed to do on that of a Bostonian.”

Sprinkled with molasses or scrunchions (small chunks of salted fat-back pork), fish and brewis was a hearty, high-calorie meal fishers could eat before a day at sea. Among the merchant class, it was a Sunday breakfast treat .

Joey Smallwood’s Book of Newfoundland called brewis as much the national dish of Newfoundland as roast beef is of England, spaghetti is of Italy, or rice is of China.

Purity has confirmed their bakery resumed production in July , so local shelves should soon be reloaded.

That’s good news for today’s hard bread die-hards.

World.title: As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it's Bridget. I recently went to Vancouver Community College to visit their auto shop and learn about how they’re teaching apprentices about electric vehicles. I was curious about efforts to train the next generation of automotive technicians, so I decided to dig a little deeper.

This week:

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

Vancouver Community College instructor Mike Coard stands with some of the electric vehicles used to train apprentices in the school's Automotive Service Tech Department. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

EV sales are ramping up — not just cars but also trucks and buses. Canada wants EVs to make up 75 per cent of new vehicle sales by 2035 to help meet its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 .

Electric school buses have gained traction in some parts of the country , but a new report suggests a challenge to keeping them running in the future — and it's one that could affect other EVs, too.

The report from the environmental think-tank Pollution Probe finds "key gaps" in training and certification of technicians to maintain and repair electric school buses.

Marc Saleh, Pollution Probe's director of transportation, said EVs require skills related to high-voltage safety, battery diagnostics, power electronics and charging infrastructure management that still aren't being taught in standard automotive service programs.

He and others in the auto service industry say this challenge applies not just to school buses but to all electric vehicles. There remain barriers to both training new automotive technicians and upgrading the skills of already certified Red Seal technicians.

Challenges for EV training

Saleh says technician training for EVs is primarily handled by manufacturers. But this will eventually need to change to properly support adoption, as there may soon be so many EVs that the dealerships can't service them all.

Emily Chung (no relation to the editor of this newsletter), president of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada, said what's involved in servicing an EV depends heavily on the make and model because EV technology, including high-voltage battery systems, is developing rapidly and varies more among manufacturers than the relatively standardized technology used in internal combustion engine vehicles.

Pictured are two of the training aids that VCC instructor Mike Coard uses to teach students about batteries. On the left is a Tesla battery, and on the right is a hybrid battery pack from a Toyota Prius. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

"There's no standardization, even amongst the car manufacturers, and everybody started doing their own thing and have their own flavour," she said.

This is why she says proprietary technology is also an issue, because shops and classrooms don't always have access to all of the information needed to understand each vehicle.

Many manufacturers refuse to provide that access, or they charge extremely high fees that repair shops can't afford.

There is also no universal certification for EV training courses or any requirement for ongoing training after technicians receive a Red Seal certification — Canada's national standard for skilled trades such as automotive.

Some solutions

Despite these barriers, both independent auto shops and community colleges are trying to fill the gap.

Andrew Ackers owns a NAPA AutoPro shop in Hamilton.

He has been training technicians who are already familiar with traditional, internal combustion engine vehicles through an EV training program called Next Drive started by NAPA, an automotive co-operative that distributes replacement auto parts.

The program has five levels — there will be six starting in September — and goes from basic electrical theory all the way to diagnosing problems inside battery packs.

Ackers says it’s about a $20,000 investment per technician but is worth the price — and each level can be done in a week, meaning they don’t have to leave their jobs for long to complete the training.

"A strong technician that is comfortable with electrical work could be up to speed within a week's worth of training to be able to handle about 90 per cent of the high-voltage repairs that are necessary on vehicles," he said.

Ackers said he's dedicated about 15 per cent of his business to electric vehicles.

Vancouver Community College trains students on a variety of EVs and hybrids. In the shop is a Ford Fusion, Tesla Model 3, Nissan Leaf, Volkswagen ID.4, Rivian pickup truck and a Toyota Mirai. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

Colleges are also stepping up to expand their clean energy programs and prepare technicians for the growing demand of EV repairs.

Vancouver Community College already has some training in place but is expanding the school’s offerings in September. To accommodate that, it is building a new Centre for Clean Energy that is scheduled to be completed in 2027. It will include space to train refrigeration technicians and electricians who will need to work on charging infrastructure.

Centennial College in Ontario is also expanding its offerings to help upskill existing Red Seal certified technicians and train new apprentices.

Pollution Probe's report recommends integrating electric vehicle content into trade curricula, and Michael Lomnicki, a professor in the School of Transportation and a Red Seal mechanic, said that's exactly what they’re working on at Centennial College.

"There's careers to be had, absolutely," he said. "I definitely think that it's important to invest in, so that all of our students can create value for themselves and lead this industry as technology evolves."

Chung of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada says this is a crucial component of the EV transition.

"Repairing and maintaining these cars is the most sustainable solution, right?" she said. "And so it goes hand in hand with the whole thought of being eco-friendly and moving towards clean energy."

– Bridget Stringer-Holden

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : Flood-prone communities are doing everything to keep water out. But as climate-fuelled storms become more severe, some architects say we need to work with water, not fight it. We learn how amphibious engineering kept Bangladeshi kids in school and allowed a Louisiana community to stay afloat.

LISTEN | What if your home could float when a flood hits?: What On Earth 23:10 What if your home could float when a flood hits?

What On Earth drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

(CBC)

Reader feedback

Last week, Emily Chung wrote about Canadian technology to cool subway stations , with the goal of recovering the heat in the future.

David Fujiwara wrote: "That’s great that energy efficient chilled water will be used in the East Broadway subway station, but nowhere do you tell us where that chilled water is coming from. If you are chilling the water with electric refrigeration is it so energy efficient? And if [the system] doesn’t yet have a district heat system to connect to, where is excess heat going in the interim?"

Yes, the system uses electric refrigeration. As mentioned in the article, because it is passive cooling without fans, it is expected to be 25 to 35 per cent more efficient and more compact than a traditional air conditioning system. During the pilot, the excess heat will be measured and vented above ground. But both the MTA and Cascara Energy are interested in making use of it in the future, to heat water (such as swimming pools) and buildings.

Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

(John Laytner/Civic Grid)

Stationary batteries are becoming a bigger part of our electricity system, helping support the use of clean but intermittent energy such as wind and solar . Batteries can store power when it's plentiful, feed extra power onto the grid when supplies are short and provide backup power during outages. But where should those batteries go?

Distributed energy storage firm Civic Grid argues they should be close to where people live and use the power. The photo above shows an example of its vision — a pilot project launched Wednesday in Cannington, Ont. The 60 kW battery is lit up beside the building on the right "transforming an invisible piece of electrical infrastructure into a public landmark," the company says. Its goal is to explore how energy storage can "move beyond industrial sites and become part of the communities it serves."

The battery is charged from the grid at night when power is plentiful. During the day, it can supply up to six hours of power to two buildings used by the Nourish and Develop Foundation, which provides local food and social services (on the right and at the back of the photo). It also supplies lighting to a privately owned public square on the property, including a sheltered seating area (back left).

— Emily Chung

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

The presence of cougars in a region can reduce the risk of car crashes, a new study finds. Here's how .

A U.S. company has effectively brought a geothermal well back from the dead to become one of the most productive pumped geothermal wells in the country.

Do small, individual green habits like recycling and taking transit distract people from taking bigger, more meaningful action? Or do they prime people to support or participate in larger climate initiatives? A new study may have solved this debate .

Big industrial offshore wind farms can impact wildlife such as birds that can fly into them. But researchers are finding they also provide habitat to creatures, from oyster larvae to porpoises. Atmos brings you up close to some of these wind farm dwellers .

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

Images of fireworks, seen in a screenshot from a YouTube video, were among those created by 100 drones as an alternative to fireworks in the Town of Three Rivers, P.E.I., on Aug. 1. (H3xan01c/YouTube)

The Town of Three Rivers in P.E.I. replaced fireworks with a drone light show for its summer festival this year.

The town's Montague Arts and Culture Festival on Aug. 1 featured acclaimed P.E.I. singer-songwriter Lennie Gallant, along with what the town believes to be Prince Edward Island’s first-ever drone light show instead of a traditional fireworks display.

Jonathon Gardner, events and facilities co-ordinator for the Town of Three Rivers, said the idea began with an email from P.E.I. CARES — the Companion Animal Rescue Education Society — outlining some of the downsides of fireworks.

"There were quite a few reasons why fireworks aren't great for the environment and animals and people," Gardner told Mainstreet P.E.I. host Nicola MacLeod.

"Originally, we thought it was going to be far too expensive as well.... After looking into it, it was mildly affordable and [we] thought it would be a really neat change."

The show used 100 illuminated drones to create animated images and patterns in the night sky, synchronized to music.

WATCH | A YouTube video that captured the drone show:

Gardner said there is also growing awareness of how fireworks can affect people who are sensitive to noise, including those who have post-traumatic stress disorder.

"With our first responders or military, the amount of PTSD, absolutely, that could trigger [it]," he said.

Karla Shalley, founder and president of P.E.I. CARES, said the organization sent the same email to every municipality on P.E.I., hoping to encourage communities to rethink fireworks.

"We know what a thunderstorm causes with animals. Imagine that tenfold with fireworks," she said.

The P.E.I. Humane Society has also welcomed the move.

Ashley Travis, the organization's development and communications co-ordinator, said it regularly sees the fallout from fireworks displays.

"Nearly every year when there's a community fireworks display, we will receive a call from someone who either wasn't aware that there was going to be fireworks that evening or who perhaps brought their animal to a fireworks display," she said.

"There have been incidents where animals have fled, and ... we've seen animals get seriously injured when fleeing from loud noises like fireworks."

People often forget that what feels festive to humans can be frightening for animals, Travis said.

"Your animal does not know what's going on. They don't understand what a firework is. They just hear a very loud noise, an explosion. They can see very bright lights sometimes and it can be very, very scary for them," she said.

"We always say that the best-case scenario is to leave your pet at home during a fireworks display to make sure that they're going to be safe."

Both Travis and Shalley hope other communities will now consider alternatives to fireworks.

Ahead of the show, Gardner said the reaction from the community was encouraging.

"There’s been a lot of positive feedback. Lots of people are saying, 'I want to come and check it out, and I want to see it,'" he said.

— Thinh Nguyen

World.title: When mom was diagnosed with dementia, we had a blueprint for her care written by her
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is the experience of Crystal MacCormac, who lives in Charlottetown. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

My mother walks into my apartment in P.E.I. for the first time after 11 years of living in Ontario. She smiles brightly as she hugs me and looks around.

Her eyes fall upon a photo on my wall: a picture of her at two years old, sitting in front of a birthday cake.

“Oh wow. Look, that's me!” she says, walking closer for a better look.

Fast forward a couple of days to her second visit. Mom looks around, another bright smile on her lips.

“Oh wow. Look, that’s me!”

It happens again a week later.

My spidey senses started to tingle and fear began to seep in.

“Well, that’s not a good sign,” I thought.

I paid closer attention after that — watching, listening to everything mom did and said. It was 2020, so I spent more time with her, thanks to the rules imposed by the pandemic. Mom became one of the 10 people in my social bubble during lockdown, and with so few distractions, I was able to put most of my focus into my mom and her declining mental capacity.

My younger sister, who’d lived with mom for a long time, noticed changes, too.

By 2024, mom’s memory continued to decline, as did other things.

She was 65 when she was diagnosed so if it were just the pain in her hip, the digestion issues or the decline in her eyesight, we may not have raised the alarm. But it all happened at once, forcing us to take notice.

Ultimately, mom was diagnosed with vascular dementia. The diagnosis took almost a year as her swift decline continued.

That’s when our lives took a detour onto an unexpected and bumpy road.

This photo of MacCormac’s mom, Barb, as a child served as one of the first indicators that her mom’s memory might be failing. (Submitted by Crystal MacCormac)

But luckily, we knew what to do because mom had already shown us. When her own mother — my grandmother — suffered an unrelated physical and cognitive decline, my mother and the rest of our family stepped up to care for Nanny for the following five years.

My mom moved into her parents home to help. She had an inside look at the struggles that came up during that time.

A couple years after losing Nanny, mom sat me and my two siblings down to talk to us. She told us what she wanted, who she wanted advocating for her, under what circumstances we were to transition her into a nursing home, who was to arrange her funeral and at what point to end care or sign a "do not resuscitate" order.

I’m grateful we didn’t have to make these decisions on the fly while juggling mom’s care and our own emotions. There is so much to learn and so much information coming in, but knowing our roles made the process so much easier.

But it left me wondering: how would we have survived if we hadn’t made plans in advance? I don’t know how I would have learned all the medical jargon while also trying to connect with the right people and agencies. Weaving through all the twists and turns would have taken my attention away from mom and her care.

Social services gave us terrific guidance. We also relied on P.E.I.’s home care program, which helped us obtain medical supplies and respite care, and connected us with medical professionals in the community to help mom at home when she was less mobile.

The Alzheimer’s Society was another lifeline. The counselling I got through them was geared toward my own mental health as a caregiver.

Because even with our blueprint, parenting my parent is so hard. The dynamic switch came with fear and so much sadness I sometimes felt like I was drowning.

The hardest is when what mom wants now doesn’t match what mom before the disease wanted.

When I told her she had to move into a nursing home, her reaction was heartbreaking.

Nanny lived at home until her death and I would have done the same for mom. But I knew I was doing what mom had wanted. She made it clear years earlier that under no circumstances were we to go against her wishes, but it took everything in me to follow through.

I’m grateful I had the support that allowed me to be vulnerable, to cry, to say the hard things out loud and to find the strength to do the next hard thing.

Now, I can cherish my time with mom because I’m confident in the decisions we made together as a family. We don’t have to guess what she would have wanted or argue amongst ourselves.

But it’s still hard. Mom is no longer mom. She is still here in body, but not cognizant of what is best for her. She has no control over her own life anymore except through the decisions she made earlier.

I love my mother, and all I want is for her to be happy and to know she is safe. Thanks to the blueprint, I am able to advocate for her with determination, with gusto and without guilt — knowing that I’m doing what I promised her I would do.

Are you an Islander with a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to CBC P.E.I.

World.title: First Nations chiefs in B.C. call on Carney, Smith to halt advancing West Coast pipeline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A group that represents numerous First Nations across British Columbia is calling on Ottawa and Alberta's government to halt efforts to advance the West Coast pipeline, saying expanding the oil industry will accelerate climate change and disasters.

"The destructive and disastrous consequences of expanding fossil fuel production extend far beyond any single territory," the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said in a letter addressed to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

"From catastrophic wildfires to destructive floods and rising seas, the impacts of climate change are already being felt across this country. Every new fossil fuel project deepens that crisis."

The letter came Sunday, a day after the B.C. government issued a state of emergency as more than 100 wildfires burned across the province, with one forcing nearly 25,000 people across two communities east of Vancouver to flee. Nearly half of the wildfires were burning out of control.

The Indigenous group said it is also publishing the letter on International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples on Sunday to reaffirm that it's against the pipeline because government has not consulted and co-operated in good faith with the First Nations.

WATCH | Canada, Alberta advance West Coast pipeline project: Canada and Alberta advance west coast pipeline project | Duration 2:12 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith discuss details of the proposed 1 million-barrel-a-day pipeline to B.C.

It said government has already developed the project's corridor, named prospective development partners and is publicly promoting its economic case.

"Consultation cannot be meaningful if First Nations are invited only to discuss how a predetermined project will proceed."

Karah Folk, spokesperson for Alberta's Ministry of Indigenous Relations, said in an email to CBC News that the project provides "long-term benefits" for Indigenous communities, who will be consulted as it progresses.

"Our government remains committed to ongoing dialogue with First Nations and all partners as this work continues," Folk said.

Carney and Smith's offices did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.

The roughly 1,250-kilometre West Coast pipeline would carry upwards of one million barrels of crude oil per day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a port near Delta, B.C., for shipment to international markets.

The Alberta government is listed as the pipeline project's proponent. The pipeline would be owned by Trans Mountain, the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission and Pembina Pipeline Corp.

WATCH | A closer look at the pipeline route: The crowded, muddy reality of Alberta’s new pipeline route | Duration 5:40 Alberta’s new southern pipeline would mostly mirror the existing Trans Mountain corridor until Hope, B.C., where it would split and send oil to a marine terminal at Roberts Bank, but as CBC’s Georgie Smyth explains, this ‘easier’ plan won’t be straightforward.

Ottawa took a step last week toward giving the proposed project a national interest designation under the Building Canada Act, which would allow government to fast-track the pipeline and skirt some environmental laws.

The government said it is accepting public feedback until mid-September on the designation.

Ottawa and Alberta have agreed the pipeline would be conditional on a carbon storage project called Pathways, and vice versa. Pathways, which is owned by various companies, would prevent emissions from increased oil production from entering the atmosphere, and is tied to the pipeline going ahead. It involves a pipeline network that would carry carbon emissions from several sites in northern Alberta to an underground storage hub near Cold Lake, Alta.

A think-tank called the Canadian Climate Institute said in July, however, that emissions from the increased production that a new West Coast pipeline would enable far eclipse what Pathways would prevent from entering the atmosphere.

The West Coast pipeline is among several projects that have been approved or proposed under Carney's Major Projects Office, which is headquartered in Calgary.

Ottawa has said the projects are meant to be of national interest and strengthen Canada's autonomy, provide economic benefits, advance Indigenous interests and meet Canada's climate change goals in a rapidly shifting global landscape.

The Building Canada Act outlines the projects' regulatory pathway.

The Conservatives helped the government pass the Building Canada Act more than a year ago, and the government has so far moved three projects toward the national interest designation under the act.

Those projects are the Grays Bay road and port project in Nunavut, the Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories and the Nuclear Waste Management Organization's deep geological repository in northern Ontario.

World.title: Adventures in Streaming: Is bad Stephen King still good?
World.content:
Article content

The dystopian thriller is technically a remake of a cheesy 1987 movie starring Arnold Schwarzenegger (streaming on Paramount+). Befitting the director of Shaun of the Dead and Hot Fuzz, Wright’s take on the material is more boisterously cinematic, and more hard-hitting in the satire of its premise: a tyrannical government employs a killer game show as one strategy to bread-and-circus the general population into complacency. (In an era where UFC fights are staged on the White House lawn to celebrate the president’s birthday, let’s just say it rings true.)
