World.title: Discovering Mexico: Puebla
World.content:
Listen to this article

Puebla is for you if you like: Colonial history, sweeping mountains, racing while holding tortillas

Mexico’s fourth-largest city, Puebla, has more going on beneath its colonial facades than most visitors realize. Its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, holds 2,619 monuments — more than any other city in the Americas — plus the tallest cathedral bell towers in the country. The city’s well-preserved architecture has also made it a go-to filming location, standing in for 18th- and 19th-century Mexico and Spain in productions including “Frida” and “Man on Fire.”

All of this is before you get out into the wider state, where sweeping mountain ranges, active volcanoes and enormous cacti dot the landscape. The state is one of the last stops in southern Mexico before the jungle claims the country. We’ve collected some of our best pieces from the last few years, to help you experience one of Mexico’s most genuine — and stunning — regions.

Puebla’s capital — also, conveniently, called Puebla — is filled with the sort of magic that only Mexico’s oldest cities can really offer. Many of the nation’s most definining moments and people have filled these streets (and the tunnels underneath them).

Puebla’s identity is tied up in origin stories, although some more verifiable than others. Its early name, Puebla de los Ángeles, traces to a 1531 account of a bishop’s vision guiding Spanish settlers to the site. Its signature dish, mole poblano, is said to have been improvised by nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa in 1680 when an archbishop arrived unannounced and the kitchen had little to offer but chilis, chocolate, nuts and stale bread. And on Nov. 18, 1910, the Serdán family home became the site of the first armed clash of the Mexican Revolution, two days before Francisco Madero formally launched the uprising; the bullet-scarred house is now a museum.

While its days of defining Mexico’s future are probably behind it, Puebla remains a fascinating destination for anyone who wants to understand how the modern country truly came to be.

While Oaxaca, Sonora and Yucatán often vie for the title of Mexico’s gastronomic heart, it’s really Puebla that deserves the credit for much of the nation’s great cuisine.

Puebla’s culinary reputation rests on three dishes with stories as rich as their flavors. Mole poblano, which rumour claims is a single flash of nun-driven inspiration, remains the most famous of Mexico’s 300-plus regional moles. Chiles en nogada, with its patriotic red, white and green color scheme, traces back to a 1821 feast honoring independence figure Agustín de Iturbide. Tacos árabes, born from Middle Eastern shawarma techniques brought by 1930s immigrants, is the progenitor of the iconic pastor.

The state is quite a bit more than just colonial architecture and great food, though. Just outside Tehuacán, Puebla’s second-largest city, sits a landscape that looks like it belongs on another planet.

The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere sprawls across 145,255 hectares of protected desert, home to more than 2,500 species of cacti — tall and candle-thin, round as beach balls, or shaped like something out of a sci-fi set. A day inside it turns into a full sensory tour of the region: 2,000-year-old salt flats still worked by hand at Zapotitlán Salinas, a lunch built around cactus flowers and hibiscus water (with insects on offer for the adventurous) and a pottery workshop in Los Reyes Metzontla where clay deposits — leftovers from an ancient sea — get shaped into earthy, hand-thrown crockery.

In a small Puebla town two hours north of the city, an entire industry is built on Christmas spirit. Chignahuapan produces an estimated 70 million hand-blown ornaments a year, and inside the country’s largest esfera factory, the process starts with nothing more than a glowing-hot glass tube and a steady breath. From there, silver coatings, hand-mixed paint and careful dabs of glitter transform each piece into something ready for the tree — some ornaments even take a year to master.

Step inside the traditional workshop where trompos, Nativity scenes and piñata-shaped baubles come to life, one painstaking layer at a time.

In the days before Day of the Dead, the Puebla town of Huaquechula holds a tradition unlike anywhere else: the trueque, an ancient barter market where locals swap goods — peanuts, sugar cane, homemade bread — for everything needed to build their altars. Families trade for marigolds and cockscomb flowers, while vendors carry stacks of pan de muerto in its many forms, from bone-topped loaves to body-shaped muertitos dusted in red sugar.

Beyond the market, the town runs on hospitality: cooks prepare meals for hundreds of festival participants around the clock, and visitors are waved into strangers’ homes to see their altars up close. Huaquechula offers a rare, local variation on Mexico’s most iconic holiday — equal parts market day, family reunion and open-door celebration of the dead.

Our glimpse into Puebla ends on a unique note. The annual Carrera de la Tortilla, a 5-km race through Tehuacán that retraces the daily walk local women make to market, tortillas and all. Most runners came from Santa María Coapan, the self-proclaimed “Tortilla Capital” of Mexico, who run decked out in traditional Mixtec dress.

Part sporting event, part tribute to the women who keep the tradition alive, it’s one of Puebla’s more charming annual customs.

Puebla, Where Magic Lives in Every Journey / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

When it comes to arriving in Puebla, it really only makes sense to arrive from Mexico City.

By air

Puebla International Airport: 45 minutes from the city center, the airport offers connections to almost every major Mexican destination, plus Newark, Houston and Los Angeles.

Mexico City Benito Juarez (AICM): The big one. About 2 hours (traffic permitting) from central Puebal. Available from everywhere in Mexico, and almost every major global airport besides.

Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA): The eternally troubled AIFA is finally beginning to come into it’s own. 2.5 hours away, it offers similar domestic connectivity to AICM and flights in from Colombia, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic and Cuba.

By road

Mexico City: 135km (83 miles) somewhere between 90 minutes and 3 hours, depending on when you travel. National holidays often lead to enormous tailbacks, but tackling the drive early on a weekday often means you can get there in less than two hours.

World.title: Ohuira Bay communities weigh federal plan for Sinaloa ammonia plant
World.content:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Mexico — When federal officials finally unveiled a plan last week to address the 12-year conflict over a nearly completed ammonia plant beside Ohuira Bay, Indigenous Yoreme activist, rural sociologist and law student Melina Maldonado did not feel relieved.

She felt crushed.

After six days of roundtable discussions, she had begun to feel hopeful; it seemed they were really taking in new information and seeing a different side to the debate. The proposal led her to believe otherwise.

“They didn’t listen to our reasons for saying no,” Maldonado said. “They listened for a way to make it a yes.”

The federal proposal promises environmental safeguards, community monitoring and public investment around the German-backed GPO-Proman plant in northern Sinaloa state. But it leaves the project’s operation largely intact — and that has exposed the fundamental divide at the heart of the conflict: The government is offering ways to make the plant safer, while the communities closest to the bay are still adamant that it should not operate at all.

Those communities must now take the proposal into their own assemblies and, using their traditional Indigenous consensus-based governance model, decide whether to accept it. Until then, the blockade outside the gate to the plant — now in its 72nd day — remains in place.

A proposal, not an agreement

The plan emerged after six days of talks involving federal and state officials, representatives of GPO-Proman and members of the ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!) collective, which is led by Yoreme-Mayo communities surrounding Ohuira Bay and has become the principal force opposing the plant.

Federal officials presented the proposal as a path toward resolving a conflict that has become one of Mexico’s longest-running and most contentious environmental battles. But movement leaders emphasized that no agreement has been reached and that they do not have the authority to accept the plan on behalf of their communities.

The proposal must first be explained and discussed in assemblies in Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas and Topolobampo. These communities surround the Santa María-Topolobampo-Ohuira lagoon system, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and would bear the plant’s most direct impacts.

Community response to the proposal

“We have to hold our own internal assemblies,” said Claudia Susana Quintero, a Yoreme educator, resident of the village of Ohuira and one of the leaders of ¡Aquí No! “We have to explain it to the community, analyze it and decide how we are going to reach consensus.”

The representatives’ role is to take the proposal home and return with a decision reached collectively — not to accept it on their communities’ behalf.

The US $1.6 billion plant, designed to produce 2,200 metric tons (2,425 tons) of ammonia a day, is reportedly about 88% complete. Opposition began soon after the project was approved in 2014 and has centered on threats to fishing, the lagoon ecosystem, industrial safety and what Yoreme communities describe as a deeply flawed Indigenous consultation.

The current protest began in late May, when residents tried to block the movement of massive absorption towers from the port. Protesters later shifted their encampment to the plant entrance, where they have remained through extreme heat and intense storms.

A project the government considers strategic

President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the plant as important to Mexico’s goal of achieving greater food sovereignty. Ammonia is a principal raw material in nitrogen fertilizers, and Sheinbaum has said Mexico currently imports nearly all the fertilizer it uses, apart from production by state-owned company Fertinal.

She has also emphasized that the plant is nearly finished, and that it underwent an environmental review and received majority support in the government-led Indigenous consultation — a process the four communities closest to Ohuira Bay continue to dispute.

The Economy Ministry says the GPO plant could reduce Mexico’s fertilizer imports by as much as 70% and keep approximately US $500 million now spent on imports within the Mexican economy.

For the federal government, the plant is part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. Opponents say that national goal does not justify concentrating the risks in their communities.

What the government put on the table

The proposal leaves the ammonia plant in place, but would significantly alter how it operates. Among its most significant provisions, the plan calls for GPO-Proman to stop drawing water directly from Ohuira Bay and instead use water discharged through a nearby Federal Electricity Commission canal.

Opponents have long warned that the plant’s authorized system would pull large volumes of seawater from the lagoon and return warmer, saltier water, potentially disrupting fish and shrimp nurseries. Under the new plan, wastewater would instead be carried offshore rather than released back into the lagoon system.

The plan also proposes a new environmental baseline study, continuous water-quality monitoring and an oversight body made up of community members, scientists, government officials and company representatives. Additional measures would address sewage and agricultural runoff already entering the bay, as well as emergency preparedness and civil protection.

Other commitments focus on longstanding community needs, including housing, education, fishing infrastructure and assistance in certifying local shrimp and crab products so they can command higher prices.

Economic development plans in Topolobampo

Federal commissioner Mauricio Rodríguez Alonso, who has led the talks, stressed at a Tuesday news conference that the plan grew out of dialogue among the communities, GPO-Proman and government agencies. He said the company had agreed in principle to its commitments.

Ulises Pinzón, Topolobampo’s municipal representative, said the package could bring meaningful benefits. He was particularly encouraged by provisions giving communities a voice over future petrochemical development.

That is especially significant in Topolobampo, which the federal government has designated as an economic development hub where chemical and petrochemical industries are among the priority sectors. The plan would also keep proposed methanol and urea plants and a port terminal on hold unless the communities agree to them.

But Pinzón noted that many of the promises involve responsibilities the government should already be fulfilling, rather than concessions from GPO-Proman itself.

“On paper, honestly, I see an attractive proposal,” he said. “The question is how we can ensure that these commitments are actually fulfilled.”

That distinction — between a promising announcement and a binding, enforceable agreement — is now one of the central questions confronting the communities.

The risk that remains

For opponents of the plant, the most troubling unresolved issue is the danger of a catastrophic ammonia release. The government proposal does include new safeguards: an emergency-response center, joint industrial-risk monitoring, water curtains around pipelines and storage tanks, and a regional civil-protection plan — something Rodríguez acknowledged does not currently exist.

But movement leaders say emergency planning and mitigation cannot eliminate the underlying danger documented in the company’s own risk assessment.

According to that assessment, a five-minute leak could create a high-impact zone extending roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the plant, encompassing Topolobampo and nearby Yoreme communities. A broader impact zone could extend as far as 45 kilometers (28 miles), reaching toward Los Mochis and other surrounding communities.

“That risk is still there, and it is still not clear to us,” Pinzón said. “The first people affected would be those of us who live in Topolobampo.”

Loss of life is not remediable

Company project documents show the plant is designed to store up to 75,000 metric tons (82,670 tons) of anhydrous ammonia near populated communities. Quintero said the proposal may reduce certain environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate the consequences of a major industrial accident.

“You can remediate many things,” she said. “What you cannot remediate is the loss of life.”

For Maldonado, this is where the government’s proposal misses the point. Her own community, the Yoreme fishing village of Lázaro Cárdenas, looks across the bay at the plant every day.

The communities’ opposition has never been limited to the plant’s effects on water quality or fisheries, she said. It is rooted in the belief that a facility carrying such risks should not operate near people’s homes. She pointed to the company’s brightly colored risk map.

“This is the risk zone the company itself identified,” she said. “And now they are minimizing it or pushing it into the background.”

A decision made under threat

The communities will not consider the proposal in a political vacuum. Several of the movement’s most visible leaders have received threats related to their opposition to the plant and now live under government protection measures.

Four of ¡Aquí No!’s most visible leaders, including Maldonado, Quintero and Ohuira traditional governor Felipe Montaño, have been enrolled in Mexico’s federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists. Protection measures can include bulletproof vests and government-issued panic buttons intended to summon help in an emergency.

But Quintero said such equipment offers little comfort as the communities prepare to deliver an answer that government officials and project supporters may not want to hear.

“I know my community is going to say no,” she said. “But now the government is putting us in the line of fire against the rest of society that says yes.”

She worries that the plan could recast defenders as obstacles to jobs and economic development, increasing the pressure on people who have already spent years facing intimidation for speaking publicly.

“A bulletproof vest and a panic button are not going to help me much if someone decides to act tomorrow,” Quintero said.

The experience, she added, has gradually consumed the rest of their identities.

“We are no longer mothers, daughters or sisters,” she said. “We are nothing more than defenders.”

From shock to strategy

By Thursday evening, the mood inside the movement had begun to shift.

Enrique Ayala, a longtime activist staying at the blockade, said movement leaders spent six hours Thursday with scientists and lawyers analyzing the proposal and plotting their next steps.

“The government proposal is one-sided,” Ayala said. “They are pushing ahead with their project.”

But after years of being ignored, Ayala sees the government’s willingness to sit down with them as progress.

“We have to get up, keep going and make proposals of our own,” he said. “After 12 years when they paid us no attention, now we have them sitting at the table.”

And despite the government’s apparent intention to move the plant toward operation, Ayala said the movement has not abandoned its original goal.

“We still believe we can get the company to leave,” he said. “Sometimes you have to dream.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: From the archive: A guide to Mexican nicknames and how they’re given
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of giving nicknames in Mexico.

If you’ve spent much time among Mexicans, you’ve probably realized something. They love to give each other — and consistently use — nicknames.

I’m not just talking about diminutives of names, though these are also popular. Guillermo, for example, is Memo for short, the same way Bob is a diminutive of Robert.

How nicknames work in Mexico

There’s Alex for both Alejandro and Alejandra, Chio for Rocío, Lalo for Eduardo, Lola for Dolores and Chava for Salvador. There’s also short versions of double names, like Mafer for María Fernanda, Majo for María José and my favorite, Lucifer for Lucía Fernanda, a name most people do not give their kids. And of course, the classic “-ito” and “-ita” can go at the end of many names. So sometimes people call me Sarita, and my partner Juanito. Careful with using these, though, as they’re often infantilizing, and as you very likely know, some people do not like being infantilized.

So you get the idea: most names here have a shortened version. But Mexicans don’t stop there!

My nicknames

I’ll admit that this makes me very happy. As a kid, I never had a nickname, and I was jealous that I didn’t. Thinking back, it’s probably better; it wouldn’t have necessarily been a nice one, as I was both a crybaby and a showoff. Come to think of it, I might still be both of those things. Thankfully, I don’t currently have any nicknames related to either of those characteristics. Yet.

I do have some other fun ones though. “Sirena polar” — polar mermaid — might be the most creative, given to me by a friend of my ex-husband who was amazed that I insisted on swimming in ice-cold water after a hike. For reasons unknown to me, this same friend also often called me “cara de nutria”: otter face. Maybe because otters swim in cold water, too? Another friend, not quite as creative, simply calls me “mi gringa favorita.” I’d be more flattered if I weren’t one of the only gringos she knows.

The futility of protesting against your nickname

Many nicknames are purposefully funny, and sometimes shocking. And from what I can tell, people don’t seem to be insulted by them. Sometimes I wonder if they actually are bothered but know that trying to fight back against the Mexican urge to make fun of everything is futile.

So when you get a name like “El Frijol” because you’re very dark-skinned, you just go along with it, I guess?

In the particular case of another acquaintance, the guy was tall and good-looking. He was married, but seemed to have no shortage of women interested in him, or of self-esteem.

I always wanted to ask him if the nickname bothered him, but we were never close, so the opportunity was lost. But I did get to ask my ex-husband, who his friends had nicknamed “el bello camello” — the beautiful camel — supposedly because they thought he looked Arab.

The new generation of nicknames

Could this be one of those cultural things that’s dying out with more socially conscious and sensitive younger generations? I don’t think it is, as my daughter, age 11, has several nicknames herself. At school, her friends sometimes call her Plana, which means flat. It’s a synonym of her name, Lisa, which means “smooth” in Spanish and is often featured on hair conditioner bottles. And in her Scout troop, every kid has a nickname, each one the name of a bird. She’ll also respond to “Mona,” which is kind of nice. “Mona” is more of a Spanish-from-Spain word for “pretty,” but in this case, of course it’s about the Mona Lisa.

So perhaps the tradition will continue?

Don’t take yourself too seriously

After several years of watching the issue of how people address them being taken very, very seriously north of Mexico, I’ll admit that I find the ability to joke around with silly nicknames refreshing. Like all humor, though, it’s very culturally specific; there are plenty of unspoken rules regarding when it’s funny and good-humored and when it’s not.

It’s not that I want the freedom to be gratuitously mean, which is something very different. But I do think that it’s always worth it to not take ourselves so seriously all the time, something most of us can agree makes us generally unlikable.

So if you get a nickname here, try to go with it. Because people don’t get nicknames when they’re not being included in a group. Even if it’s not one you’d have chosen for yourself, it’s a signal that you are part of a community; people know you.

They might be making fun, but it’s affectionate fun. Try to take it that way.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: US suspends avocado certs, fracking studies continue and Peru rift ends
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conferences set much of the week’s agenda, moving from children’s social media use to a government transparency decree, a high-profile murder, fracking policy and a diplomatic breakthrough with Peru. Economic data told a mixed story too, with a strengthening peso set against a sharp drop in Pemex profit and a battered Sinaloa economy.

Security developments also kept pace, including the arrest of a former Guerrero governor on Ayotzinapa-related charges, a jump in U.S. rewards tied to CJNG’s new leadership, and a fresh U.S. suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán. On the public health and safety front, a UNAM cheating scandal, a UNESCO deadline to protect the vaquita and a cyclosporiasis scare linked to Riviera Maya travel all drew attention.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Economy: Peso strengthens and avocado trade swings

Mexico’s currency extended a 10-day rally to reach its strongest level since February, helped by the Bank of Mexico holding its benchmark rate at 6.5% and a weaker US dollar following a soft American jobs report. The gains came even as Pemex reported a 70% annual drop in second-quarter net profit, which the state oil company attributed to higher financial costs, tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate. Economic disparities varied widely by region, with Sinaloa’s economy posting the worst quarterly contraction of any Mexican state, a result economists linked to the ongoing cartel conflict in the region.

Tourism data added to the mixed picture: Tourism GDP fell 0.8% quarter-over-quarter in the first three months of the year, according to INEGI, driven by a 5.9% quarterly drop in spending by foreign visitors, even as domestic tourism consumption rose 0.5%.

Mexico’s avocado trade also had a volatile week. New data showed exports to the U.S. jumped 35% in the first quarter compared to the previous year, according to Sader. Days later, however, the United States suspended avocado export certifications in Michoacán, citing an unspecified “threat against U.S. interests” — the third such suspension in just over four years. Michoacán’s governor deployed additional state security operatives and the Defense Ministry sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the region in response.

Energy: Government edges toward fracking while banning it in Mexico’s top basin

A government expert committee tasked with assessing “sustainable fracking” recommended prohibiting hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, Mexico’s largest-potential shale region, citing environmental, social and biodiversity concerns. Sheinbaum said her government would respect that recommendation, which she reaffirmed at Friday’s mañanera.

However, the committee recommended continued evaluation of two other northern basins. Reuters reported that pilot projects in Coahuila and Tamaulipas could begin as soon as next month if approved, as Mexico looks to reduce its reliance on natural gas imports from the United States.

Security: Pressure builds on cartels and past officials

U.S. authorities raised the reward for CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, to $25 million following the February death of cartel founder “El Mencho,” as part of more than $100 million in reward offers and new visa restrictions. Domestically, federal agents dismantled four illicit fuel processing centers in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Morelos, seizing roughly 1 million liters of fuel. In Sinaloa, Sheinbaum acknowledged the murder of content creator César Gastélum, the ninth social media personality killed in the state since 2024. And in a case tied to one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved crimes, federal authorities arrested former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre on charges of concealing video evidence related to the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students; Sheinbaum said the arrest was not politically motivated.

Public health, environment and education

Sheinbaum laid the cornerstone for a new IMSS hospital in Oaxaca, part of a three-facility “Health City” complex the government frames as a step toward its planned Universal Health Service. And after the U.K. reported dozens of cyclosporiasis cases among travelers, Mexico stepped up health inspections at Riviera Maya hotels, while officials said the country has not been identified as the outbreak’s source.

Officials at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) confirmed that nearly 60,000 applicants must retake its entrance exam after widespread cheating undermined its first-ever online exam.

Separately, UNESCO gave Mexico until February to show concrete action to protect the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which only seven to 10 are believed to remain.

Diplomacy and governance

Sheinbaum signed a decree aimed at strengthening federal government transparency, which officials said would compel departments to disclose more information following the 2024 elimination of the INAI watchdog agency.

On the diplomatic front, Sheinbaum announced that Mexico and Peru would restore relations severed since November, after former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was granted safe passage from asylum in Mexico’s Lima embassy.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test several threads left open this week: whether Mexican and U.S. officials can resolve the security concerns behind the avocado certification suspension, whether President Sheinbaum’s panel of experts finds acceptable conditions in northern Mexico to move fracking pilot projects forward, and how UNAM’s rescheduled in-person exams — set for mid-to-late August — play out after the cheating controversy. Mexico also faces UNESCO’s February deadline on vaquita protections and continued scrutiny of Sinaloa’s cartel-driven economic slowdown.

World.title: Colombia’s 2027 Budget Reaches Congress With a US$9.5bn Gap
World.content:
Colombia · Economy

Key Facts Budget total — The 2027 spending plan totals COP 575.6 trillion, roughly 27% of GDP, according to La República.

— The 2027 spending plan totals COP 575.6 trillion, roughly 27% of GDP, according to La República. Financing gap — The Comptroller’s Office flags a COP 30.2 trillion shortfall (about US$9.5 billion) that needs new legislation.

— The Comptroller’s Office flags a COP 30.2 trillion shortfall (about US$9.5 billion) that needs new legislation. Contingent income — The budget relies on COP 30.2 trillion in contingent revenues from a yet-to-be-approved financing law.

— The budget relies on COP 30.2 trillion in contingent revenues from a yet-to-be-approved financing law. Uncovered spending — Of that gap, COP 8.292 trillion (around US$2.6 billion) has no identified source, per Infobae’s calculations.

— Of that gap, COP 8.292 trillion (around US$2.6 billion) has no identified source, per Infobae’s calculations. Political friction — The Centro Democrático party asks to return the bill to the Finance Ministry for corrections and better justification.

— The Centro Democrático party asks to return the bill to the Finance Ministry for corrections and better justification. Leadership change — Minister Germán Ávila resigned effective 7 August 2026; Miguel Gómez Martínez is the designated successor.

— Minister Germán Ávila resigned effective 7 August 2026; Miguel Gómez Martínez is the designated successor. Legal deadlines — Congress must set the budget amount by 15 September and vote by 20 October, reports Infobae.

The outgoing government’s spending plan faces a financing gap. It also faces political pushback.

This sets up a tense fiscal debate. Investors and residents will watch closely.

Colombia’s 2027 national budget landed in Congress. It has a COP 575.6 trillion price tag.

That is about US$181 billion. But it carries a COP 30.2 trillion financing hole.

That is around US$9.5 billion. The outgoing government hopes to fill it with a new tax law.

The Comptroller’s Office flagged that gap. La República and El Espectador reported it.

This means your taxes and utility bills will be affected. The pace of public investment in Colombia will also change.

A tense legislative fight will shape all of this. It will last over the next two months.

Colombia’s Congress in session. The 2027 budget arrives with a financing gap that lawmakers must close. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Understanding Colombia’s 2027 National Budget

Every year, the national government drafts a General Budget of the Nation, a document that lays out all public spending for the following year: salaries, infrastructure, health transfers, defence, and debt payments. The Finance Ministry submits it to Congress, where the third and fourth committees of both the Senate and the House review the numbers, debate the sources of income, and vote on the total amount.

The key dates are set: Congress must fix the budget amount by 15 September and vote the final text no later than 20 October, according to Infobae. That gives lawmakers roughly eight weeks to pick apart a document that represents about 27% of the country’s GDP, as La República notes.

Where the Money Comes From — and Where It Doesn’t

The 2027 budget proposal, presented by the outgoing administration of Gustavo Petro, leans on a mix of tax revenue, royalties, and debt. But COP 30.2 trillion of that income is what officials call contingent: it only materialises if Congress approves a separate financing law, a kind of tax reform that the government has not yet secured.

The Comptroller’s Office, the independent audit body, has already warned that this creates a structural shortfall. According to El Espectador’s reporting on the radicado bill, the project requires those additional revenues to balance the books. La República cites the same COP 30.2 trillion figure as the desfinanciación, or unfinanced portion, of the budget.

Colombia’s 2027 budget proposal was filed at COP 575.6 trillion (about US$181 billion), with a financing gap of COP 30.2 trillion (about US$9.5 billion). The government wants to close that hole with a separate financing law, but lawmakers have asked the finance ministry to revise or return the project before debate begins.

The outgoing administration identified COP 21.9 trillion (about US$6.9 billion) in funding sources, leaving roughly COP 8.3 trillion (about US$2.6 billion) with no clear backing. Under the plan, Congress must approve the new revenue measures, but the discussion has yet to start, and some legislators want the accounts recalculated first.

The Hole Within the Hole

The picture gets worse when you look closer. Infobae, citing calculations around the government’s coverage plan, reports that the outgoing administration identified financing for only COP 21.9 trillion of that gap. That leaves COP 8.292 trillion — roughly US$2.6 billion — with no source of funding identified at all.

In practice, this means the budget as submitted is not fully backed by real revenue. If Congress does not pass the financing law, or if the promised income falls short, the government would face a shortfall that could force spending cuts, delays in transfers to regions, or new debt issuance on less favourable terms.

Colombia’s 2027 National Budget Faces Political Storm and a New Minister

The political climate is tense. The Centro Democrático party has filed a motion to return the bill to the Finance Ministry, demanding that officials correct and properly justify several funding sources, as reported by Semana. The discussion has not even formally started in the plenary committees, yet the pushback is already loud.

Adding to the uncertainty, Finance Minister Germán Ávila resigned with effect from 7 August 2026, the same day the budget was filed. Miguel Gómez Martínez is the designated minister in the incoming government, meaning the person defending the numbers in Congress may shift mid-debate.

Why This Matters for You

If you live in Colombia or hold assets here, this budget is your forecast for inflation, interest rates, and public services. A wider fiscal deficit typically pressures the peso, raises the cost of government borrowing, and can push the central bank to keep rates higher for longer — directly affecting your mortgage, your car loan, and the yield on your local bonds.

The COP 30.2 trillion gap is not an accounting footnote; it is roughly 1.2% of GDP. If it is not closed with clean revenue, the adjustment could come through spending freezes that delay highway projects, or through higher taxes on businesses and individuals later. For investors, the signal is simple: watch the congressional calendar, especially the first two weeks of September, because the outcome will set the tone for the Colombian peso and the local equity market through 2027.

The Road Ahead

The next steps are procedural, but the politics are heavy. The third and fourth committees of the Senate and the House will hold hearings, likely calling the new minister to defend each line item. The Centro Democrático’s request to return the bill will be voted on early in the process.

If the bill survives intact, the financing law becomes the next battleground — and that is where the real fiscal fight will happen. For now, the numbers on the table are COP 575.6 trillion in spending, COP 30.2 trillion in hoped-for revenue, and a political calendar that runs to 20 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

This represents roughly 27% of the country’s GDP, according to La República. How big is the financing gap in the 2027 budget? The Comptroller’s Office has flagged a financing gap of COP 30.2 trillion, approximately US$9.5 billion. This amount depends on a separate financing law that Congress has not yet approved, and part of it — COP 8.292 trillion or about US$2.6 billion — has no identified source, per Infobae. Who is the new finance minister handling this budget? Germán Ávila resigned with effect from 7 August 2026. Miguel Gómez Martínez is the designated minister in the incoming government, and he will likely be the one defending the budget in Congress. When must Congress approve the 2027 budget? Congress must set the budget amount by 15 September and vote on the final text by 20 October, according to Infobae. The Centro Democrático party has already asked to return the bill to the Finance Ministry for corrections.

Sources: Ministerio de Hacienda y Crédito Público; Contraloría General de la República; El Espectador; La República; Portafolio.

World.content:

— US avocado inspections in Michoacán resume partially on Saturday, August 8, 2026, after a three-day suspension. Key fact — Mexico deployed 1,557 soldiers and National Guard personnel on August 6 to secure key avocado towns.

— Mexico deployed 1,557 soldiers and National Guard personnel on August 6 to secure key avocado towns. Key fact — Michoacán produces about 75–80% of Mexico’s avocados, according to a Reuters-linked report.

Partial resumption of USDA inspections in Mexico’s avocado heartland follows a three-day suspension over inspector safety, easing fears of another export freeze.

US resumes avocado inspections in Michoacán. The United States has partially restarted official checks in the state.

Michoacán supplies most of the avocados Americans eat. The pause had lasted three days, over inspector safety.

The US embassy said activities would resume on Saturday, August 8, in several avocado-growing areas. That eases fears of another export freeze that could hit prices and supply.

The partial resumption builds on a security agreement that includes the deployment of 1,557 soldiers and National Guard personnel. A move intended to reassure US inspectors and maintain the flow of a trade worth billions.

What happened

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) suspended phytosanitary inspections on August 5, 2026, after a security alert that raised concerns for US inspectors working in the region. Reuters reported that the US embassy said operations would partially resume as of Saturday, citing Mexican security commitments and continued coordination on conditions on the ground.

The partial restart covers key production towns, including Tancítaro, Tacámbaro, Uruapan, and the corridor between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, according to a Spanish-language report quoting US Ambassador Ronald Johnson. The ambassador praised President Claudia Sheinbaum’s leadership and the security agreements that allowed the resumption.

The resumption is limited to these areas, with other zones potentially included later if security remains stable. The US embassy emphasised that the decision was made after evaluating that safety conditions had improved sufficiently to allow inspectors to return.

Why it matters

If you live in the US, this directly affects your grocery bill. Avocados are a staple in millions of kitchens, and Michoacán is the dominant supplier – it accounts for about 75% to 80% of Mexico’s avocado production, according to a Reuters-linked report. A prolonged suspension could have sent prices soaring and emptied shelves, as happened during an earlier safety-related pause.

For investors and businesses in Latin America, the episode is a reminder of how security risks in Mexico’s countryside can ripple through international supply chains. The quick resumption, though, suggests both governments are keen to avoid disrupting a trade that is worth billions annually.

The avocado trade is a key economic lifeline for Michoacán, where thousands of jobs depend on the export chain. Any extended halt would have immediate consequences for local economies and for US retailers that rely on steady shipments.

Michoacán accounts for roughly three-quarters of Mexico’s avocado output, and the US takes nearly 90 per cent of Mexican exports by volume—worth US$3.653 billion in 2025, according to Mexico’s Agriculture Ministry. The week-long suspension of USDA inspections, from August 5th, threatened to freeze that flow entirely, risking perishable losses for growers who depend on the border crossing for their main revenue.

Washington halted checks after a security alert, but partial activity resumed on August 8th in towns like Tancítaro and Uruapan following Mexican security pledges and the deployment of 1,557 troops and National Guard personnel. The US embassy credited President Claudia Sheinbaum’s leadership, yet the pause underscores how vulnerable the trade remains to local crime and diplomatic frictions, leaving exporters to hope the restart sticks.

Security response

To make the resumption possible, Mexico deployed 1,557 soldiers and National Guard personnel on August 6, 2026, to secure the avocado hub, Reuters reported. The deployment was aimed at reassuring US inspectors and ensuring they could carry out their work safely.

The US embassy said the partial restart was based on Mexican security commitments and continued coordination on conditions on the ground. Ambassador Johnson noted that the resumption began in areas including Tancítaro, a town long associated with avocado production and cartel activity.

The security operation is a joint effort between federal and local authorities, with the goal of creating a safe environment for inspectors and workers across the avocado supply chain.

What’s at stake

The numbers underline the stakes. Mexican avocado exports to the US reached US$3.653 billion in 2025, according to Mexico’s Agriculture Ministry. Nearly 90% of Mexican avocado exports by volume go to the US, Reuters reports – a dependency that makes any disruption feel immediate for American consumers.

Michoacán alone produces roughly three-quarters of Mexico’s avocados, so any prolonged halt in inspections would have quickly drained US inventories. The partial resumption is welcome news, but it remains conditional on security conditions holding up.

Beyond the immediate supply impact, the episode highlights the fragility of cross-border trade in agricultural goods when security issues arise, underscoring the need for sustained cooperation between the two countries.

What to watch

The US embassy said activities would resume in some avocado-growing areas as of Saturday, but not all – so the situation is still fragile. Both sides will be watching closely to see if the security commitments hold and inspections can expand to full capacity.

For now, the immediate crisis appears averted, but the episode shows how quickly trade can be disrupted by insecurity. If you’re in the avocado business – whether as a buyer, shipper, or investor – keep an eye on security reports from Michoacán.

The US and Mexico have pledged to maintain communication and adjust the inspection schedule as conditions evolve, which means the current arrangement is subject to change without notice.

US resumes avocado inspections in Michoacán

The partial resumption follows a security agreement between the US and Mexico, allowing USDA inspectors to return to key avocado-producing areas. The move is expected to stabilise supply and prevent price spikes in the American market.

Both governments have emphasised the importance of maintaining the flow of avocados, which is a multi-billion-dollar trade. The continued cooperation on security will determine whether inspections can be fully restored.

This development is a positive sign for the industry, but it also serves as a reminder that the security situation in Michoacán remains a critical factor for the long-term reliability of avocado exports.

Frequently Asked Questions

The suspension was lifted partially on August 8 after Mexico deployed security forces and made security commitments. Which areas are included in the partial resumption? The resumption covers Tancítaro, Tacámbaro, Uruapan, and the corridor between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, according to reports citing US Ambassador Ronald Johnson. Other areas may follow if security conditions improve. How much avocado does Michoacán export to the US? Michoacán produces about 75–80% of Mexico’s avocados, and the US takes nearly 90% of Mexican avocado exports by volume. In 2025, Mexican avocado exports to the US were valued at US$3.653 billion, per Mexico’s Agriculture Ministry. What happens if inspections are suspended again? A prolonged suspension would likely lead to avocado shortages and higher prices in the US, as seen in past incidents. The partial resumption is conditional on security, so any new security incident could trigger another halt.

His death marks the end of an era for the Messi family and for Argentinian football. Tributes pour in from around the world.

For decades, Jorge stood as a steadfast pillar, navigating contracts, medical battles. Media scrutiny, ensuring his son could focus solely on the game.

The news has prompted an outpouring of grief from fans and players alike. Underscoring his impact not only on Lionel’s life but on the sport itself.

Who was Jorge Messi?

Jorge Horacio Messi was more than just a father to Lionel Messi – he was the architect behind one of football’s greatest careers. From the dusty pitches of Rosario’s Abasto neighbourhood, he recognised his son’s prodigious talent early, becoming his agent and manager when Lionel was still a boy. His dedication and foresight transformed a shy, small boy with a growth hormone deficiency into a global icon, overcoming numerous obstacles along the way.

He negotiated Lionel’s first contracts with Barcelona, famously saving the deal on a napkin when the club hesitated, and stood by his son through every transfer, trophy, and controversy. For years, Jorge was a constant presence on the touchline and in the boardroom, earning respect as a shrewd and devoted guardian of his family’s name. His role extended beyond business, as he often served as a calming influence and a link between Lionel and the press. Even after stepping back from day-to-day management, his guidance remained a quiet constant in Lionel’s professional decisions.

Born in a modest household, Jorge worked as a steel factory foreman while raising three children. He and his wife Celia instilled in Lionel a humility that would later define his public persona. When the family relocated to Barcelona to support Lionel’s treatment, Jorge gave up his job, a sacrifice that highlighted his unwavering commitment. This background in adversity helped him relate to the challenges of young players, and he often mentored other parents navigating football’s complex world. His death has prompted tributes from across the football community, with many recalling his warmth and approachability.

The final goodbye in Rosario

The wake took place on Saturday evening at El Prado Cementerio Parque in Pérez, a town near Rosario, with only close family and friends in attendance, according to Clarín and Infobae. Lionel Messi, along with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children, flew from the United States on a private flight to be there. The family has maintained a low profile, with security personnel managing the crowd of reporters and supporters who gathered outside the cemetery gates. Mourners left flowers and handwritten notes, creating a makeshift shrine that reflected the deep affection many held for Jorge.

The Sanatorio Centro, where Jorge had been treated, issued a brief statement expressing condolences and said no further medical details would be provided out of respect for the family’s privacy, as reported by La Nación. The football world has since sent an outpouring of support, but the Messi family has asked for calm and discretion during this difficult time. Many former teammates and rivals have shared tributes on social media, highlighting Jorge’s kindness and his instrumental role in shaping Messi’s career. Inter Miami, Lionel’s current club, also released a statement expressing their deepest condolences and offering support to the family.

Jorge Horacio Messi served as both father and long-standing representative to Lionel, guiding his son’s career from an early age until his death in Rosario on 8 August 2026 at 68. His passing, following a prolonged illness, prompted a private family farewell attended by Lionel and his loved ones.

Jorge Messi dies at 68: Why it matters for Latin America

For you living in or invested in Latin America, the death of Jorge Messi marks the end of an era not just for football, but for the region’s cultural identity. Lionel Messi is a source of immense pride across the continent, and Jorge was the quiet force behind that success – a symbol of how a family’s sacrifice can elevate a talent to global stardom. His story is a testament to the power of parental support and unwavering belief, values that resonate deeply in Latin American societies. The mention of ’Jorge Messi dies at 68’ in headlines has become a rallying point for collective mourning, with vigils spontaneously forming in Rosario and Buenos Aires.

His story resonates beyond the pitch: it’s about migration, ambition, and the bonds that hold families together through wealth and fame. As Argentina mourns, the legacy of Jorge Messi will live on in every child who kicks a ball in a Rosario street, dreaming of following in Lionel’s footsteps. For the broader region, his life exemplifies the opportunities and challenges that come with global fame, serving as an inspiration for generations to come. From his humble start in a factory to the corridors of football power, his journey mirrors the aspirations of millions across South America.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused Jorge Messi’s death? The family has not disclosed a specific cause, but reports from Infobae and La Nación mention he had a long illness. The Sanatorio Centro said no further medical details would be released. Where is the wake being held? The private ceremony is at El Prado Cementerio Parque in Pérez, near Rosario, with restricted attendance limited to close family and friends, as reported by Clarín. Did Lionel Messi attend the funeral? Yes, Lionel Messi flew from the United States on Saturday evening with Antonela Roccuzzo and their children, landing in Rosario to join the family, according to Infobae and Clarín. How old was Jorge Messi? He was 68 years old at the time of his death on 8 August 2026, as confirmed by multiple outlets including La Nación and BBC Mundo.

Sources: Infobae; Clarín; Olé; La Nación.

World.title: Brazil Court Bars Bolsonaro Family Visit for Father’s Day
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts Denied request — Brazil’s Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected a defence plea for Bolsonaro to see his sons on Father’s Day.

— Brazil’s Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected a defence plea for Bolsonaro to see his sons on Father’s Day. Ongoing suspension — Non-essential visits have been suspended for 30 days since July 17, 2026, over social media violations.

— Non-essential visits have been suspended for 30 days since July 17, 2026, over social media violations. Domiciliary arrest — Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year, 3-month sentence for leading an attempted coup.

— Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year, 3-month sentence for leading an attempted coup. Legal exceptions — Only medical staff, physiotherapists, and lawyers may visit during the ban.

— Only medical staff, physiotherapists, and lawyers may visit during the ban. Defence argument — Bolsonaro’s lawyers called the request ’strictly humanitarian and family-related’.

— Bolsonaro’s lawyers called the request ’strictly humanitarian and family-related’. Prejudiced ruling — Moraes declared the request ’prejudiced’ (invalid) because the visits were already suspended.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected Bolsonaro’s request. He denied the former president’s defence plea.

Brazil’s Supreme Court has denied a Bolsonaro Father’s Day visit. Justice Alexandre de Moraes ruled on Saturday, 8 August 2026.

He rejected a request from former President Jair Bolsonaro’s defence. It sought to let his sons visit him at home.

The sons are Carlos, Flávio and Jair Renan. The visit was for Father’s Day on Sunday, 9 August.

Moraes called the request ’prejudiced’ (invalid). Non-essential visits were already suspended by a prior decision, according to Agência Brasil and other Brazilian media.

The denial underscores the strict conditions of Bolsonaro’s detention as he serves a lengthy sentence for attempting to subvert Brazil’s democratic order.

Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who denied the request from Bolsonaro’s defence. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Who is Alexandre de Moraes?

Alexandre de Moraes is a justice of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court. That court is the STF, the country’s highest judicial body.

He has been central in cases involving political figures. This includes Bolsonaro.

Moraes is the rapporteur for the coup attempt case.

Moraes previously ordered Bolsonaro’s preventive detention. He also imposed restrictions on his communications.

For example, Bolsonaro cannot use social media. This is part of the ongoing proceedings.

His decisions always protect the judicial process. They put the integrity first, not personal matters.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes is a Brazilian Supreme Court justice. He oversees the criminal case against former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro is under house arrest for leading an attempted coup. On 8 August 2026, Moraes rejected a defence request.

The request was to allow Bolsonaro’s sons to visit him for Father’s Day. All non-essential visits were already suspended.

This was due to Bolsonaro’s breach of social media restrictions.

Bolsonaro Father’s Day visit denied: what was requested

The defence asked the court for exceptional authorisation. They wanted Bolsonaro’s sons to visit him.

The visit was for Father’s Day afternoon and evening. The family wanted to celebrate the occasion.

But the court had suspended all non-essential visits. That suspension lasts 30 days, starting 17 July 2026.

Moraes denied the request, stating that ’all visits are suspended’ except for those from medical staff, physiotherapists, and lawyers. Poder360 reported that Moraes said authorising the encounters would contradict the restrictions imposed on the former president.

The decision was handed down just one day before the intended visit, leaving no room for appeal in time.

Bolsonaro’s Supreme Court case stays with Justice Alexandre de Moraes. He is the rapporteur.

Bolsonaro is under domiciliary arrest. His sentence is 27 years and three months.

Non-essential visits are suspended for 30 days. This started on 17 July 2026 after a social media breach.

Moraes denied a Father’s Day visit on 8 August. The ban allows only medical staff and lawyers.

On 8 August 2026, Justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected a request. Bolsonaro’s defence wanted his sons to visit.

They asked for Carlos, Flávio and Jair Renan. The visit was planned for Father’s Day.

Moraes ruled the request ’prejudiced’. All non-essential visits were already suspended.

Only medical staff, physiotherapists and lawyers were exempt.

The 30-day suspension, in place since 17 July, followed a finding that Bolsonaro breached his social media restrictions through third parties. It is due to lift on 16 August, and the defence retains the option to seek alternative relief through the appeal process.

Bolsonaro Father’s Day visit denied: why the visits are suspended

The suspension followed a decision on 17 July 2026. Moraes had found that Bolsonaro violated restrictions on his social-media use through third parties.

Specifically, a letter signed by Bolsonaro was published on the social networks of his son Flávio.

The court deemed a breach of the conditions.

The 30-day ban blocks visits from family and friends, with exceptions for necessary medical personnel and legal representatives. Bolsonaro is under domiciliary arrest, serving a sentence of 27 years and 3 months for leading an attempted coup.

The ban is scheduled to lift on 16 August 2026, just days after Father’s Day.

Bolsonaro Father’s Day visit denied: legal standing and context

Bolsonaro was president from 2019 to 2022. He was convicted in a sweeping case over efforts to overturn Brazil’s election results.

He is now under house arrest while appealing the conviction, according to UPI and other international outlets.

The Supreme Court case keeps drawing attention. It tests accountability for political leaders.

For Brazilians, this affects political stability. It also impacts the regional balance.

Brazil’s decisions often echo across Latin America. Legal experts say the denied visit fits the court’s stance.

They see no leniency towards Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro Father’s Day visit denied: why this matters

If you live in or invest in Latin America, Brazil’s political dramas matter beyond the headlines. The case against Bolsonaro, including the strict enforcement of his detention conditions, signals how Brazil’s institutions handle challenges to democracy.

This affects everything from policymaking to market sentiment. It matters in the region’s largest economy.

The Supreme Court shapes the rule of law. That is critical for business in Brazil.

A denied family visit may seem minor. It reflects the broader legal and political environment.

Investors and residents must navigate it.

This decision signals strict limits on Bolsonaro’s detention. It comes ahead of the October polls.

The judiciary keeps tight control over his conditions. This reinforces the former president’s political isolation.

Legal constraints shape his reduced role. He remains sidelined in Brazil’s electoral landscape.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Alexandre de Moraes in simple terms? He is a justice on Brazil’s highest court, the Supreme Federal Court (STF). He is known for taking a tough line in cases involving political figures, and he is the judge in charge of the coup attempt case against Bolsonaro. What is the STF? The STF is Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court, the top judicial authority. It handles constitutional issues and high-profile cases involving political figures. Is Bolsonaro in prison? No, he is under house arrest. He was convicted of leading an attempted coup and sentenced to 27 years and 3 months, but he is serving his sentence at home while he appeals. Can Bolsonaro receive visitors at all? Yes, but only certain people. Currently, his medical team, physiotherapists, and his lawyers can visit. All other visits, including from family, are suspended until mid-August 2026.

Sources: Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF); O Globo; G1.

World.title: São Paulo Confirms Second Wild Bird Flu Case of 2026
World.content:
Brazil · Agriculture

Key Facts Second case — São Paulo confirmed its second avian influenza case of 2026 in a wild irerê duck at Ibirapuera park.

— São Paulo confirmed its second avian influenza case of 2026 in a wild irerê duck at Ibirapuera park. Wild bird — The infected bird was found in the park, with no link to commercial poultry or farms.

— The infected bird was found in the park, with no link to commercial poultry or farms. No embargo — The state agriculture secretariat said the case does not trigger any export embargo on chicken or eggs.

— The state agriculture secretariat said the case does not trigger any export embargo on chicken or eggs. Sanitary status — Brazil’s and São Paulo’s WOAH sanitary status remains unchanged.

— Brazil’s and São Paulo’s WOAH sanitary status remains unchanged. No human cases — Officials reported no human influenza cases in the state so far.

— Officials reported no human influenza cases in the state so far. Isolated event — The secretariat described the case as isolated, with no impact on the poultry production chain.

— The secretariat described the case as isolated, with no impact on the poultry production chain. Global context — Brazil is the world’s largest chicken exporter, making avian flu a closely watched issue.

A wild duck at Ibirapuera park tests positive for avian influenza, but officials stress it is isolated and poses no threat to commercial poultry or exports.

Brazil confirmed a bird flu case on Friday (7 August). It involved a wild irerê duck.

The duck was found at Parque Ibirapuera. The species is Dendrocygna viduata.

The state agriculture secretariat called the case isolated. There is no link to commercial poultry.

No export embargo was placed. Brazil’s sanitary status stays unchanged.

This was announced before the World Organisation for Animal Health.

A poultry processing line in Brazil. Officials say the isolated wild-bird case in São Paulo does not affect commercial flocks. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

São Paulo Bird Flu Case: What Happened at Ibirapuera Park

The infected bird was a wild duck common in South America. It was found in the park.

It was isolated, examined, and sampled for testing. The Secretaria de Agricultura e Abastecimento de São Paulo reported this.

They confirmed the case on Friday. The news came out on 8 August 2026.

This is the state’s second avian flu case in 2026, but officials emphasise it is an isolated finding in a wild bird. There are no commercial poultry establishments within 10 km of the detection site, the secretariat said.

The detection happened during routine wild bird surveillance. This program has run since the first case earlier this year.

The duck was found in a pond near the park’s main entrance. Park staff immediately contacted veterinary authorities.

Bird samples went to the state’s reference lab. Molecular tests confirmed influenza A subtype H5N1.

The bird was euthanised to prevent spread. Risk to wildlife or visitors stays minimal.

Officials increased monitoring of waterfowl in the park. No other birds show signs of infection.

The park remains open. Signs advise visitors not to feed or approach wild birds.

This is customary in such situations.

Why It Matters for Brazil’s Poultry Exports

You might wonder why a single sick duck in a park makes headlines. The reason is simple: Brazil is the world’s largest chicken exporter, and any avian flu detection can send ripples through global markets.

This case is not a commercial outbreak. The state government says it has no link to commercial farms.

It does not involve food production either. It does not affect the poultry or egg chain.

In plain terms, there is no embargo. No ban applies to chicken meat or egg exports.

This covers Brazil and São Paulo.

Avian influenza, or bird flu, is a viral disease that primarily affects birds, but certain strains can occasionally infect humans. The state government reported no human influenza cases in São Paulo so far, reassuring residents and visitors alike.

International buyers have historically reacted swiftly to avian flu news from Brazil. But trade analysts note isolated cases in wild birds.

These cases have not led to lasting restrictions. The secretariat signals this detection is low-risk.

The key metric for global poultry is whether commercial flocks are affected. This case involves only a wild duck in an urban park.

It does not change the risk assessment for Brazilian poultry products. These products remain in high demand worldwide.

Sanitary Status and Official Response

The secretariat stressed that the finding does not impact the sanitary status of São Paulo or Brazil before WOAH. That means Brazil’s official status as free of highly pathogenic avian influenza in commercial poultry remains unchanged.

Enjoy Ibirapuera Park, but don’t touch wild birds. That’s standard for any park.

This advice is unchanged for São Paulo residents and expats. The secretariat keeps monitoring the situation.

There is no cause for alarm.

The state’s animal health agency has activated its emergency response. Surveillance is heightened within a 10 km radius.

Nearby poultry farms are being checked. None exist in the immediate area.

Wild birds in other parks are tested.

Officials have also communicated the detection to national authorities, who in turn have informed WOAH and Brazil’s trading partners. This transparency is part of Brazil’s commitment to maintaining its sanitary credentials and avoiding trade disruptions.

The federal agriculture ministry issued a statement. It supports the state’s actions.

The case matches global avian flu patterns. These patterns are in wild birds.

No more restrictions are expected. That is unless new cases appear.

What This Means for You

If you live in or invest in Latin America, this case is a reminder of how closely Brazil’s agricultural sector is watched. But it also shows that officials act swiftly and transparently when a detection occurs.

Your chicken dinner and Sunday roast are safe for now. The poultry industry is unaffected.

Brazil’s export machine runs as usual. That’s how it has been in past wild-bird cases.

Regular visitors to Ibirapuera Park may notice extra officials in eathwear. Daily operations are unchanged.

The park’s wildlife remains part of its charm. This includes the irerê ducks sharing ponds with other species.

Avian flu is a disease of birds. The risk to humans stays negligible.

Follow standard hygiene practices. Cook poultry thoroughly.

This always eliminates any potential virus.

As Brazil moves through its agricultural calendar, the secretariat will provide updates if the situation evolves. For now, the São Paulo bird flu case is a footnote in the country’s ongoing surveillance efforts, and life goes on.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this bird flu case dangerous to humans? No human cases have been reported in São Paulo, and the case involves a wild bird, not commercial poultry. The risk to humans remains very low. Will this affect Brazil’s chicken exports? No. The state government said the case does not trigger any export embargo on chicken meat or eggs. Brazil’s sanitary status is unchanged. What is avian influenza? Avian influenza, or bird flu, is a viral disease that mainly affects birds, but some strains can occasionally infect humans. It spreads among wild birds and can sometimes reach poultry farms. Should I avoid Ibirapuera Park? No, the park remains open. Just avoid touching wild birds, as you would in any park. Officials are monitoring the situation.

Sources: Secretaria de Agricultura e Abastecimento de São Paulo; Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária; WOAH (OMSA).

World.title: Lula to Send Trump Amazon Data in Tariff Spat
World.content:
Brazil · Trade

Key Facts New tariffs — The US imposed a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports, with some exceptions like beef and coffee.

— The US imposed a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports, with some exceptions like beef and coffee. Deforestation cited — Washington said illegal deforestation was one reason for the measures, a claim Lula disputes.

— Washington said illegal deforestation was one reason for the measures, a claim Lula disputes. Data to send — Lula will forward Inpe figures showing a 36.87% drop in Amazon losses from August 2025 to July 2026.

— Lula will forward Inpe figures showing a 36.87% drop in Amazon losses from August 2025 to July 2026. Lowest since 2016 — The deforestation rate is the lowest in the series since 2016, according to Inpe.

— The deforestation rate is the lowest in the series since 2016, according to Inpe. Diplomatic tensions — The US also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador, adding to the strain.

— The US also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador, adding to the strain. No retaliation yet — Lula has not announced immediate countermeasures, focusing instead on rebutting the US rationale.

— Lula has not announced immediate countermeasures, focusing instead on rebutting the US rationale. Trade at stake — Brazilian exporters face higher costs in the US market, a key destination for manufactured and agricultural goods.

Brazil’s president will challenge Washington’s tariff case. He will send the latest deforestation figures, after a 25% duty on most Brazilian goods.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spoke on Saturday. He will send Donald Trump the latest Amazon deforestation figures.

This aims to undercut a key justification for the new US tariffs. Those tariffs target Brazilian goods.

Lula will send Trump the Amazon data in this tariff spat. It is a direct challenge to Washington’s claims.

Lula spoke in Taboão da Serra, São Paulo. He pointed to fresh data from Brazil’s space agency, Inpe, released on Friday.

It shows deforestation fell 36.87% between August 2025 and July 2026. That is the lowest in the series since 2016.

“I want to send these numbers to the US government,” Lula said, according to local media.

The US cited illegal deforestation as a reason for the tariffs. The package imposes a 25% duty on most Brazilian imports.

Some products, like beef and coffee, are exempt. The dispute raises costs for investors and exporters.

It makes doing business with the US more expensive. The US is Brazil’s second-largest trading partner.

Uncertainty now hits supply chains that rely on cross-border trade.

Lula’s move is a diplomatic gambit: rather than escalate with retaliation, he is betting that hard data can change the narrative. But the tariff dispute is not just about forests – Washington has also raised concerns about digital trade, intellectual property, and ethanol.

The coming weeks will show whether data can cool a trade war that is already affecting real money.

President Lula. He again attacked the US tariffs on Brazil and vowed to send Trump fresh Amazon deforestation data. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Are the New US Tariffs on Brazil?

In July 2026, the United States imposed a 25% tariff. It applies to most goods imported from Brazil.

The measure is sweeping and affects many sectors. Some products were exempted, like beef and coffee.

But the broad scope shocked Brazilian export industries.

Washington cites several trade grievances. They include digital trade barriers.

Intellectual property protections are another. Ethanol tariffs also matter.

Forest-related policies are included. Handling illegal deforestation is part of it.

For a Brazilian exporter, this means a 25% surcharge on goods. They are sent to the US market.

This can erode profit margins. It may force price increases.

Higher prices reduce competitiveness. The tariff rate is significant.

It is not a symbolic gesture. It is a substantial barrier.

It could reshape trade flows.

Most Brazilian exports to the US now face the higher duty. Some products are spared.

This creates a clear incentive for companies. They may seek alternative markets.

Or they may renegotiate contracts.

What the US Tariffs on Brazil Put at Stake

The US cited illegal Amazon deforestation as one reason for the tariffs. It linked environmental policy to trade.

This is sensitive for Brazil. The Amazon is a global symbol of climate action.

It is also a source of national pride.

Lula has made cutting deforestation a cornerstone of his government. The latest Inpe data supports his claim of progress.

It shows a 36.87% drop from August 2025 to July 2026. That is the lowest level in the series since 2016.

Lula sent these figures to Trump. He directly challenges the US justification’s factual basis.

He called Trump ’my friend’ in his remarks. VEJA reported this.

This signals he wants open dialogue. Tensions are rising, but he keeps talking.

The deforestation argument matters to investors. It could decide if tariffs stay or go.

Brazil can prove its environmental record. That may weaken the case for duties.

But the US may have other motives. Data alone cannot address those economic reasons.

For Brazilian exporters, a 25% US tariff on most goods is a direct hit to margins—steel, aircraft. Processed foods, and manufactured goods face a surcharge that can price them out of a key market.

The Amazon-deforestation justification is contentious because Brasília can point to a 36.87% drop in clearances. The lowest since 2016, which undercuts Washington’s stated rationale and suggests protectionist motives.

Investors face uncertainty over trade flows and diplomatic friction, as seen in the ambassador’s visa row. Brasília could negotiate bilaterally, escalate at the WTO, or impose reciprocal tariffs—though Lula’s immediate move is data, not retaliation, keeping de-escalation alive.

Lula to Send Trump Amazon Data in Tariff Spat

The tariff package is part of larger US trade pressure. Washington has acted on other fronts too.

This week, the US revoked Brazil’s ambassador visa. G1 reports this responded to Brazil’s delay.

Brazil delayed approving Trump’s ambassador-designate, Daniel Perez.

This diplomatic friction adds another layer to the economic conflict, making it harder to separate trade from politics.

For Latin American markets, the Brazil-US dispute is a reminder of how tariff decisions in Washington can ripple across the region. Brazilian exporters face higher costs, which could slow growth in key sectors like manufacturing and agriculture.

Lula’s data strategy could help de-escalate. But it is untested.

If tariffs persist, Brazilian companies must adapt. Investors should watch for signs of retaliation.

Lula has not yet announced any.

The stakes are high. The US is a major market for Brazilian goods.

Any sustained tariff could reshape trade relations. This could last for years.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the current US tariff on Brazilian goods? The US imposed a 25% tariff on most Brazilian imports in July 2026, with exceptions for some products such as beef and coffee. The rate applies broadly, affecting a wide range of sectors. How is deforestation linked to the tariffs? Washington cited illegal deforestation in the Amazon as one reason for the tariffs. Lula is challenging this by sending Inpe data showing a 36.87% drop in deforestation from August 2025 to July 2026, the lowest since 2016. Why did the US revoke Brazil’s ambassador’s visa? The US revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador in Washington as a response to Brazil’s delay in approving Trump’s ambassador-designate to Brasília, Daniel Perez, according to G1. This has added to diplomatic tensions between the two countries. Is Lula planning to retaliate against the US tariffs? As of August 2026, Lula has not announced immediate retaliation. Instead, he is focusing on rebutting the US justification by sending deforestation data, though the dispute remains unresolved.

Sources: Presidência da República (Planalto); Reuters; G1.

World.title: Panama Canal Deepens Draft to 48 Feet, Boosting Cargo Limits
World.content:
Latin America · Trade

Key Facts Draft increase — maximum authorised draft rises to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters) from August 26, 2026.

— maximum authorised draft rises to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters) from August 26, 2026. Further rise — draft climbs to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) from September 3, 2026.

— draft climbs to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) from September 3, 2026. Lake recovery — Gatun Lake levels have recovered after severe drought, enabling deeper transits.

— Gatun Lake levels have recovered after severe drought, enabling deeper transits. No transit cut — ACP confirms daily transit numbers remain unchanged.

— ACP confirms daily transit numbers remain unchanged. Cargo boost — deeper draft allows Neopanamax ships to carry more containers or gas.

— deeper draft allows Neopanamax ships to carry more containers or gas. Regional impact — lower freight costs and improved reliability for Latin American exporters.

The Panama Canal Authority is raising the maximum draft for Neopanamax locks from August 26, easing drought-era restrictions and allowing ships to carry more cargo.

If you’re shipping goods through Latin America, the Panama Canal draft increase is about to let bigger ships through again. On August 26, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) will raise the maximum authorised draft for Neopanamax locks to 48.0 feet (14.63 meters).

Followed by a further rise to 48.5 feet (14.78 meters) on September 3.

Exporters and shippers get more cargo per vessel. Freight costs drop per container.

Drought-driven restrictions ease. This helps regional trade after months of pressure.

Draft means the water depth a ship needs. A deeper draft allows a heavier load.

Gatun Lake recovered after last year’s drought. The El Niño-driven drought forced the ACP to cut vessel numbers and draft limits.

Now the canal can return to near-normal operations. The ACP said the adjustment reflects current water levels.

It also reflects projected conditions. The ACP confirmed daily transits will not be reduced.

A ship transits the Panama Canal’s locks, where the maximum draft has been raised to 48 feet. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
