World.title: Teachers offered $2000 sign-on bonus as Labor fights to stop third strike
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsVictoriaEducation Teachers offered $2000 sign-on bonus as Labor fights to stop third strike Alex Crowe Updated August 10, 2026 — 1:39pm ,first published 12:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorian educators would get a $2000 bonus with the signing of a pay and conditions offer from the state government, as the new education minister attempts to avoid statewide school strikes planned for next Wednesday. Teacher, principal and education support staff salaries would still rise by at least 28.3 per cent over the next four years as per the previous offer, but those at the top of their salary bands would receive a 1 per cent annual lump-sum payment, plus the one-off payment at the start of the new agreement. Education Minister Gabrielle Williams and Premier Ben Carroll. Eddie Jim Australian Education Union Victorian president Justin Mullaly said the offer came a day after the premier committed the state government to signing a full funding agreement with the federal government before the November state election. “Victoria needs full funding for public schools and pay and conditions that reflect the value of the important work public school staff do for Victorian families and communities,” Mullaly said.





Lucy Honan, a spokesperson for the union’s left faction, said they will vote against recommending the deal to members and will call to push on with industrial action. Teachers, principals and support staff will stop work for 24-hours on August 19, the third strike this year, if it is rejected. The union had originally sought a 35 per cent pay increase over three years, which would mean graduate teachers would start on more than $107,400 by 2028 and experienced teachers would earn more than $159,300 by 2028. Members rejected an in-principle agreement endorsed by 120 of its elected council members in June, under which teachers’, assistant principals’ and principals’ salaries would have increased by between 28.3 per cent and 32.4 per cent over four years.



Under the in-principle schools agreement, a graduate teacher’s pay would have increased from the current $79,589 to more than $114,731 by 2029 and an experienced classroom teacher’s pay would have increased from the current $118,063 to $151,419 by 2029. Teachers would also have received a lump sum payment of 1 per cent of their salary each year. Thousands of Victorian teachers and support staff walked off the job in July as part of their campaign for better wages and conditions. Wayne Taylor Union leadership has signalled that signing a long-term agreement with the Commonwealth to fully fund public schools, as set out by the Gonski reforms, is crucial to pay negotiations. Victoria’s two-year federal funding agreement is set to expire at the end of 2026. It is the only state or territory not to reach an agreement with the Commonwealth, though both parties have signalled that a deal is imminent. Premier Ben Carroll said negotiations with the Commonwealth were ongoing and it remained a top priority.



Related Article Updated

Education Teachers prepare to strike again as pay negotiations falter “I said to the prime minister when I spoke to him during the week, education was one of my priorities,” he said. Carroll said he’d always wanted to work constructively with the union and his door was always open to its representatives. “I am urging them not to strike next week. Kids should be in the classroom learning,” he said. “It was a very close vote last time, and I’m sure we can get there.” The public school educators’ pay negotiations have broader implications for the sector and its about 40,000 Catholic school staff, who are currently negotiating their own enterprise agreement. Catholic teachers have had pay parity with Victorian public school teachers since the 1990s.

World.title: Want to travel with a tennis champion or famous author? Board a ship
World.content:
Last week anyone who happened to be sailing with Explora Journeys in the Mediterranean had a brief chance to encounter tennis superstar Jannik Sinner, on board Explora II sailing between Genoa and Marseille for an overnight stay to promote his wellness collaboration with the cruise line.

Sinner participated in a Q&A session and charity gala dinner, and made appearances at private coaching and wellness sessions available to a few select guests. No word on whether he’ll make further appearances but, as brand ambassador for the cruise line, I expect he will.

Jannik Sinner aboard Explora II.

Jannik Sinner is one of the biggest stars to recently grace a cruise ship, but in the past Katy Perry, Kelly Clarkson, Sheryl Crow and yes, even Taylor Swift have performed at sea. Themed cruises have seen the likes of Beach Boys, Kiss, The Walking Dead, New Kids on the Block, and the cast of Star Trek make appearances.

You’ll have to keep a lively lookout for the release of such cruises, which are booked out by fans before you can shout “anchors aweigh”. Many cruise lines, however, have special guests on board who, while they mightn’t have the same celebrity status, are equally experts in their field.

World.title: Council pushes Ohakune's water restoration another 24 hours
World.content:
The Ruapehu District Council is now saying another 24 hours will be needed before Ohakune's water network is safely back online.

The council had earlier been confident supply would be restored around 5pm on Monday.

But it says if the pipeline that carries water from its source to the treatment plant is repressurised too quickly, it could fracture, and cause even longer delays.

Earlier on Monday morning the district's mayor had said the problem was more serious than originally thought and could not confirm when the town will have water again.

But Ruapehu District Mayor Weston Kirton told Midday Report that although earlier today he had not been confident the water would be back on by 5pm, it had now been suggested that this was achievable with experts coming in from all around the country.

Ruapehu Mayor Weston Kirton discusses Ohakune water issues Midday Report Download MP3 4m

Water supplies to the central North Island town were turned off after last month's earthquake near Taumarunui likely damaged a major water pipeline.

The town's water reservoir is down to 12 percent.

RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Kirton had first Morning Report it had been more difficult to fix the piping than had been initially thought.

"We've found the leak, we've actually fixed the leak, we've then tried to flush the system out and it's not working that well... and so we're obviously working hard to overcome that problem."

On Monday afternoon the council's chief executive Clive Manley said service contractor Veolia was able to locate hidden valves and was installing new ones to help release trapped air from the system.

"Restoring the supply has been complicated by sections of the raw water pipeline being buried and located in heavy bush, making valves difficult to find.

"Veolia has developed a plan for recharging the water network that includes introducing water from the treatment plant end of the system."

One of many closure notices in Ohakune today. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Manley said this was expected to get water to properties faster and council was aiming to get water back by 5pm Monday but has now pushed it another 24 hours.

Additional staff and resources were brought in from Whanganui, Auckland and Central Hawke's Bay to help with the repairs, he said.

Residents were asked to keep all taps inside their properties turned off while network restorations where ongoing.

Manley said the water may have a "milky appearance" when it first returns, caused by air bubbles trapped in the water as the network is recharged, which are "harmless".

Evie Story says she's been bathing 18-month-old Thea by using bottled water during Ohakune's outage. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Mayor had been unsure when water would be back

Kirton had said there was about 5km of concrete piping that was about 70 years old and may have been affected by the earthquake.

But it was in difficult-to-access terrain which was hard to flush out, he said.

Angelina Reyes has filled up water bottles from the council-supplied tank in Ohakune. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

"As soon as we get on top of the airlocks then we'll be able to manufacture the water and then open the systems up for the town, but it's certainly concerning."

The water had previously been expected to be back on by Monday afternoon, but Kirton told Morning Report that was no longer the case, and he did not want to speculate on when it would be back on.

Weston Kirton says it will take longer than initially expected to get the town's regular water system fixed. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The water plant was brand new and the issue was actually getting the water to the plant, he said.

The emergency situation was worsening and they would be dealing with that this morning, Kirton said.

"It could well be that we have an emergency situation to actually get water from elsewhere, through tankers or the like."

It would take longer than expected to get the existing plant up and running, he said.

Colin Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

It may be necessary to put an emergency water system in place before Ohakune's regular system can be fixed, he said.

"So I can't speculate whether it's a state of emergency yet, but that's one of the considerations you know whether we call on the government for help to actually overcome the issue with our town."

There was an influx of people in Ohakune at this time of year and there were businesses that wanted to be open and operating, he said.

"So we've got to have a Plan B and we'll take whatever measure it takes to make sure we actually get water to the households."

Currently there are emergency porta-loos around the town and water tankers which could be used in emergency situations, he said. They were setting up a centre at the Ruapehu District Council where people could come and collect as much water as they liked.

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

World.title: 'Stop the rot': Protesters fear Auckland's Carrington Hospital facing 'demo by neglect'
World.content:
What happened to Auckland's former Carrington Hospital? Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The vast brick exterior of the former Carrington Hospital in the Auckland suburb of Mt Albert is an impressive sight - from a distance.

But up close, windows are smashed or boarded up, graffiti is strewn across the building's facade, and whole rows of roof tiles are missing.

Built in 1865, the Category 1 historic place opened as the Whau Lunatic Asylum, and was used for psychiatric and mental heathcare for more than 120 years, and then was part of tertiary institute, Unitec, until 2021.

For the past five years, it's sat empty, and deteriorating.

Tired of watching the heritage building's decline, a group has gathered in front of the building on Saturday mornings through the winter.

The building has been a target for theft and vandalism. RNZ / Erin Johnson

"We hold our little placards that say 'Stop the rot', and 'Fix the bloody roof' and 'Shame this' and 'Shame that'," said Chris Casey, a trustee of The Cachet Foundation, a charity which aims to support artists and protect heritage buildings.

"We protest weekly just to highlight the fact that we think it's shameful that government and the managers are not protecting the building."

Protest signs near the heritage building. RNZ / Erin Johnson

He told RNZ the group was prepared to fundraise to weatherproof the building, and in particular, to fix the roof where rows of tiles have been removed, exposing interior timber.

"If it's a case of money, well then speak to the community. We're good fundraisers, we know where we can get money from. I don't think it's a huge amount of money to weatherproof it," Casey said.

The former psychiatric hospital's main building is an impressive sight - from afar. RNZ / Erin Johnson

The Crown acquired the site in 2018, as part of a 40-hectare parcel that is part of Treaty of Waitangi redress, and where 4000 homes are planned to be built in coming decades.

As part of development preparations, Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga recommended four buildings across the wider site, including the former Carrington Hospital main building, be protected with heritage covenants.

Only one building, the Pumphouse, now has that. Another, Penman House, was demolished last year.

Once Unitec moved out of the building, the former Ministry for Housing and Urban Development (now part of the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Roads and Transport, MCERT) took over responsibility for its maintenance.

Chris Casey, trustee of The Cachet Foundation, says the community is willing to fund raise to replace tiles missing from the roof of the former Carrington Hospital main building. RNZ / Erin Johnson

An MCERT spokesperson said the ministry did reactive maintenance while it held the building, including boarding up broken windows, but it wasn't responsible for decisions about the building's future.

"We initially boarded up only broken windows, to avoid fully concealing a heritage building, but later boarded up all ground-level doors and windows, to improve security.

"We also employed CCTV and fulltime security guards 24/7, 365 days a year. Unfortunately, the building was a constant target for theft, vandalism, and other criminal activity, as vacant properties often are. The initiatives above did not prevent people from breaking into the building."

Graffiti is strewn across the building's facade. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

In October, responsibility transferred to Marutūāhu Rōpū, the iwi group that has development rights for the site - and their partner, Ockham Residential.

"As part of the transfer of the building to Marutūāhu Ockham No 6 Limited Partnership, the developer advised they could improve the boarding up of the building and we provided them funding for this," the ministry spokesperson said.

The hospital building's Category A heritage status in the Auckland Unitary Plan means it needs to comply with Auckland Council planning rules.

In recent months, Auckland Council has issued two bylaw notices, under the Property Maintenance and Nuisance Bylaw 2015, demanding the developers secure entry points.

Rows of tiles have been removed from the heritage building's roof. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Some of the removed tiles are stacked on the third storey roof. RNZ / Erin Johnson

They complied with the first notice in July, and must comply with the second by 10 August.

Council compliance manager Adrian Wilson said the developers had "gone to considerable lengths" to comply with the first notice.

"In response to recent break-ins, we have issued an additional bylaw notice to secure several additional windows, doors and a grate that we identified as allowing reasonably easy access into the building," Wilson said.

"Ultimately, if people are both reckless and determined enough to bring a large ladder to the site and access the building via holes in the roof, that is criminal behaviour and not something the council can reasonably require the property owners to prevent."

Meanwhile, Casey's group continues to protest.

"Our main thing at the moment is we're really wanting to stand up and protect Carrington heritage from degrading, and what would formerly be called demo by neglect."

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Also concerned about the building's deterioration is Allan Matson, president of the Civic Trust Auckland, which has focused on protecting heritage buildings for decades.

Matson said the community shouldn't bear the cost of fixing the roof, when the developers would profit from the associated housing project on adjacent sites.

"They've got a job to do to look after it in the meantime. Clearly the job's not being done and the asset is degrading, and they'll all just point the finger at the other party and say, 'oh no, it's not our responsibility'."

Marutūāhu director Paul Majurey has not responded to RNZ's questions about the building, and Ockham Residential chief executive William Deihl declined to comment.

Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga said it had encouraged proactive maintenance at the site, and more broadly, had advocated for measures to address demolition by neglect, as well as incentives for owners to conserve heritage places.

HNZTP director northern Bev Parslow said the organisation had raised the possibility of a heritage covenant for the building with the iwi developers "who expressed openness to the idea at that time".

"We would welcome further discussion with them about that possibility, however we have no ability to require this," Parslow said.

On Monday, Wilson said the council had conducted a compliance inspection, and confirmed the second Bylaw Notice had been complied with.

World.title: The impact of central Christchurch's surge in newbuild apartments
World.content:
By Bill Morris for Frank Film

"That's not what a thriving inner city looks like." Christchurch City Councillor Nathaniel Hertz Jardine is standing in the residential heart of a rebuilt Christchurch.

During the earthquake recovery phase, this, it was promised, would be a place for people - the "most liveable city in New Zealand." The problem is that most of the time it appears empty.

A wide swathe of the centre of Christchurch is now made up of rank upon rank of newbuild apartments. But most look shuttered and barely-used. Green areas designed for people to gather are empty. Streets are devoid of foot traffic. "It's just a sense of blankness," says Jardine. "There's no washing out. Where are the kids? Where are the families?"

Over this scene of unease looms the new One New Zealand stadium, projected to generate more than $50 million dollars annually for the local economy. For a few hours on game days, which come around once a week at best, the streets here are pumping. But when the crowd goes home, silence returns. And herein lies the problem.

Frank Films

Jardine says Christchurch's rebuild happened at the same time that Airbnb arrived in New Zealand, and the rising city was primed for a short-stay rental takeover. Many of the apartments in the new Christchurch, he says, have been built and marketed with this in mind. "The surge pricing on Airbnb and other websites," he explains, "is so extreme that as long as you hit those big nights-Robbie Williams, Six60 and the Crusaders-you can just leave it empty the rest of the time."

One statistic says it all- 484 new dwellings have been built in the inner city in the last year, but only 50 people have moved into the area. "Some of the ones that are being built now aren't even really studio apartments," says Jardine. "They just have a bed that falls down over the couch."

When Frank Film visits this desolate dormitory town, there are few people about, but producer Gerard Smyth manages to find a couple of permanent residents, who seem somewhat bemused by where they've found themselves living. "I wanted to live in a community, and a neighbourhood with permanent residents," says Bernard.

"You sort of give up talking to people," Dale says, "because you're going, "oh, this is a new neighbour, but it's not. It's someone who's here for 24 hours or 48 hours."

It's not necessarily the developers' Jardine says. "They're just doing what the market tells them." The blame, he says, lies with the Central Government, which has allowed this situation to unfold without giving City Councils the necessary tools to override the process.

Apartments in Central Christchurch. Frank Films

Jardine is asking for a bed register and a bed tax, so that property owners can be taxed correctly based on the usage of the dwelling, and for that money to be made available to support local infrastructure. The Council, he says, has been seeking this for a decade now.

He's also asking for more power in zoning, so that "as a Council, we can actually say, 'this area is for residents. We are not going to have any short stay accommodation in this area.'" This approach, he says, has been taken in other cities around the world, and "it brings vibrancy back to the inner city."

It's not too late to save Central Christchurch, Jardine says. "We can have this amazing, thriving inner city if we just change the incentives. There is still so much land in Christchurch where we can build medium-sized, two-three bedroom homes, where families can live."

He says existing apartments can be used to home single people and students.

World.title: Long Covid sufferers call on politicians to do more to help those with the disease
World.content:
People with Long Covid are calling on politicians to collect better data on the disease, and enable those with it to access disability support services.

Politicians from Labour, ACT, the Greens, New Zealand First and Opportunity attended an online panel on Monday morning, hosted by Long Covid Support Aotearoa.

Advocate Renee Dingwall, who also has Long Covid, said their members still reported seeing doctors who did not believe in or understand the condition, and struggling to get the support they needed.

According to the latest New Zealand Health Survey, 4.3 percent of adults reported living with Long Covid - roughly 185,000 people.

Larissa Hockey, chair of Long Covid Support Aotearoa, told the panel these weren't small numbers, "and behind every statistic is a person".

"Someone like me who still needs a rest after washing my hair, my children who missed years of education, and Renee who was a city councillor and is now housebound in a wheelchair," she said.

There were now treatments and medications available which could ease symptoms and prevent deterioration, she said. "So we need to ensure access to these options and bring new research developments into treatments."

What would each party do for those with Long Covid?

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong said its tax policy - a universal basic income for everyone, funded by a new land tax - would help to support those with Long Covid.

"If you find yourself with an unexpected illness or having to look after a loved one, those choices around our loved ones having to take time out to look after us and be paid for it, imagine if that was supported as well by a citizen's income, which makes it a lot less challenging," she said.

Andy Foster from New Zealand First said it was important to build understanding of Long Covid and related conditions among clinicians, and maintain funding for medicines.

"This government's increased the funding for Pharmac very, very significantly. That was something New Zealand First did, or championed. I know ACT is championing to take it further as well. We support that."

Todd Stephenson from ACT said it was important to make sure the taxpayer was getting good value for money.

"Plenty of money is being spent in health, but what we do not think is that we're necessarily getting value from that".

Dingwall asked him about plans to increase MSD doctor appointments for people on benefits.

"Having a chronic illness is a full-time job," she said. "You are often seen by a wide range of doctors and specialists. These appointments take months of trialling different remedies to relieve different symptoms. At the same time, you're navigating a stretched welfare system.

"You often have to wait on the phone for an hour just to make an appointment with MSD. These are precious hours that people living with chronic illness simply don't have. So why are you proposing to add mandatory extra appointments with MSD doctors and how are you proposing to resource that?"

Stephenson replied most people were receiving benefits appropriately, "but there are some who do not have a proper an independent review of their circumstances" and it was about making sure taxpayers' money was well spent.

But Labour's Ingrid Leary said she didn't accept the claim that people were exploiting the system.

"It's going to be much harder for disabled people to access the care they need," she said. "If you can imagine them trying to apply chronic illness where there is a paucity of good research and data and we've all recognised that, then I think that's going to be really, really problematic."

She urged people to look at the track records of different governments, rather than listen to their promises.

"In real terms, we have seen a between 6 and 14 percent loss to each region in real terms of health funding over the last term of government. So Labour would commit to putting the capital gains tax money into the health system."

Huhana Lyndon from the Green Party said patient voices should be central, and it was matter of creating better understanding and accountability across the system.

It was also important for families to access a fair income to support whānau, alongside the cost of treatment and medicines.

World.title: Delmore housing development with plan to truck wastewater away gets fast-track approval
World.content:
Fast-track approval has been granted for the development of more than 1200 homes in North Auckland, where treated wastewater will be trucked off-site when needed.

The 61-hectare Delmore development has been proposed for farmland in Ōrewa. As well as the residential development, it includes a commercial area, and an interchange with State Highway 1.

The proposed water and wastewater systems for the development have attracted criticism.

Both Auckland Council and Watercare opposed the development. Their submissions to the independent expert panel considering the fast-track application said that it was out of sequence with council growth and infrastructure plans.

Minister of Infrastructure Chris Bishop said the panel had granted approvals for the development, subject to comprehensive conditions.

Bishop said the panel had decided the consent conditions will appropriately manage the off-site effects of the proposed wastewater system.

"For the first stage of the development, wastewater will be treated and discharged on site, with treated wastewater transported off site during summer periods when necessary.

"Before the second stage of the development can proceed, the applicant will be required to obtain further approvals for a long-term wastewater solution, including on-site disposal, continued transport off site, or connection to the public network if capacity becomes available."

Developer Vineway Limited lodged its fast-track application in January.

Before getting into the body of its decision, the expert panel took "the opportunity to clarify" the proposal to tanker treated wastewater off-site.

"The implication taken is that this approval enables continual, regular tankering off-site, at volume and with minimal pre-treatment - and that Whangārei is to be the destination for those tankers.

"That is not what has been approved."

The panel said off-site tankering of wastewater had been approved under specific scenarios.

The first scenario is if connection is available to the public wastewater network for stage 1A of the development (up to 264 dwellings) by 31 December 2031, where "interim short term tankering off-site" makes sense, rather than constructing a private wastewater treatment plant.

The other scenario is in drier, summer months "during Stage 1 when low-flow conditions in the stream network make irrigation/infiltration discharge volumes inadvisable".

Consent conditions set a maximum on-site discharge of 101.5m3/day from December to February, with any remainder to be discharged off-site.

That is estimated to be five to seven tankers per day once Stage 1 is complete, and is unlikely to be needed until around 475 homes are built, the panel said.

Tankering "would likely occur under emergency" if there was a significant outage of the on-site wastewater treatment plant, "but that is not subject to the approval given", it said.

The panel said no authorisation has been given for wastewater options for Stage 2 of the development, "other than recognising that a second wastewater treatment plant module would be required in the absence of public connection".

World.title: Tree felling death of Southland man highlights DIY risks, coroner says
World.content:
A coroner is cautioning against a "do-it-yourself" attitude for risky work at home, following the death of a Southland man in a tree felling accident.

Edwin Coulter, 54, was struck by a branch at the Invercargill property where his mother-in-law lived in May 2021.

He had been climbing and topping pine trees at the back of the section using a pruning belt and chainsaw.

To make sure the trees fell into an empty paddock, Coulter had been cutting directional notches, then his wife pulled them with a rope attached to their four-wheel-drive.

Associate Coroner Dan Moore said the couple had been unable to find an arborist.

Coulter was struck while he was eight metres off the ground, working on the biggest tree on the property.

"Mrs Coulter started driving forward in the vehicle, but she could tell the top was not moving. She put the handbrake on and got out of the car to tell Mr Coulter this. As she did, the treetop fell sideways in the direction of where Mr Coulter was positioned, hitting him in the chest," he said.

The coroner found Coulter lacked enough tree felling experience for the job.

"Mr Coulter was carrying out what was clearly high-risk tree felling without having any form of training or formal experience in this area. This 'do-it-yourself' attitude is not uncommon in New Zealand; as a previous ad campaign has noted, it is practically part of the Kiwi DNA," he said.

"It is also an approach that works perfectly safely in many circumstances. However, it also needs to be tempered with recognising when it is appropriate to engage someone with expertise and training."

Moore said people should employ a qualified arborist for trees that were on a lean, work that involved climbing or trees or that required assisted felling techniques like pulling with a rope.

World.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
World.content:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

World.title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
World.content:
Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

World.title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
World.content:
Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

AAP

World.title: Walker announces retirement after one last shot at AFL premiership
World.content:
Adelaide Crows great Taylor Walker has announced the 2026 AFL season will be his last, saying he hopes to end his career as a premiership winner.

The Crows today announced the veteran of 316 games would bring an end to his playing career, where he has kicked a club-record 706 goals to date.

Affectionately known as Tex, the 36-year-old told media after the announcement that the decision to step away had been "probably the hardest one of my life".

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club that I retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership cup or a medallion around my neck," he said.

"I don't want to be that player that goes that extra year or probably outstays their welcome.

"The closer I've got to the end, it's probably become a little bit more evident that it might be this year, but I've sort of treated it like my last year for the past six years."

Walker was drafted by the Crows in 2007 and made his AFL debut during the 2009 season.

He captained the club from 2015-2019, where he was twice named the AFL Players Association Best Captain in 2016 and 2017. He also led the Crows to the 2017 grand final, the club's most recent appearance in the sport's biggest game.

Today Walker was asked about one of the low points in his career — when he was fined and suspended for using a racial slur in 2021.

The Crows great described the incident as the "one thing I wish never happened".

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and I, and I suppose the biggest thing I learnt was that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people, and I feel like I'm a better person for that mistake that I made," he said.

While Walker's sights remain firmly fixed on the remainder of the season, he said his hometown of Broken Hill had been very much in his thoughts as he looked both back and forward.

"I grew up barracking for the Adelaide footy club. It was my dream. I had Crows posters all through my room as a little kid," he said.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year."

The Crows currently sit fifth on the AFL ladder, level on points with fourth-placed Brisbane on percentage.

Adelaide travels to Perth for a Friday night blockbuster against ladder-leaders Fremantle, then hosts GWS in the final round of the home and away season at Adelaide Oval.

World.title: Aussie high jumper wins gold at under-20 world titles
World.content:
Australian high jumper Izobelle Louison-Roe has won gold at the World Athletics U20 Championships.

The 19-year-old came into the championships in Eugene, Oregon as the leading under-20 jumper this year, twice hitting a personal best of 1.95 metres.

She would not need a personal best to win gold on Sunday (local time), with a jump of 1.92m enough to be crowned champion, adding to the silver she won at Lima during the 2024 championships.

Hungary's Lilianna Bátori claimed silver and Spaniard Aitana Alonso won bronze, both jumping 1.90 metres.

"It was such an exciting competition, one of the moments of my life," Louison-Roe said.

"It was an incredible feeling when I won.

"I was crying so much I couldn't keep it together, it was amazing."

Louison-Roe was not the only Australian to medal on Sunday, with the 4x400m relay team securing a silver.

The Aussie quartet of Shari Hurdman, Xanthee Watts, Charlotte McAuliffe and Alice Hill ran a 3:31.39 to finish second behind the United States.

"Honestly, it's surreal to just go out there and get the job done," McAuliffe said post-race.

"I think we knew coming into this what we were all capable of, and we knew a medal was definitely possible.

" To go out and do the job is just amazing. "

Australia's men's 4x400m relay team — Seth Kennedy, Fred Hamblin, Dylan Hall and Chase Grant — came agonisingly close to also winning a medal, missing out on the podium by four-hundredths of a second.

Grant produced a brilliant final leg of 44.85 seconds, but was just pipped at the line by the French runner.

The women's 4x100m team — Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed — were also pipped at the line and placed fourth.

Kieran Shepherd ran a personal best of 3:42.25 to place eighth in the men's 1,500m, while Milla Roberts overcame a mid-race fall to be 14th in the women's 1,500m.

Elijah Wilson placed 13th in the men's discus final with a best throw of 56.47m.

World.title: AFLW double-header season opener left fans with 'lots of mixed feelings'
World.content:
As young Carlton star Poppy Scholz launched the ball into the stands at Docklands Stadium to kick the first goal of the 2026 AFLW season, fans were asking each other: "What do you think this crowd is?'"

The Blues were playing against St Kilda in the season opener in one of five double-headers between the men's and women's competitions this season.

Players, clubs and fans have been calling for regular double-headers to be introduced by the AFL to help grow the women's game.

This was in a bid to increase exposure of the women's game, try to adopt more fans across, give a unified club identity (one club, two teams approach) and allow the women to play on better conditions to allow for a better product.

St Kilda puts up a late challenge against Carlton but the Blues never give up their lead. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

By half-time on Sunday evening there were 11,000 people in the crowd, 2,000 more than the sold-out Australia vs Ireland game at North Sydney Oval a week earlier.

Halfway through the final quarter, that number had ballooned to 20,455.

For St Kilda veteran and former captain Hannah Priest, they gave "a nice unity for an all-club approach".

"I look at the idea of all of your teams playing on the same day and celebrating each other," she told ABC Sport, acknowledging that a lot of club staff worked across both the men's and women's programs.

"To open the season at [Docklands] is a testament to every single AFLW supporter who has advocated for this sort of growth, and everyone who's been on board since the start. It's a celebration for all of us."

Blues' 26-point win over Saints Carlton has held off a St Kilda fightback to claim the opening win of the new AFLW season by 26 points in an entertaining game that made a case for more double header fixtures.

Across the stadium and fan sections, fans enjoyed the pizzazz of the bigger stadium, crowd noise and being sheltered from the rain.

However, there were also some who missed the community element of the suburban grounds and felt like AFLW was the main event.

Carlton AFLW fan Asha Ziffer, who has a membership for the women's team but not the men's, said she probably wouldn't have gone to the double-header had it not been the opener.

"I've got a lot of mixed feelings about it, but I don't think that this showcases it as it should be," Ziffer told ABC Sport.

"I think that it is presenting it as second to the men's game, and certainly for a season opener, W should be the focus."

There were 20,455 in the last quarter of the AFLW opener between St Kilda and Carlton. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Ziffer said her 14-year-old daughter, Lily, said "it's like when you go to a concert and there's a support act that only half the people come to and then there's the main event".

"I think even if a 14-year-old can identify that, then it does say something more broadly to the community about where the women's game sits," Ziffer said, during the third quarter.

"Look, it's great and the game is going our way, which is great, even better. But it does feel, because it's such a big venue, I think 11,000 turnout is great but it just doesn't feel like a big crowd because the venue is so big. And you know, I'm sure it's a great ground for them to play on. And you know, it's nice to have a roof over our heads, given the weather's average."

Long time AFLW St Kilda fan Shae Williams said although her side didn't come away with the win, she hoped the team left the evening with a few more fans.

"It was exciting walking in and the thought of W starting … [although it] felt weird not being in a more intimate setting like Moorabbin.

"Twenty thousand attendance was a great result [and a] good experience for the players to play on a bigger stage," Williams told ABC Sport.

"The idea of double-headers are great, [although] I understand the need for W to have its own space as well."

Carlton won its opening match against St Kilda at Docklands. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

Another Saints supporter, Dylan Cross, who got into both the games with his men's and women's membership, was pleased with the early turnout for the women's game.

"I heard a few people comment around me that haven't watched much women's footy that it was better than they expected," Cross told ABC Sport.

"So, hopefully it [double-headers] grow the game.

"I will say personally I still prefer the AFLW games at smaller grounds like Ikon or Moorabbin due to the more local footy vibes and that it's so family friendly. The crowd felt a bit reserved tonight.

"But all in all, I think it was a success and hopefully we see more double-headers in the future."

World.title: Carlton fans chant 'we want Fraser', talks on coaching future imminent
World.content:
Carlton fans are chanting Josh Fraser's name and a similar endorsement from the club's hierarchy for the Blues' interim coach to take the reins full time could follow as soon as this week.

Fraser has mounted an irrepressible case to take on the vacant head coach role, having delivered 10 wins and just two losses since stepping up when Michael Voss was sacked in mid-May, with the Blues at 1-8.

The interim coach, who earned "we want Fraser" chants from Carlton fans after last night's 44-point win, is yet to officially throw his hat in the ring — but that conversation is imminent.

Loading...

"At some stage this week there'll be an opportunity to have some conversations with the club," Fraser said.

"It'll be sometime this week."

Half-back Adam Cerra joked whether the interim boss taking the reins was the hardest question at the club at the moment.

"Obviously the club's got their processes. We've got full faith in that process and their decision and we'll support whatever they pick. 'Frase' has been great," he said.

"The boys obviously love playing with him. We'll leave that to the club."

Cerra put Carlton's turnaround down to a combination of Fraser's influence and how the playing group lifted him — with experienced players leading from the front and young players expressing themselves.

"Frase has probably allowed a bit of freedom for us to do that, a bit of simplicity in the way we're trying to play," Cerra said.

"It hasn't set too many boundaries on us. It's more trying to explore what our best football looks like and building that week to week.

"These last couple of weeks we've been getting more confidence in our process and our trust and executing."

Fraser was asked whether part of his thinking in holding off on nominating was around managing if he missed out on the job while preparing the team for a potential wildcard match.

Blues plant one foot in the AFL finals as Saints lose star to hamstring Carlton plants one foot in the AFL finals series with a statement victory over the Saints at Docklands.

"It's a fair question, but no, I haven't thought too deeply about that," the 43-year-old said.

"I've just tried to stay as narrow as I can and it's been challenging with a lot of the questioning and different things, but I still feel such a responsibility to this role as interim coach.

"That's what I needed to, and have, focused all of my energy on — because I would be doing a disservice, not only to our players, but our staff and everyone, if I started to stray away from that.

"Clearly I've had to think through some things, but that hasn't occupied a lot of my thinking and all the hypotheticals haven't either. Most of my energy has been focused on this playing group and footy club."

The Blues sit eight points clear in 10th with games against the Western Bulldogs and Fremantle to come.

"[It's] not about daring to dream, I think the thing that's taking us forward is we are just attaching ourselves to the work that we need to do," Fraser said.

AAP

World.title: 'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open
World.content:
Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner has pulled out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

The 24-year-old, who claimed his fifth grand slam title at Wimbledon last month, had also pulled out of the Canadian Open, a key warm-up event for the US Open at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Sinner won the Cincinnati title in 2024 and finished runner-up to seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz there last year.​‌

"After consulting with my doctors and my team, I have to announce that I need to withdraw from the Masters 1000 tournament in Cincinnati," Sinner said in a statement.

"My right knee has been bothering me and even though we have been working hard with my medical team, I have to accept that I'm not ready to compete yet.

"I'm very disappointed not to be able to play in Cincinnati … I can't wait to be back next year and I'm now focusing on getting ready for the U.S. Open."

Sinner's withdrawal further depletes the field in Cincinnati, with US Open champion Alcaraz also sidelined by a wrist injury.

The Cincinnati Open main draw begins on August 13, while the US Open main draw gets underway on August 30.

Reuters

Tech.title: No Dogs in Space is a music history podcast for true obsessives
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Sadly, there hasn’t been a new episode of No Dogs in Space since July of 2024. Part four of the podcast’s series on Can wrapped up an abbreviated season three, which focused on experimental rock. Don’t get me wrong, I loved seasons one and two, but the show seemed to be gearing up for a deep dive into Krautrock, and I was hype. Unfortunately, that episode ended with hosts Marcus Parks (Last Podcast on the Left) and Carolina Hidalgo declaring they were going to do another season on punk (the topic of season one), only for the feed to go quiet.

If you’re a music obsessive, this is a must-listen podcast. Over the course of 73 episodes, the husband-and-wife duo digs into the careers of the Beastie Boys, The Velvet Underground, Joy Division, and more. Even if you think you know everything there is to know about iconic bands like The Stooges, I guarantee there will be new info here.

The show dedicates multiple hours over the course of several episodes to its subjects. Its two-part intro to Krautrock, which heavily focuses on Amon Düül II is over three hours long, and that’s on the shorter side. The Replacements series is nearly nine hours long, and Beastie Boys is even longer still.

Over these exceptionally long series, it never gets dull, though. The two balance scripted info-dense sections with more improvisational sidebars expertly. They also, as you’d expect from a married couple, have great chemistry on mic. They also make sure to share all their sources at the end of the episode in case you want to track down the primary source or do your own fact-checking.

The show isn’t officially over. As recently as a couple of months ago, Carolina was responding to Instagram comments saying she’d love to do more episodes. And the possibility of the show returning has come up multiple times on live streams. But as of this writing, we’re still waiting on that Punk Rock 2.0 series.

Tech.title: Zuckerberg’s yacht was closer, but someone else saved a stranded boat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this week, the Alaskan cruise ship Wilderness Legacy rescued a small skiff stranded near Farragut Bay after running out of fuel. But, according to tracking data reviewed by the Alaska Beacon and Halifax Shipping News, the closest vessel was actually Mark Zuckerberg’s super yacht, Launchpad.

Michael Love, a passenger on the Wilderness Legacy, posted on Bluesky that the captain announced the Launchpad was closer, but “repeatedly refused to respond,” which was met with booing from the passengers. The AIS tracking (embedded below) seems to support that the Launchpad was closer to the vessel in trouble, but then stopped near the entrance of the bay. The Wilderness Legacy can be seen passing Launchpad, then turning around and towing the stranded boat back to safety.

The US Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard told the Alaska Beacon that “at approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf.”

Brian Baker, spokesperson for Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, told The Verge that “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe.”

Tech.title: 49ers coach says his Tesla was on Autopilot when he crashed
Tech.content: “I’ve had Autopilot for nine years, so I’m pretty comfortable with it and, you know, who knows what happened when I turned around? Whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off? That’s something I don’t know yet. But regardless, that’s… it is always your fault, whether you’re on Autopilot or not. You can’t take your eyes off the road. It’s a partnership driving, you don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Tech.title: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
Tech.content:
In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year.

It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice.

I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep.

Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts.

My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance.

There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do.

I can’t recall a single time the service failed

I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there.

Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud.

And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected.

That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.

Tech.title: AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more news about how AI is changing our daily lives, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Long before ChatGPT became a thing, educators and editors frequently used anti-plagiarism tools to see if writers were being honest about their work. These tools work by comparing a written work against a database filled with content from across the web, scholarly articles, and more to check for matching sentences and phrases. Some, like Turnitin, offer a percentage that claims to illustrate how much of the student’s writing overlaps with other works. Between potential false positives and uncertainty about whether work was duplicated intentionally, some educators have backed away from using that particular tool.

But now, the hunt for copied content is evolving into a war on AI-generated work. As quickly as students have picked up ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, teachers have adopted so-called AI detectors just as fast. A survey from the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 43 percent of sixth to 12th grade teachers in the US regularly used AI detectors between 2024 and 2025. Some universities already using Turnitin in their learning management systems found that the service automatically enabled AI detection when the tool launched in 2023.

Instead of comparing pieces of written content, AI detectors like GPTZero, Pangram, and the one created by Turnitin rely on their own AI models to guess whether something might not be human-written — a process that’s arguably even murkier than matching text on the web. As noted by GPTZero, AI detectors use an algorithm to analyze a text’s wording, rhythm, and structure, as well as to pick up on patterns in length and tone that may be more common in AI-written text. This relatively subjective evaluation isn’t as solid as something you could back up by matching text online, and can get tripped up by writers who speak English as a second language. Despite this, Turnitin has said that its AI detector falsely flags less than 1 percent of human-written content as AI, while Pangram claims its false positive rate is just 1 in 10,000. GPTZero claims it has a similarly low rate of mistaking human content for AI.

How it’s going

People online are already accusing each other of “sounding like AI,” but the ready availability of AI detection tools is only adding fuel to the LLM witch hunt. In some high-profile cases, AI writing accusations have directly impacted people’s livelihoods and reputations. Last month, the publisher Minotaur dropped a $2 million book deal over concerns that its author, Jerry Falade, used AI — something he vehemently denies.

There’s Thierry Rignol, a French national who sued Yale last year after a professor accused him of writing portions of his final exam with AI, resulting in a failing grade and a one-year suspension. The professor used GPTZero to scan Rignol’s writing for signs of AI, but the lawsuit argues that “AI surveillance and detection tools are known to unfairly target non-native English speakers” like Rignol. In February, a student at Adelphi University won a lawsuit against the school after his professor similarly claimed he used AI to write an essay. Though the lawsuit doesn’t say which AI tool the professor used to examine the student’s essay, Adelphi University has a licensing agreement with Turnitin.

As pointed out by the University of California, Los Angeles, AI detection tools are trained to pick up on patterns that could indicate AI use, such as repetitive terms and phrases, text that sounds too formal or informal, and nonsensical phrasing. Some, like QuillBot, also measure the “unpredictability” of text, as “AI tends to make the most ‘obvious’ or most common language choices as compared with human-produced writing,” according to UCLA. They may also look for sentence structure that remains the same throughout as another sign of AI. But these measurements aren’t indicative of AI on their own, as some people may just have a writing style with these qualities.

Even though Turnitin touts low false positive rates, it maintains that its tool “may not always be accurate” and shouldn’t be used to take actions against a student. Grammarly warns that users “should never rely on the results of an AI detector alone,” while GPTZero says “no AI detector can ever truly be 100% perfect.” OpenAI even shut down its own AI writing detector in 2023 due to low accuracy.

But AI writing accusations are still being flung across the web. Last week, in a video broadcast to the more than 3.5 million followers across his social channels, Ozzy Osbourne’s son, Jack, accused journalist and Verge contributor Kat Tenbarge of using AI to write an article for Rolling Stone, while flaunting the results from an AI detector, Getsolved, as “proof” of his claim. Tenbarge has refuted the claim in a video and a post on her website, but Osbourne hasn’t retracted his accusation or deleted the video, leaving Tenbarge to deal with the trolls.

There are numerous examples of false accusations, from writers to students, with many accusers failing to acknowledge the disclaimers that come along with some of these AI detection tools.

What happens next

The uncertainty surrounding AI detectors is enough for some educational institutions to stop using them altogether. Yale University, Johns Hopkins University, Vanderbilt University, Georgetown University, and others have disabled or restricted the use of AI detection tools. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology also warns that “AI detectors don’t work.”

Instead of relying on tools to weed out AI, many schools are encouraging educators to rethink their lessons. The University of Chicago, for example, suggests telling students to slow down their reading, breaking up longer writing assignments, and requiring students to reflect on their work. Stanford University says professors can consider holding assessments in classrooms, while MIT advises professors to leave room for students to disclose whether they used AI for help on an assignment, without penalty.

With AI becoming more prevalent in and outside the classroom, efforts to suss out what’s written by a human or a machine are ramping up as well. Some online platforms are only exacerbating suspicions surrounding AI use. Substack has built Pangram into its app, allowing users to scan blogs for suspected AI-generated content, while LinkedIn added a “seems like AI slop” button on posts. The result is a new era of distrust, where readers constantly question whether what they’re reading is AI and real human writers try their best not to sound like it.
